course.title: System Design
course.description: Learn to design a system the way a working engineer does: state the requirements, estimate the load, and justify every component with a number, from caches and shards to retries and error budgets.
course.audience: A capable adult who can read code and has met databases and web requests. Assumes How Computers and Networks Work (latency, TCP, HTTP, DNS) and the SQL course for basic queries. Software Design and Architecture covers how code inside a service is structured and how styles such as microservices are chosen, and this course does not repeat it; the two meet at the lesson on availability and at the architecture-style trade-offs.

paragraphs: A service that handles a thousand requests a day and one that handles a thousand requests a second have the same purpose, but they cannot have the same design. The second has to decide where its data lives, which work is repeated for every request, and what happens when one of its machines stops, and each of those decisions is costly to reverse once other parts of the system rely on it. System design is the study of how a service too large for one machine is divided into parts, and of how each choice is judged against the number of users, the amount of data and the failures that the service must survive.

Most of those judgements come down to arithmetic. The number of requests per second shows whether one machine is enough, the share of lookups that a cache answers shows how much load still reaches the database, and the availabilities of two components show how often a service built from both will be down. A design checked in this way is an argument, with each part present because a figure called for it, and when the figure changes you can see which parts have to change with it.
outcomes: You'll be able to turn a vague request into measurable requirements and estimate load, storage and bandwidth.
You'll be able to use percentiles, Little's law and fan-out arithmetic.
You'll be able to size a fleet and predict how delay grows with utilisation.
You'll be able to compute the effect of a cache, an index and a shard key.
You'll be able to choose quorum sizes, explain what CAP says, and compute retry amplification, availability and error budgets.
You'll be able to carry a design from requirements to failure handling, justifying each part with a number.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on How Computers Solve Problems, How Computers and Networks Work, SQL: From Rows to Reports, Probability and Statistics.

modules.title: Method and numbers
modules.description: A repeatable way to approach a design, and the arithmetic of load, storage and delay that decides what is needed.

modules.title: Serving traffic and storing data
modules.description: Load balancing, caching, indexes, replication, partitioning and consistency, each with the numbers that justify it.

modules.title: Asynchrony, failure and operation
modules.description: Queues, retries and timeouts, redundancy, and the measurements that tell you whether a system is healthy.

modules.title: Worked designs
modules.description: Two complete designs and a review of a flawed one, using every earlier tool.

concepts.title: Functional requirement
concepts.summary: A behaviour the system must provide, such as 'a user can shorten a URL'.

concepts.title: Quality target
concepts.summary: A measurable property such as 'p99 latency under 200 ms' or '99.9% available', which usually decides the design.

concepts.title: Read/write ratio
concepts.summary: How many reads occur per write, which determines whether to optimise for reads, as caches do, or for writes.

concepts.title: Design method
concepts.summary: Clarify scope, estimate load, define the interface and data, sketch the components, then probe bottlenecks and failures.

concepts.title: Queries per second
concepts.summary: Total requests in a period divided by the seconds in it; a day has 86,400 seconds.

concepts.title: Peak factor
concepts.summary: Traffic is not flat, so peak load is commonly assumed to be two to three times the average.

concepts.title: Storage estimate
concepts.summary: Records per period times bytes per record times retention.

concepts.title: Bandwidth estimate
concepts.summary: Requests per second times bytes per response times 8 bits.

concepts.title: Percentile
concepts.summary: The value below which a given share of requests fall; p99 is the latency that 99% of requests beat.

concepts.title: Little's law
concepts.summary: The average number of requests in the system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends there.

concepts.title: Tail amplification
concepts.summary: A request that waits for n parallel calls is slow if any one is, so the chance of a slow response is 1 − (1 − p)^n.

concepts.title: Horizontal and vertical scaling
concepts.summary: Vertical scaling buys a bigger machine, horizontal scaling adds more machines behind a load balancer.

concepts.title: Stateless service
concepts.summary: A server that keeps nothing between requests, so any server can handle any request and a failed one can simply be replaced.

concepts.title: Utilisation and delay
concepts.summary: In a simple single-server queue the mean time in system is 1 / (service rate − arrival rate), which grows without bound as utilisation approaches 100%.

concepts.title: Load balancer
concepts.summary: A component that spreads requests across servers by round robin, least connections or hashing, and removes servers that fail health checks.

concepts.title: Hit rate
concepts.summary: The fraction of lookups answered from the cache.

concepts.title: Cache-aside
concepts.summary: The application checks the cache, on a miss reads the database, then stores the result in the cache.

concepts.title: Invalidation
concepts.summary: Entries expire after a time to live or are removed when the data changes, and the choice trades freshness against load.

concepts.title: Stampede
concepts.summary: Many requests miss on the same expired key at once and all hit the database.

concepts.title: Access pattern
concepts.summary: How data is read and written: by key, by range, by join or by traversal, which decides the store.

concepts.title: Index
concepts.summary: A sorted structure such as a B-tree that finds rows without scanning the table, at the cost of space and slower writes.

concepts.title: B-tree depth
concepts.summary: With a fan-out of f, a tree of n keys needs about log base f of n levels, so 1,000,000 keys at a fan-out of 100 need 3.

concepts.title: N+1 queries
concepts.summary: Fetching a list and then querying once per item costs 1 + N queries instead of one or two.

concepts.title: Replication
concepts.summary: Keeping copies of the data on several machines for availability and read capacity.

concepts.title: Replication lag
concepts.summary: Followers apply changes after the leader, so a read from a follower may return older data.

concepts.title: Sharding
concepts.summary: Splitting data across machines by a key so that each holds a part.

concepts.title: Consistent hashing
concepts.summary: Placing keys and nodes on a ring so adding a node moves only about 1/N of the keys.

concepts.title: CAP
concepts.summary: When a network partition separates replicas, a system must choose between answering every request, with possibly stale data, and refusing some to stay consistent.

concepts.title: Quorum
concepts.summary: With N replicas, W acknowledgements for a write and R replicas read, R + W > N guarantees that a read overlaps the latest write.

concepts.title: Consensus
concepts.summary: Agreement among nodes on a value despite failures, which requires a majority: 3 of 5 tolerates 2 failures.

concepts.title: Queue
concepts.summary: A buffer between a producer and consumers that lets the producer continue and the consumers work at their own rate.

concepts.title: Delivery semantics
concepts.summary: At-most-once may lose messages, at-least-once may repeat them, and effectively-once needs an idempotent consumer.

concepts.title: Backpressure
concepts.summary: When consumers fall behind, the system must slow producers or shed work, because an unbounded queue only postpones failure.

concepts.title: Event stream
concepts.summary: An ordered, retained log of events that many consumers read at their own positions, with order guaranteed within a partition.

concepts.title: Timeout
concepts.summary: A limit on how long to wait, without which a slow dependency ties up resources until the caller fails too.

concepts.title: Retry amplification
concepts.summary: If each layer in a chain of k layers makes up to a attempts, the last service may see a^k calls.

concepts.title: Backoff with jitter
concepts.summary: Waiting longer after each failure, with a random offset, so that clients do not retry in step.

concepts.title: Circuit breaker
concepts.summary: After repeated failures it stops calling a dependency (open), then lets a trial request through (half-open) before resuming (closed).

concepts.title: Availability
concepts.summary: The fraction of time a service works; 99.9% allows 43.2 minutes of downtime in 30 days.

concepts.title: Series and parallel
concepts.summary: Components that all must work multiply their availabilities; independent replicas fail together only if all fail, so two 99% replicas give 1 − 0.01^2 = 99.99%.

concepts.title: Failure domain
concepts.summary: The set of things that fail together, such as a machine, rack or region, which limits how independent replicas really are.

concepts.title: RPO and RTO
concepts.summary: The recovery point objective is how much data may be lost, and the recovery time objective is how long the outage may last.

concepts.title: Logs, metrics and traces
concepts.summary: Logs record events, metrics record numbers over time, and traces follow one request across services.

concepts.title: Four golden signals
concepts.summary: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation.

concepts.title: SLI, SLO and error budget
concepts.summary: An SLI is a measurement, an SLO a target for it, and the error budget the amount of failure the target allows.

concepts.title: Burn rate
concepts.summary: How fast the budget is being spent compared with spending it evenly over the window.

concepts.title: Identifier space
concepts.summary: With 62 characters and length k there are 62^k identifiers, and 62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208.

concepts.title: Redirect status
concepts.summary: 301 may be cached by browsers and so hides repeat visits; 302 is not cached and lets the service count them.

concepts.title: A worked design
concepts.summary: Each decision traces back to a requirement or an estimate.

concepts.title: Fan-out on write
concepts.summary: When a user posts, copy the post into each follower's feed, making reads cheap and writes costly.

concepts.title: Fan-out on read
concepts.summary: Build the feed at request time from the posts of everyone followed, making writes cheap and reads costly.

concepts.title: Hybrid
concepts.summary: Fan out on write for ordinary accounts and on read for accounts with huge followings.

concepts.title: Design review
concepts.summary: Walk a design with failure questions: what is the single point of failure, what is unbounded, what is unmeasured?

lessons.title: Requirements and scope

lead.text: Return to the one-sentence request, a service that shortens links, and ask what a team would have to agree on before building anything. Some of the answers describe behaviour: a user gives the service a long URL and receives a short one, and anyone who opens the short one is sent to the long one. Statements of this kind are called **functional requirements**, because they say what the system *does*.

Other answers describe quality: how quickly the redirect arrives, how often the service can be reached, and whether a link survives the failure of a disk. These are **quality targets**, and they say how *well* the behaviour must be delivered.

afterFigure.text: The sorting matters because the two kinds shape a design in different ways. The behaviours are few and easy to satisfy on a single machine, and the quality targets are where the effort goes, because a requirement such as *never lost* forces the system to keep several copies of every link.

diagram.caption: Four statements about the shortener. Use the buttons to see them sorted into what the service does and how well it must do it.

reveal.text: It names something the service does and gives no figure, which is the mark of a functional requirement. The quality targets for the same behaviour, such as how fast it must happen, are separate statements.

lead.text: "Fast" and "scalable" read like requirements, but no measurement could ever show that they had been met. Compare "redirects should be fast" with "99% of redirects complete in under 100 ms, measured at the server". The second names a quantity (time), a threshold (100 ms), a share of requests (99%) and so a test: collect a day of redirect times, sort them, and check whether the slowest 1% begin above the line.

Four properties turn up in nearly every design, and each takes its own kind of number. **Latency** is how long a request takes, stated for a share of requests. **Availability** is the fraction of time, or of requests, that succeed, such as 99.9%. **Durability** is whether data that was accepted can still be read later, which is where "a created link is never lost" belongs. **Consistency** is whether a reader sees the most recent write, and it can differ between two systems of the same size: a chat message should reach everyone almost at once, whereas a short link that appears a second late to one reader does little harm.

afterFigure.text: Numbers of this kind are what make a design arguable. If the target is 100 ms for 99% of requests, a design that sometimes waits on a distant disk can be rejected by arithmetic; if the target is only "fast", nothing can be rejected, because nothing was promised.

reveal.text: The key phrase is *shows the new name*, which concerns which version a reader sees. Durability would have been the answer had the statement said that the name is still there after a disk fails.

The reads outnumber the writes a hundred to one, and the two rates multiply, because every creation brings its own 100 opens: 10 creations a second mean about 1,000 redirects a second. The next screen gives this multiplier a name and shows what it implies for the design.

lead.text: The choice you just made rests on one number, the **read/write ratio**, which counts the reads for every write. A ratio of 100 to 1 means that each time a link is created it is opened 100 times, so 10 writes per second imply 100 × 10 = 1,000 reads per second. The ratio fixes one rate from the other: you usually know one rate from the product's numbers, and the ratio supplies the second.

afterFigure.text: The ratio points to where the effort should go. When reads dominate, the same answers are requested again and again, so keeping copies of answers close to the reader pays off. When writes dominate, the cost of storing every item safely and in order is what limits the system.

steps.headline: A service has 5 writes per second and a ratio of 200 reads to 1 write. Find the read rate and the share of requests that are writes.

workedSteps.text: The ratio of 200 to 1 means 200 reads for each write.
Use the ratio to turn the write rate into the read rate.
Add the two rates to get the total that arrives at the service.
Divide the writes by the total to see how small a share they are.

steps.headline: Now find the read rate for 12 writes per second at a ratio of 150 reads to 1 write.

workedSteps.text: The [[read/write ratio|How many reads arrive for each write. Met earlier in this lesson.]] is 150 to 1, so there are 150 reads for each write.
Use the ratio to turn the 12 writes per second into a read rate.

lead.text: Every design in this course follows the same order, and it is worth stating once. First you **clarify the scope**: the behaviours, the quality targets and what is deliberately left out. Second you **estimate the load**, in requests per second, storage and bandwidth, which the next lesson teaches. Third you **define the interface**, the calls that clients make, and fourth the **data**, what is stored and how it is found. Only fifth do you **sketch the components**, and sixth you **probe** the sketch for its bottleneck at the busiest point and for what happens when a part fails.

afterFigure.text: The order is not arbitrary: the load cannot be estimated until the scope says what counts as a request, and a component cannot be chosen until the load says how much work it has to do.

reveal.text: Components are justified by numbers, so a design drawn before any estimate has nothing to be checked against. Asking for the ratio and the rate is the quickest way to restart such a review.

lead.text: After the behaviours and the targets, a design states its **assumptions**, the facts it takes as given because nobody has measured them yet, such as "each link is opened 100 times", and its **non-goals**, the things it deliberately will not do, such as "links cannot be edited after they are created" or "no record of who clicked". Assumptions are numbers that can be revised later, whereas non-goals are boundaries that save work.

afterFigure.text: When the estimate turns out to be wrong, the assumption names exactly which figure to revise, and when someone asks for a feature, the non-goal shows that leaving it out was a decision and not an oversight.

reveal.text: Dividing by the ratio recovers the write rate, 3,000 ÷ 150 = 20, which is under the 25 the leader is sized for. Product numbers often give the larger rate, such as page views, so this direction is as common as multiplying.

lessons.orientation: Sort statements into behaviours and quality targets, and derive read and write rates from a ratio.
lessons.nextAction: Estimate requests per second, storage and bandwidth from user numbers.

blocks.text: The request is one sentence long: build a service that shortens links. Nothing in it says how many links there will be, how fast a short link must open, or whether a link may ever be lost, and each of those answers leads to a different system.
Design begins by turning such a sentence into statements that can be checked, which means separating what the system does from how well it does it and putting a number on the second.

intro.promise: By the end you'll sort requirements into behaviours and measurable targets, and derive a service's read and write rates from its ratio.
intro.whyItMatters: Requirements decide which components a design needs, so a mistake made here is the most expensive to repair.

recap.keyIdea: A design starts from measurable requirements and a read/write ratio, not from a list of technologies.

blocks.text: A request such as "shorten links" becomes a design problem once it is split into functional requirements, which say what the system does, and quality targets, which carry a number such as 99% of redirects in under 100 ms. The read/write ratio then turns one known rate into the other, so that 10 writes per second at 100 to 1 means 1,000 reads per second, and the order of scope, load, interface, data, components and probing follows from those numbers.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns user numbers into requests per second, storage and bandwidth, which is the estimate that the second step of the method calls for.

lessons.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimation

lead.text: Take a service with 10 million users a day, each making 20 requests. Multiplying gives 200,000,000 requests in a day, a figure too large to compare with anything, so the next step is to turn it into a **rate**, by dividing by the number of seconds over which the requests arrive. A day has 24 × 60 × 60 = 86,400 seconds, and the quotient, about 2,315, is the average number of requests per second, usually written **QPS**, for queries per second.

Nothing in this calculation needs to be exact, and that is the second idea. A day is close to 100,000 seconds, and dividing by 100,000 instead gives 2,000, which differs from 2,315 by about 14% and shares its order of magnitude. Since every input to an estimate is itself a guess, a result is judged by its **order of magnitude**, the power of ten it lands near, and round numbers are chosen on purpose because they keep the arithmetic doable in your head.

afterFigure.text: The test of a good estimate is whether a different answer would change the design. A system for 2,000 requests per second and one for 2,300 are the same system, while one for 230,000 is a different one, so an error of 15% is harmless and an error of a factor of ten is not. This is why you should be more careful about the unit of a number than about its last digits.

diagram.alt: A chain of arithmetic: 10,000,000 daily users times 20 requests each gives 200,000,000 requests a day, which divided by 86,400 seconds gives about 2,300 requests per second. A third view rounds the day to 100,000 seconds and gets 2,000.
diagram.caption: The estimate as a chain of operations. Use the buttons to see the division by seconds, and then what rounding the day to 100,000 seconds does to the result.

reveal.text: The daily total is 4,000,000 × 30 = 120,000,000, and dividing by the 86,400 seconds in a day gives about 1,390 per second. Had you divided by 100,000 instead you would have reached 1,200, the same order of magnitude but about 14% low.

lead.text: People use a service when they are awake and near a screen, so the busiest hour carries far more traffic than the quietest, and a fleet that handles the average load exactly will be overloaded for part of every day. Designers therefore multiply the average by a **peak factor**, commonly assumed to be between two and three, and size the system for the result.
For the service above, the average of about 2,300 requests per second becomes 2,300 × 3 = 6,900 at the upper end of that assumption.

afterFigure.text: The average still has a use, since it determines the daily totals for storage and cost. It is the peak, though, that determines how many machines must be running at the busiest moment, which is the number a design has to meet.

reveal.text: The fleet was planned for the average, so it is overloaded whenever traffic runs above it. With a peak factor of 3 the target would have been 4,200 requests per second, and a factor of 2 would give 2,800, a range that is still the same order of magnitude.
The two numbers multiply to 50 billion bytes, and the unit conversion is the only delicate part. The next screen puts the units on a scale so that you can check an answer by its size.

lead.text: A storage estimate multiplies three quantities: how many records arrive in a period, how many bytes each record takes, and for how long they are kept, which is the **retention**. For 100 million records a month at 500 bytes each, a month adds 100,000,000 × 500 = 50 billion bytes, or 50 GB, and keeping them for a year gives 12 × 50 GB = 600 GB.
The units step by factors of 1,000: a kilobyte is a thousand bytes, a megabyte a thousand kilobytes, a gigabyte a thousand megabytes, and so on to terabytes and petabytes.

afterFigure.text: The scale of units gives a quick check on an answer: if a month of 500-byte records came out in megabytes or in petabytes, the slip would be visible at once.

steps.headline: Find the storage for one year of 40 million records a month at 2,000 bytes each.

workedSteps.text: Start with the records added in one month.
Multiply by the size of one record to get the bytes added in a month.
Divide by a billion bytes per gigabyte to convert the unit.
The data is kept for 12 months, and each month adds the same amount.

steps.headline: Find the storage for 5 years of 2 million records a day at 1,000 bytes each.

workedSteps.text: A day adds 2,000,000 records of 1,000 bytes, so the bytes added in a day follow by multiplying.
The retention is five years of 365 days.
The total held is the daily amount for every day that the data is kept.

lead.text: Bandwidth is the amount of data that must flow each second. Suppose a service answers 2,000 requests per second and each response is 100 KB, which is 100,000 bytes. The data flowing out is 2,000 × 100,000 = 200,000,000 bytes per second, or 200 MB per second, and that is where most people stop, one step short of the number that can be compared with a network link.
Network capacity is quoted in *bits* per second, while sizes are counted in *bytes*, and a byte is 8 bits. Multiplying by 8 gives 1,600,000,000 bits per second, or **1.6 Gbit/s**.

afterFigure.text: The factor of 8 is the most common slip in this kind of estimate, and it is easy to catch by writing the unit at every step.

diagram.alt: The bandwidth estimate as a chain of arithmetic ending in 1.6 gigabits per second, and a drawing to scale showing that figure as a bar longer than a 1 gigabit per second link.

reveal.text: Dividing by 8 gives 1,250 MB/s, so the 200 MB/s of the previous example would fit easily on this link, although it would not fit on a 1 Gbit/s link, which carries only 125 MB/s.

lead.text: An estimate becomes a decision once it is set against what a machine can do. Suppose, as an assumption you would later check, that one machine has a 1 Gbit/s link, 10 TB of disk and enough processing for 5,000 requests per second. The example service then needs 2,000 requests per second, which fits, 600 GB of storage for a year, which fits, and 1.6 Gbit/s of bandwidth, which does not, so the network is the first resource to run out.
That answer is more useful than a count of machines, because it says what to change. The resource that runs out first is the one the design has to be built around, and it is often not the processor.

afterFigure.text: The assumptions about the machine are part of the estimate and are stated with it, in the same way that the peak factor is.

reveal.text: At 180 MB/s the network is overloaded by about 44% while the processor has headroom, so a faster processor would not help and more links or smaller responses would.

lessons.orientation: Estimate requests per second, storage and bandwidth from user numbers, and compare them with one machine.
lessons.nextAction: Measure delay in percentiles, relate it to load with Little's law, and see why the slowest requests matter.

blocks.text: Ten million people use a service each day and make 20 requests apiece, which comes to 200 million requests, a number too large to feel. Divide it by the 86,400 seconds in a day and it becomes about 2,300 requests per second.
Estimates of this kind need only multiplication and a handful of round constants, and what they have to get right is the power of ten.

intro.promise: By the end you'll estimate requests per second, storage and bandwidth from user numbers, and say which resource a single machine would exhaust first.
intro.whyItMatters: An estimate in minutes can rule out a design that would take weeks to build, so it is the cheapest check there is.

recap.keyIdea: An estimate multiplies a few stated inputs, is judged by its order of magnitude, and is compared with one machine to find the first resource that runs out.

blocks.text: Requests per second come from daily totals divided by 86,400, and the design is sized for the peak, which is commonly two to three times the average. Storage multiplies records, bytes per record and retention, and bandwidth multiplies responses per second by bytes and then by 8, because links are rated in bits. Setting each result against the limits of one machine shows which resource gives out first, and so what the design must change.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the time each request takes, and at why the slowest requests, not the average ones, decide how a system feels.

lessons.title: Latency, throughput and tails

reveal.text: The mean is 29.8 ms. It is a legitimate number, and the next screen shows what it does and does not tell you about this sample.

lead.text: In that sample the mean of 29.8 ms is about three times what 98 of the requests took, yet 33 times smaller than what the other two took, so it describes none of them. A **percentile** avoids the problem by sorting the requests from fastest to slowest and reading off the value at a chosen position. The **p50**, or median, is the latency that half the requests beat, and here it is 10 ms. The **p99** is the latency that 99% of requests beat.

To find it by the *nearest-rank* method, multiply the share by the number of requests and round up, so that 0.99 × 100 = 99 and the p99 is the 99th value in the sorted list. Positions 99 and 100 are both slow requests, so the p99 is 1,000 ms.

afterFigure.text: The figure marks all three numbers on the same 100 requests. The mean lies beside the fast cluster and corresponds to no request that a user experienced, while the p99 points at the slow ones, which is why a latency target is stated as a percentile, as in "p99 under 200 ms". The tail also matters more than its share suggests, because a user who makes many requests will meet the slow ones: a page that needs 100 calls will include at least one of the slowest 1% far more often than once in a hundred pages.

diagram.alt: A histogram of 100 request times on a millisecond axis from 0 to 1,000. A tall bar of 98 requests sits at 10 ms and a very short bar of 2 requests at 1,000 ms. Views mark the mean at 29.8 ms, the p50 at 10 ms and the p99 at 1,000 ms.

reveal.text: The mean is 0.98 × 20 + 0.02 × 900 = 37.6 ms, a figure that matches no group of requests at all, whereas the p99 is 900 ms. Only the percentiles tell you how many users saw each speed.

lead.text: Latency says how long one request takes, and **throughput** says how many requests finish each second. One more quantity links them: the number of requests that are inside the service at once. If 200 requests arrive each second and each stays for 50 ms, then at any moment the requests of the last 50 ms are still inside, and that is 200 × 0.05 = 10 of them.
This is **Little's law**, which says that the average number in the system, L, equals the arrival rate, written λ, times the average time W that each request spends there: L = λW.

afterFigure.text: If a dependency becomes slow and each request stays twice as long, the same arrival rate puts twice as many requests inside, each holding a connection, a thread and some memory, and those resources run out long before the arrival rate has changed.

reveal.text: The count is 400 × 0.25 = 100, more than the 80 threads. Keeping the units consistent is most of the work: a rate per second needs a time in seconds.
The answer is far larger than 1%, because a request that waits for many parts is only as fast as the slowest of them.

lead.text: Each backend is fast with probability 0.99, and the request is fast only if all 100 are, so for independent backends the probabilities multiply: 0.99^100 ≈ 0.366. The request is slow for the remaining 1 − 0.366 = 0.634 of the time, so **63.4%** of requests are slow although each backend is slow only 1% of the time. The effect is called **tail amplification**: the tail of the whole is much worse than the tail of any one part.

In general, a request that waits for n backends, each slow with probability p, is slow with probability 1 − (1 − p)^n. Dean and Barroso gave this case, with 100 servers and 63%, in *The Tail at Scale* (2013).

afterFigure.text: A single slow call among the hundred is enough to make the whole request slow, and the 100 calls are all fast only about 37% of the time. This is why a p99 that looks acceptable for one service can ruin the page that depends on a hundred of them.

steps.headline: Find how often a request is slow when it waits for 5 backends, each slow 1% of the time.

workedSteps.text: Each backend is fast with probability 0.99, and the request is fast only if all 5 are.
The request is slow when at least one backend is slow, which is the opposite event.
Written as a percentage, a fivefold fan-out makes slow requests about five times as common as a single backend does.

steps.headline: Find how often a request is slow when it waits for 20 backends, each slow 1% of the time.

workedSteps.text: Each backend is fast with probability 0.99, and the request is fast only if all 20 are.
The request is slow when at least one backend is slow, which is the opposite event.

lead.text: In 1 − (1 − p)^n there are two numbers to reduce. Lowering n means asking fewer backends, and lowering p means making each backend's slow responses rarer.

In a **hedged request** the caller sends the same request to a second replica, another server holding the same data, if the first has not answered within a short delay, and uses whichever answer arrives first. A **timeout** sets a limit on how long the caller waits at all.

afterFigure.text: Each remedy has a price: fewer calls may mean a less complete answer, hedging adds load at exactly the moment a backend is struggling, and a timeout turns a slow answer into a missing one.

reveal.text: The count follows both quantities, so it grows with the load even when the speed of each request is unchanged.

Fewer backends and rarer slow calls both pull the result down, but a tenfold change in p is worth more than cutting n to a third. The price of fewer calls is a less complete answer, and the price of rarer slowness is engineering effort at every backend.

lessons.orientation: Compare a mean with percentiles, apply Little's law, and compute how fan-out amplifies a rare slow call.
lessons.nextAction: Add machines to carry a load, spread requests across them with a load balancer, and see why delay grows steeply near full utilisation.

blocks.text: Of 100 requests to a service, 98 finish in 10 ms and two take a full second. The usual way to summarise such a sample is its mean, but a mean describes no request that actually happened, and here it would hide the two that a user would remember.
A fair summary of delay has to say what the slowest requests do.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read percentiles from a sorted sample, apply Little's law, and compute how fan-out turns a rare slow call into a common one.
intro.whyItMatters: Latency targets are stated in percentiles, and the fan-out sum explains why large systems feel slower than their parts.

recap.keyIdea: Percentiles describe the tail that a mean hides, and a request that waits for many calls is slow whenever any one of them is.

blocks.text: The mean of a sample can sit beside the fast requests and describe none of them, so latency is reported as percentiles such as the p99. Little's law, L = λW, links the number of requests in flight to the arrival rate and the time each one stays, and the formula 1 − (1 − p)^n shows that a request waiting for n backends is slow far more often than any one of them. Fewer calls, rarer slowness and hedged requests each reduce that chance.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson adds machines to carry a load, and shows why delay grows steeply as they approach full use.

lessons.title: Scaling and load balancing

lead.text: There are two ways to carry more load. *Vertical* scaling replaces a machine with a bigger one, which is simple but has a ceiling and leaves one machine to fail. **Horizontal scaling** adds more machines of the same kind behind a **load balancer**, a component that receives every request and hands it to one of them, so that capacity grows by about the capacity of each added server, and when one breaks the others carry on.

The balancer has to choose, and three rules are common. *Round robin* sends requests to the servers in turn, *least connections* sends each one to the server with the fewest requests in progress, and *hashing* sends requests with the same key, such as a user id, to the same server each time. The balancer also runs **health checks**, small requests sent to every server at intervals, and stops sending traffic to any server that fails them.

afterFigure.text: Balancers work at two layers. A layer 4 balancer decides from the connection alone, so it is fast and knows nothing about the request, whereas a layer 7 balancer reads the HTTP request and can route by path or header.

diagram.alt: A load balancer receiving 900 requests per second and sending them round robin to three servers. In the first view each server gets 300 per second. In the second, server 3 fails its health check, and the other two get 450 per second each.

reveal.text: The six servers ran at 80%, and the five that remain run at 96%. A failure at peak pushes the survivors close to saturation, which is the reason a fleet is sized with spare capacity.
The delay was 100 ms, five times the delay at 50 requests per second, although the load rose by less than a factor of two. The next screen gives the formula and the reason.

lead.text: Adding servers does not make each one faster, so the next question is how busy each may safely be. The **utilisation** of a server is its arrival rate divided by the rate at which it can serve, and in a simple model with one queue and random arrivals the mean time that a request spends in the system, waiting and being served, is 1 ÷ (service rate − arrival rate). A server that handles 100 requests per second serves one in 10 ms, and at 50 arrivals per second the formula gives 1 ÷ 50 = 20 ms; at 90 per second it gives 1 ÷ 10 = 100 ms, and at 95 per second 1 ÷ 5 = 200 ms.

The delay does not rise in proportion to the load. As the arrival rate approaches the service rate the denominator tends to zero, and the delay grows without limit. At 90% utilisation the delay is already ten times the 10 ms service time, so a server at 90% is not efficient but fragile, and Little's law shows why it is also crowded: 90 per second times 0.1 s leaves 9 requests inside at any moment.

afterFigure.text: The model is simple, and the numbers it gives are not exact for any real server, but the shape is general. A burst that arrives while the server is busy has nowhere to go but to wait behind the others, and the nearer the server is to full use, the less chance it has to catch up. Designers therefore set a **target utilisation** at peak, commonly well below 100%, such as 70%, where the model gives 33 ms, and treat the unused 30% as the price of low delay.

diagram.alt: A curve of mean time in the system against utilisation for a server that handles 100 requests per second. It is flat at low utilisation and rises steeply: 20 ms at 50%, 100 ms at 90%, 200 ms at 95%. A second view shades the region below a planning target of 70%, where the delay is 33 ms.

lead.text: Sizing combines the three ideas so far. Take the peak load from the estimate, which is the average times the peak factor, and take what one server handles at saturation. A server that handles 500 requests per second should be planned to carry only 70% of that at peak, which is 500 × 0.7 = 350 requests per second. If the peak is 4,500 requests per second, the fleet needs 4,500 ÷ 350 ≈ 12.9 servers, and because servers come whole the result is rounded *up* to 13.

The rounding goes up for a reason. With 12 servers each one would carry 4,500 ÷ 12 = 375 requests per second, which is 75% of its capacity, five points over the plan, and on the steep part of the curve being over is not free.

afterFigure.text: The target of 70% is a decision that belongs in the design's assumptions, in the same way as the peak factor.

steps.headline: Size a fleet for a peak of 6,000 requests per second, where each server handles 500 per second and the target utilisation is 70%.

workedSteps.text: Start from what one server can saturate at, and the share of it you are willing to use.
Divide the peak load by what each server should carry.
Servers come whole, and rounding down would run each above the plan, so round up.
Check the result by sharing the peak across the fleet.

steps.headline: Size a fleet for a peak of 8,000 requests per second with servers that handle 600 per second each and a target utilisation of 60%.

workedSteps.text: Work out what each server should carry at the target utilisation.
The peak is shared among servers that each carry 360 requests per second, and servers come whole.

lead.text: Suppose a user adds an item to a cart and the server that handled the request keeps the cart in its own memory. The next request goes, by the balancer's choice, to a different server, which has no cart, and the item seems to have vanished. The server was holding **state**, information that has to survive from one request to the next, and a service that does this cannot just be copied behind a balancer.

A **stateless** service keeps no such information between requests. What must survive is held where every server can reach it: in a signed cookie that the client sends back with each request, in a shared cache, or in a database. Then any server can answer any request, a failed server loses nothing that was not already stored elsewhere, and capacity grows by adding servers.

afterFigure.text: The state has not disappeared. It has moved to a shared store, and that store is now the part that has to be fast, large and safe.

reveal.text: Where the session state goes decides the design. A shared store keeps the servers interchangeable, at the cost of one more component to run.

lead.text: Every request passes through the load balancer, so a single balancer is a single point of failure, however many servers stand behind it. The usual remedy is to run two or more, with one taking over when its partner fails or with traffic shared between them.

**Autoscaling** adds and removes servers according to a measured signal, such as processor use or the number of requests in flight, and it always lags behind the load. A new server needs time to start and warm up, so a sudden surge is met first by the servers that already exist, and the margin of a target utilisation below 100% is what carries the service across that gap.

reveal.text: Fifteen servers carry 400 requests per second each, which is 80% of their capacity against the 70% planned, so the update uses up the margin that the plan kept. A smaller batch, or an update outside the peak, keeps the servers near 70%.

lessons.orientation: Size a fleet from the peak, explain why stateless servers scale out, and compute queueing delay.
lessons.nextAction: Keep copies of answers closer to the reader with a cache, and compute what a given hit rate saves.

blocks.text: A server that can handle 100 requests per second answers in about 10 ms when it is idle, and when 50 requests arrive each second the average request already takes 20 ms.
How quickly that delay grows as a server fills is what decides how many servers a design needs, since the aim is to have enough machines that none of them comes near the steep part of the curve.

intro.promise: By the end you'll size a fleet from peak load and a target utilisation, say why stateless servers scale out, and predict how delay grows as a server fills.
intro.whyItMatters: Running a fleet at the wrong utilisation costs either money, when it is too low, or delay and outages, when it is too high.

recap.keyIdea: A fleet is sized from the peak at a target utilisation well below full, with stateless servers behind a balancer, because delay climbs steeply as a server fills.

blocks.text: Capacity grows by adding stateless servers behind a load balancer that spreads requests and removes servers that fail their health checks. In a simple queue the mean time in the system is 1 ÷ (service rate − arrival rate), so delay climbs steeply as utilisation nears 100%, and the fleet is sized by dividing the peak by what each server should carry at a target such as 70% and rounding up. The state that statelessness removes from the servers lives in a shared store, which becomes the next thing to make fast.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson keeps copies of popular answers close to the reader, and computes what a given hit rate saves.

lessons.title: Caching

lead.text: A **cache** is a small, fast store of copies, kept so that repeated requests do not repeat the work. The usual arrangement is **cache-aside**: the application looks the key up in the cache first, and if the answer is there, which is a **hit**, it returns it. If not, which is a **miss**, the application reads the database, stores the result in the cache, and then returns it.

afterFigure.text: Because every entry is a copy, the database remains the **source of truth**: when the two disagree, the database is right and the cache is out of date. A design that treats the cache as the only place a value lives will lose data when the cache restarts, or when it evicts the entry to make room for another.

reveal.text: The average is the lookup plus the miss rate times the database time, here 1 + 0.1 × 20 = 3 ms. The next screen draws it for three hit rates.

lead.text: Every request pays for the lookup, and only the misses go on to pay for the database as well. The **hit rate** is the fraction of lookups that the cache answers, and the misses are the rest. With a 1 ms lookup, a 20 ms database read and a hit rate of 95%, the misses are 5% and the average latency is 1 + 0.05 × 20 = 2 ms. At a hit rate of 80% the misses are 20% and the average is 1 + 0.2 × 20 = 5 ms, two and a half times slower, though the hit rate has fallen by only fifteen points.

afterFigure.text: The last view of the figure shows the case that the idea of a cache hides. If only 5% of lookups hit, the average is 1 + 0.95 × 20 = 20 ms, exactly what the database alone would take, and any lower hit rate makes every request slower, because each pays for a lookup that mostly finds nothing. The break-even hit rate is the lookup time divided by the database time, here 1 ÷ 20 = 5%, so a cache helps only when it hits often enough to earn back its own cost.

diagram.alt: A request goes to a cache with a 1 ms lookup, and the misses continue to a database with a 20 ms read. At a 95% hit rate the average is 2 ms, at 80% it is 5 ms, and at 5% it is 20 ms, no better than the database alone.

reveal.text: On a miss the application reads the database, stores the result in the cache and then returns it. The database stays the source of truth, and the next reader of that product is a hit.

lead.text: The same fraction decides the load that reaches the database, which is what a cache is usually there to reduce. Of 10,000 requests per second, a hit rate of 95% lets 5%, or 500 requests per second, through, and a hit rate of 80% lets 2,000 through. A fall of fifteen points in the hit rate therefore quadruples the load on the database, because the load follows the *miss* rate, and the miss rate went from 5% to 20%.

afterFigure.text: A freshly restarted cache has a hit rate of zero, so the database must briefly serve all 10,000 requests per second, which is 20 times the 500 that it was sized for.

reveal.text: A freshly restarted cache has a hit rate of zero, so the database must briefly serve all 10,000 requests per second, 20 times the 500 it was sized for.

lead.text: A copy goes out of date the moment the data changes, and the policy for removing it sets how long a reader may be shown the old value. The simplest policy is a **time to live**, or TTL: each entry expires a fixed time after it is stored. If a product page is cached for 60 seconds and its price changes 10 seconds after the page was cached, readers see the old price for the remaining 50 seconds, so the page is late by at most 60. Two alternatives are *explicit invalidation*, in which the code that changes the data also removes the cached entry, and *write-through*, in which a write updates the cache and the database together.

afterFigure.text: The choice trades freshness against load. A short TTL keeps answers fresh but sends more requests to the database, and a long one saves load at the price of older answers. Explicit invalidation gives the freshest answers, but every code path that changes the data must remember to use it.

reveal.text: The old price shows from second 120 until the entry expires at second 300, which is 180 seconds. A TTL bounds how stale an answer can be, and removing the entry on every change removes the window.

lead.text: Consider a key that is requested 1,000 times per second, whose database read takes 200 ms. When the entry expires, the first request misses and starts the read, and so does every request that arrives before the result has been stored, since none of them can tell that a refresh is under way. In 200 ms, 1,000 × 0.2 = 200 requests read the same row at once. This is a **stampede**.

Three remedies are standard. In *request coalescing*, one request refreshes the key while the others wait for its result, so the database sees one read. In *serving stale*, the others are given the expired value while the refresh runs. And *jittered TTLs* add a random amount to each expiry so that keys stored together do not expire together: 10,000 keys with a 60-second TTL all expire at second 60, whereas the same keys with a random extra of 0 to 9 seconds expire at about 1,000 per second.

reveal.text: Each remedy removes a different cause: coalescing the duplicate reads, serving stale the waiting, and jitter the simultaneous expiry.

steps.headline: Find the average latency and database load at 20,000 requests per second, with a 2 ms lookup, a 30 ms read and a 90% hit rate.

workedSteps.text: Every request pays for the lookup, and the 10% of requests that miss also pay for the database.
Add the lookup to the miss rate times the database time.
Multiply the request rate by the miss rate to get the load on the database.
Compare with the database alone, which would have served every request in 30 ms and carried the full 20,000.

steps.headline: Find the average latency for a 1 ms lookup, a 20 ms database read and a 99% hit rate.

workedSteps.text: The miss rate is the share of lookups that the cache does not answer.
Every request pays for the lookup, and the requests that miss also pay for the database.

reveal.text: The break-even hit rate is the lookup time divided by the database time, 4 ÷ 40 = 10%. At 8% the average is 4 + 0.92 × 40 = 40.8 ms, slower than reading the database directly.

lessons.orientation: Compute the effect of a hit rate on latency and database load, and choose how to keep entries fresh.
lessons.nextAction: Choose a store from the access pattern, and count the page reads an index saves.

blocks.text: A database takes 20 ms to answer a read, and a cache that sits beside it answers in 1 ms. A request whose answer is already in the cache costs 1 ms, while one whose answer is not pays for the lookup and then for the database as well, 21 ms in all, so the average cost of a request depends on how often the cache already holds what is asked for.
A cache is therefore a bet on repetition, and its value can be worked out before it is built.

intro.promise: By the end you'll compute the average latency and database load for a given hit rate, say how stale a TTL allows an answer to be, and name the remedies for a stampede.
intro.whyItMatters: A cache is the cheapest way to cut load and delay, and the arithmetic tells you whether it will pay off.

recap.keyIdea: A cache lowers latency and load in proportion to its hit rate, at the price of stale copies, and it helps only when the hit rate repays the lookup.

blocks.text: In cache-aside the application checks the cache, reads the database on a miss and stores the result, so the database remains the source of truth. The average latency is the lookup time plus the miss rate times the database time, and the database load is the request rate times the miss rate, so a small fall in the hit rate multiplies the load. A TTL bounds how stale an answer can be, and coalescing, serving stale and jittered expiry stop a popular key from sending a stampede to the database.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at what sits behind the cache, choosing a store from the access pattern and using an index to turn a scan into a few page reads.

lessons.title: Databases and indexes

lead.text: Before choosing a database, write down how its data will be read. Four patterns cover most cases. A lookup *by key* fetches one record from its id, and a key-value store is built for it. A *range* query reads the records between two keys, such as one customer's orders in a month. A *join* combines rows from several tables by a shared value, which a relational database does well, and a *traversal* follows links from one record to the next, such as the friends of friends of a user, which is what a graph store is for. The set of patterns a system has to serve is called its **access pattern**.

reveal.text: Every request fetches one record from its token, which is a lookup by key. Before choosing a database, the access pattern is what to write down.

The table fills 1,000,000 ÷ 100 = 10,000 pages. Every added row adds work to a scan, which is the reason that a query fast on a small table can fail on a large one. The next screen shows how an index avoids it.

lead.text: A query such as "find the order with id 123" can be run in two ways. A **scan** reads every page of the table until it finds the row, and for 1,000,000 rows at 100 rows per page that is 10,000 page reads. An **index** is a separate sorted structure that maps keys to where the rows live, so the database can go straight to the row. In PostgreSQL the default index is a **B-tree**, which keeps its keys in sorted order across pages arranged as a tree: the root page points to pages at the next level down, each of those to the next level, and so on until the leaf pages, which hold the keys with pointers to the rows.

A lookup walks one page at each level, from the root to a leaf, which is the highlighted path in the figure. With 1,000,000 keys and 100 keys to a page the walk reads 3 pages, and one further read fetches the row, so 4 pages answer a query that the scan answered with 10,000.

afterFigure.text: The scan grows with the table, but the walk hardly does, so a query that is fast on 1,000 rows can be hopeless on 100 million when it has no index, and fast on both when it has one. This is also why the index must match the query: a B-tree sorted by order id can find an order id at once, but it does not help a search for a customer name.

lead.text: How many levels does an index need? If a page holds f keys and so points to f pages below it, then a tree with L levels reaches f^L keys. With f = 100, two levels reach 100^2 = 10,000 keys and three reach 100^3 = 1,000,000. The number of levels is the smallest L for which f^L is at least the number of keys n, which is about log base f of n, and it is called the **depth** of the tree.
Depth grows very slowly. A hundredfold increase in the table, from 10,000 keys to 1,000,000, adds one level, from 2 to 3, because 100^3 = 1,000,000.

afterFigure.text: Real pages hold hundreds of keys, so a fan-out of 100 is a modest assumption, and a lookup through an index costs a handful of page reads however large the table becomes.

reveal.text: A hundredfold increase adds one level, because 100^3 = 1,000,000 and 100^4 = 100,000,000, so the lookup reads 4 index pages and one for the row. A scan of the same table would read 1,000,000 pages.

lead.text: An index is not free. Every insert, update or delete that touches an indexed column has to change the index as well as the table, so a table with five indexes turns each insert into one write to the table and five more to the indexes, and every index takes space of its own.

A **composite index** sorts on several columns in order. An index on `(customer_id, created_at)` sorts by customer and, within each customer, by date, so it serves "orders for customer 7" and "orders for customer 7 in March". It does not serve "orders created in March" for all customers, because the dates are in order only inside each customer, and the order of the columns is therefore part of the design.

afterFigure.text: One further property affects the choice of store. A **transaction** groups several changes so that they all happen or none does, as when a transfer must both debit one account and credit another, and relational databases provide this as standard.

reveal.text: An index is built for the queries that will be run, so the access pattern comes before the index, just as it comes before the store.

lead.text: A page lists 50 orders and shows each customer's name. The code runs one query for the 50 orders and then, for each order, a separate query for its customer, which is 1 + 50 = 51 queries. This pattern is called **N+1**. Each query may be fast, but each also pays a round trip to the database.
The cure is to ask for the related rows together: a join returns each order with its customer in one query, or a second query can fetch all 50 customers by their ids at once, for a total of two.

steps.headline: Compare a scan and an index lookup on 100,000,000 rows, with 100 rows per page and a fan-out of 100.

workedSteps.text: A scan reads every page, so divide the rows by the rows per page.
An index needs the smallest number of levels whose reach is at least the number of keys.
The lookup reads one page per level and one more for the row.
Divide the scan by the lookup to compare them.

steps.headline: Compare a scan and an index on 30,000,000 rows with 100 rows per page and a fan-out of 100.

workedSteps.text: The index needs the smallest number of levels whose reach covers the keys. Since 100^3 is 1,000,000 and 100^4 is 100,000,000, it needs 4 levels.
workedSteps.math: 4 levels, so 5 page reads with the row

workedSteps.text: A scan reads every page of the table.

reveal.text: Every index is one more structure to update on each insert, so seven indexes would turn 20,000 inserts a second into 140,000 writes a second. An index earns its place by the reads it serves.

lessons.orientation: Choose a store from the access pattern, compute B-tree depth, and count the queries a page runs.

blocks.text: A query for one order in a table of 1,000,000 rows can be answered in two ways. The database can read the table page by page until it meets the row, or it can walk a sorted index that leads to the row in a handful of page reads, and a table a hundred times larger needs only one page more.
That difference decides whether a design survives its own growth, and it follows from two numbers, the fan-out of a page and the number of keys.

intro.promise: By the end you'll choose a store from the access pattern, compute how many levels an index needs, and count the queries a page runs.
intro.whyItMatters: Most slow systems are slow at the database, and the cause is usually a scan or a count of queries that this lesson teaches you to spot.

recap.keyIdea: An index turns a scan that grows with the table into a walk of a few pages, at the price of space and slower writes.

blocks.text: The way data is read, by key, range, join or traversal, decides the store, and an index turns a scan of every page into a walk of a few. A B-tree of fan-out f reaches f^L keys in L levels, so 1,000,000 keys need 3 levels and 100,000,000 need 4, while each index costs space and slows writes. A page that fetches a list and then queries once per item runs 1 + N queries, where a join runs one.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson copies data to several machines for availability and splits it across machines when one cannot hold it, and shows what that does to reads.

lessons.title: Replication and partitioning

lead.text: **Replication** keeps copies of the data on more than one machine, so that the data survives the loss of a machine and the copies can serve reads. In the commonest arrangement, **leader-follower** replication, one machine, the leader, accepts every write and sends the changes to the others, the followers, which apply them in the same order. Reads can go to any copy, so the read capacity grows with the number of copies.
The copying takes time. A follower applies a change only after the leader has made it, and the gap, called **replication lag**, may be a few milliseconds or a good deal more under load.

afterFigure.text: Two consequences follow. Replication does not make writes faster, since every write must still be made by the leader and then repeated on every follower, so adding followers adds read capacity and survives failures but leaves the write capacity where it was. And a user who saves a profile and is then sent to a follower that has not caught up will see the old one, because the system has no *read-your-writes* guarantee.

reveal.text: The data is not lost; it has not arrived yet, which is why the same read a little later returns the new value.
To raise the write limit, the data itself has to be divided among several machines, which is what the next idea does.

lead.text: When one machine can no longer hold the data or carry the writes, the data is split by a key. In **sharding**, each machine, called a shard, holds the records whose keys fall in its part. The simplest rule is **hash-mod**: compute a hash of the key, a number that looks random but is always the same for the same key, and take it modulo the number of shards N, so that shard = hash(key) mod N. With N = 4 and small numeric keys standing for their own hashes, key 13 lives on shard 13 mod 4 = 1, and any machine can work out where a key lives without asking anyone.

Unlike replication, sharding does scale writes, because each write goes to just one shard and different shards work at the same time. It has costs of its own: a query over keys on several shards has to ask each of them, and a transaction that spans shards is harder to make safe than one inside a machine.

afterFigure.text: Each shard is usually replicated as well, so the two ideas combine: the data is divided for capacity and every part is copied for availability.

reveal.text: The answer is small, and the next screen shows what it means for a cluster that is growing.

lead.text: Take the 20 keys 0 to 19. With 4 shards a key k lives on shard k mod 4, and with 5 shards on shard k mod 5. The two rules agree only for keys 0 to 3, so 4 keys stay and **16 move**, which is 80% of the data, for a cluster that has grown by only a quarter. Every key that moves must be copied to its new shard, so a small change in the cluster causes a large transfer, and the first view of the figure and the second show the keys that change.

**Consistent hashing** avoids this. Place the keys and the nodes on a circle, a ring of hash values, and give each key to the first node met moving clockwise from it. A node that joins takes over only the arc between itself and its predecessor, so the keys that move are those of that arc, about 1/N of them for N nodes after the join: a fifth node moves about 1/5, or 20%, and no key moves between the old nodes. Karger and his co-authors described it in 1997, and Dynamo uses it to place data.

afterFigure.text: The third view of the figure places the twenty keys in arcs, one arc per node, and gives the new node the end of each arc. Four keys move, all of them to the new node, against sixteen under hash-mod. The ring is what lets a cluster grow by one node at a time without moving most of its data.

reveal.text: Under hash-mod only 8 of every 72 keys keep their shard, so nearly 89% move, whereas consistent hashing moves the arc of the new node, about 1/9, or 11%. Dynamo places data with consistent hashing for this reason.

lead.text: Hashing gives each shard about the same *number* of keys, but not the same *load*. If one key, such as a celebrity's profile, receives a thousand times as many requests as an ordinary one, the shard that holds it is overloaded however even the key counts are, and the imbalance is called **skew**. A hot key can be eased by copying it to several shards or by caching it, since adding shards does nothing for a single key.

The choice of shard key follows from the access pattern. Sharding orders by customer id keeps all of one customer's orders on one shard, while sharding them by date would instead send all of today's writes to the shard that holds today, which becomes a hot spot while the others sit idle.

lessons.orientation: Explain leader-follower replication and lag, and compare how many keys move under hash-mod and consistent hashing.
lessons.nextAction: State what CAP does and does not say, and compute quorum sizes and fault tolerance.

blocks.text: When a database keeps a copy of its data on a second machine, the copy is always a little behind, and a read that lands on the copy returns the value from before the write.
Copying is one of two ways for data to outgrow a single machine, and splitting it by a key is the other.

intro.promise: By the end you'll explain replication lag, count how many keys move when a shard is added under hash-mod, and say why consistent hashing moves only about 1/N.
intro.whyItMatters: Copies and shards are how data outgrows one machine, and both choices decide what a reader can see and what a growth step costs.

recap.keyIdea: Followers add reads and resilience but lag behind the leader, and hash-mod sharding moves most keys when the shard count changes, which a ring avoids.

blocks.text: Leader-follower replication copies each write from the leader to the followers, which adds read capacity and survives failures but leaves writes at the leader's limit, and a read from a follower within the replication lag can return old data. Sharding by hash(key) mod N splits the data and so scales writes, but changing N moves most keys, for instance 16 of 20 going from 4 to 5 shards, whereas consistent hashing moves only about 1/N. Hashing balances the keys and not the load, so the shard key follows the access pattern.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson asks what a system should guarantee when its copies disagree, and counts how many copies must answer to be sure.

lessons.title: Consistency and quorums

lead.text: How a system answers a read after a write is described by its **consistency**. A **strongly consistent** system behaves as if there were a single copy: once a write has been acknowledged, every later read returns it or something newer. An **eventually consistent** system promises less: if no further writes arrive, all copies will in time hold the same value, but a read in the meantime may return an older one.

Between the two lies a useful middle, *read-your-writes*, which promises only that a user sees their own writes at once. Eventual consistency is sometimes taken to mean "wrong", and it is not: a like count that is a few seconds behind is harmless, and the weaker the promise, the cheaper it is to keep.

reveal.text: The weaker promise is cheaper to keep, and for data such as a like count it is enough.

lead.text: Suppose the network between two replicas of a value fails, so that each can still reach its own clients but not the other. This is a **network partition**. A client writes a new value through one replica, and the other replica cannot hear about it. A client reading from that other replica must be either answered, with the value it holds, which may be out of date, or refused. A system that refuses stays consistent, because no stale value is ever returned, but it is no longer *available* on that side. A system that answers stays available and may return stale data.

That choice is the content of **CAP**. Eric Brewer stated it as a conjecture in 2000, and Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch proved a precise form in 2002: when a partition separates replicas, a system cannot both answer every request and always return the latest write. The popular summary "pick two of three" misleads, because a designer cannot decline to have partitions. The choice arises only *during* one, and when the network is healthy a system can be both consistent and available.

afterFigure.text: CAP says nothing about speed, and nothing about the other trade-offs that systems make, such as latency against consistency even when no partition is present. It is a narrow result, which is its value: it names the one decision that cannot be avoided when the network splits.

diagram.alt: A network partition between two replicas, drawn as a dashed line. When the system chooses consistency, the write from client B on side B is refused and both replicas keep x = 1. When it chooses availability, replica 2 accepts x = 2 while replica 1 still has x = 1, so a read on side A is out of date.
diagram.caption: The same partition under two policies. Use the buttons to compare refusing with answering.

reveal.text: The two policies are the two halves of the choice, and which one is right depends on what a wrong answer costs.
The reasoning counts the replicas that can miss the write, and the next screen turns it into a rule.

lead.text: A **quorum** system sets two numbers. A write is acknowledged once W of the N replicas have it, and a read asks R replicas and takes the newest value it receives. Any set of W replicas and any set of R replicas share at least one replica when R + W > N, because together they would otherwise need more than N distinct replicas. With N = 3, W = 2 and R = 2, the sum is 4, which exceeds 3, so every read sees at least one copy of the latest write. With W = 1 and R = 1 the sum is 2, and the read can land on a replica that never got the write.

The figure draws the idea for five replicas. With W = 2 and R = 3 the sum is 5, which does not exceed N, and the write and the read can use different replicas, as the first view shows. Raising R to 4 gives 6, and the sets must share one. By the rule, with N = 5 and W = 2, R must be greater than 5 − 2 = 3, so the smallest R is 4.

afterFigure.text: The numbers trade cost against safety. A larger W makes writes slower and makes them fail when too many replicas are down, since a write needs W of them, and a larger R does the same for reads. A write can tolerate N − W unavailable replicas and a read N − R. Not every choice of W and R gives a consistent read, so the sum has to be checked and not assumed. The guarantee also needs a strict quorum, in which the W and R replicas are always counted among the same N, since a system that lets other nodes stand in for failed replicas loses the overlap.

diagram.alt: Five replicas R1 to R5. In the first view the write reached R1 and R2 and the read asks R3, R4 and R5, so the read misses the write. In the second the read asks R2 to R5 and includes R2. In the third the write reached R1 to R3 and the read asks R3 to R5, sharing R3.
diagram.caption: Which replicas hold the latest write and which are asked by a read. Use the buttons to compare three choices of W and R.

lead.text: Quorums give an overlap for reads and writes of a value, but some decisions, such as which node is the leader, need every node to agree on one answer even when some of them fail. This is **consensus**, and algorithms for it, such as Raft, rest on **majorities**. In Raft a leader adds each change to a log and counts it as committed once a majority of the nodes have stored it, and any two majorities of the same group share a node, so a later leader always knows about every committed change.

A majority of n nodes is more than half of them, so a group keeps working while a majority is up. Five nodes need 3, and so tolerate 2 failures. Four nodes also need 3, and so tolerate only 1, the same as a group of three, which is why consensus groups usually have an odd size.

afterFigure.text: A group that could not reach a majority stops accepting changes, which is CAP's choice made visible: it keeps the one history by refusing to make progress.

diagram.alt: Five nodes of a consensus group drawn as circles. With two nodes down, three are up, which is a majority, so the group continues. With three nodes down, only two are up, which is not a majority, so the group stops.

reveal.text: A group of 7 needs a majority of 4 and tolerates 3 failures, and the same reasoning shows that 4 nodes tolerate 1 and 5 tolerate 2, which is why odd sizes are the rule.

lead.text: The right guarantee depends on the data. An account balance needs strong consistency, because a stale read can let a withdrawal go through twice. A like count can be eventually consistent, because a number a few seconds behind harms no one.

The Dynamo paper described a shopping cart that is always writable: during a failure, the cart accepts additions on either side and merges them afterwards, since a customer who cannot add an item loses more than one who sees a briefly different cart.

steps.headline: Choose W and R for N = 5 so that reads and writes both survive two unavailable replicas and every read sees the latest write.

workedSteps.text: A write needs W replicas up, so it survives N − W unavailable ones, and likewise for a read with R.
workedSteps.math: tolerated down = N − W for writes and N − R for reads

workedSteps.text: To survive two unavailable replicas, both W and R can be at most 3.
workedSteps.math: 5 − W ≥ 2 and 5 − R ≥ 2, so W ≤ 3 and R ≤ 3

workedSteps.text: Take W = 3, and find the smallest R that overlaps every write set.
The choice W = 3 and R = 3 satisfies all the conditions.
workedSteps.math: 3 + 3 = 6 > 5, with two replicas allowed to be down for either

steps.headline: Find the smallest R for N = 7 and W = 4.

workedSteps.text: The condition for the read and write sets to overlap is R + W > N, which here reads R + 4 > 7.
R has to be a whole number of replicas that makes the sum exceed 7.

reveal.text: With W = 3 the writes can tolerate N − W = 0 unavailable replicas. The setting makes reads fast and consistent and puts the cost on the availability of writes.

lessons.orientation: State what CAP says, compute quorum sizes, and count the failures a consensus group tolerates.
lessons.nextAction: Decouple producers from consumers with a queue, and say what happens when a message is delivered twice.

blocks.text: When the network between two replicas of a value fails, a client that has just updated one of them leaves the other holding a value that is out of date. A second client that reads from that other replica can be given the stale value or be told that no answer is available, and no system can avoid the choice, because its users would like both an answer to every request and an answer that is always the latest.

The choice comes with arithmetic: how many replicas must acknowledge a write, and how many a read must ask, decide how many failures a service survives and whether a read is certain to see the latest write.

intro.promise: By the end you'll state what CAP does and does not say, compute the read size that overlaps a write, and count how many failures a consensus group tolerates.
intro.whyItMatters: These numbers are how designers decide how many copies to keep and how many must answer, so that data stays correct and the service stays up.

recap.keyIdea: During a partition a system must choose between consistency and availability, and quorums with R + W > N and majorities are the arithmetic that makes the choice precise.

blocks.text: CAP, conjectured by Brewer in 2000 and proved in a precise form by Gilbert and Lynch in 2002, says that when a partition separates replicas a system cannot both answer every request and always return the latest write, and the choice arises only during a partition. In a quorum system a write acknowledged by W replicas and a read of R replicas overlap whenever R + W > N, and consensus rests on majorities, so 5 nodes tolerate 2 failures. Which guarantee a feature needs depends on what a stale answer would cost.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson decouples the part of a system that produces work from the part that does it, with a queue, and asks what happens when a message arrives twice.

lessons.title: Queues and event streams

lead.text: When a user signs up, the service must store the account and also send a welcome email. Putting the email request into a **queue** lets the sign-up code hand it over and return at once, while a separate worker, the **consumer**, takes requests from the queue one after another and sends them. The code that adds them is the **producer**.

afterFigure.text: A queue also absorbs bursts. If requests arrive faster than the consumer can handle them for a minute and then slow down again, the queue holds the excess where otherwise the producer would fail.

reveal.text: The backlog is a running difference between two rates, here 50 messages per second, which makes 6,000 after two minutes. The next screen draws it for steady rates.

lead.text: The queue's length, its **backlog**, changes by the difference between the two rates. If messages arrive at 120 per second and the consumers handle 100 per second, then 20 more arrive each second than leave, and after 10 minutes, which is 600 seconds, the backlog is (120 − 100) × 600 = 12,000 messages. If the rates are the other way round, with arrivals at 80 per second, the backlog shrinks by 20 per second, and the 12,000 messages are gone after 12,000 ÷ 20 = 600 seconds.

afterFigure.text: A queue is therefore safe only while the arrival rate stays below the consumers' capacity on average, and a longer queue means a longer wait: a message that joins behind 12,000 others, with consumers handling 100 per second, waits 12,000 ÷ 100 = 120 seconds before it is processed.

diagram.alt: A graph of messages waiting against time over 600 seconds. With arrivals at 120 per second and capacity of 100, the backlog rises in a straight line to 12,000. With arrivals at 80 per second and a starting backlog of 12,000, it falls in a straight line to zero at 600 seconds.
diagram.caption: The backlog under steady rates. Use the buttons to compare arrivals above capacity with arrivals below it.
