reveal.text: The queue fills at the difference of the two rates, so a modest excess is enough to reach a limit in under an hour. A queue is safe only while arrivals stay below the consumers' capacity on average.

lead.text: Suppose the arrival rate stays above capacity. The backlog grows without limit and so does the wait of every message. The system has to respond, and the response is called **backpressure**: telling producers to slow down, for example by rejecting new requests with an error that asks the client to try again later; dropping the least valuable work, which is called *shedding load*; or adding consumers so that capacity exceeds arrivals, which helps only if the work can be shared between them.

afterFigure.text: Draining takes time, and the time depends on the spare capacity. With a backlog of 12,000, arrivals at 80 per second and capacity of 100 per second, the spare 20 per second clears the backlog in 600 seconds. A system that is sized exactly for its average load has no spare capacity, so a backlog never drains.

steps.headline: With capacity 100, find the backlog after 5 minutes at 150 per second, then its drain time once arrivals fall to 60.

workedSteps.text: During the first 5 minutes the queue grows by the difference of the rates.
After arrivals fall to 60, the queue shrinks by the spare capacity each second.
Divide the backlog by the rate at which it shrinks to get the drain time.
The queue is empty about six minutes after arrivals fell.

steps.headline: Find how long a backlog of 9,000 messages takes to drain when arrivals are 60 per second and consumers process 100 per second.

workedSteps.text: The backlog shrinks by the processing rate minus the arrival rate.
The backlog is 9,000 messages, and it shrinks at that rate until none remain.

lead.text: A queue sits between machines, so a message can be lost or repeated, and the promise a system makes about this is its **delivery semantics**. With **at-most-once** delivery a message is sent once and never resent, so a failure can lose it but it is never repeated. With **at-least-once** delivery the message is resent until it is acknowledged, so it is never lost but may arrive more than once, because an acknowledgement that goes missing makes the sender try again. The third, exactly once, is attractive and much harder than it sounds, because a sender cannot tell a lost message from a lost acknowledgement.

What systems achieve in practice is **effectively-once** processing: at-least-once delivery together with a consumer that is **idempotent**, which means that processing a message twice has the same effect as processing it once. Some systems offer exactly-once inside narrow bounds, such as within one broker, but a message that causes an effect outside it, such as charging a card, still needs a consumer that can cope with repeats.

afterFigure.text: The choice follows from what each failure costs. For a stream of temperature readings, losing one is harmless and at-most-once is cheap. For a payment, losing a message is unacceptable, so at-least-once is used, and the consumer is made idempotent so that a repeat is harmless.

diagram.alt: Three messages M1, M2 and M3 sent to a consumer under three guarantees. With at-most-once, M2 is lost and has no effect. With at-least-once, M2 is delivered twice and applied twice. With at-least-once and an idempotent consumer, M2 is delivered twice and applied once.

reveal.text: The guarantee gives up delivery to avoid repeats, and the opposite choice gives up the absence of repeats to avoid loss.

lead.text: How does a consumer become idempotent? It records the id of every message it has handled, and checks the record before it acts. The record has to be written in the same transaction as the effect: if the effect and the record could succeed separately, a crash between them would leave either a missed effect or a repeated one. A payment that is retried after a timeout carries an *idempotency key* in the same way, and the payment service stores it, so that the card is charged once however many times the request arrives.

Some messages can never be processed, because they are malformed or trigger a bug, and a consumer that retries such a **poison message** for ever blocks everything behind it. After a set number of attempts the message is moved to a **dead-letter queue**, where it can be inspected, and the main queue moves on.

A queue deletes a message once it has been consumed, whereas an **event stream** keeps it. A stream is an ordered log, retained for a set time, in which each event has a position called its **offset**. Each consumer keeps its own offset, so many consumers can read the same events at their own pace, and a new one can start from the beginning and replay the history. To scale, the log is divided into **partitions**, each its own ordered log, and the consumers in a **consumer group** share the partitions, each partition being read by one consumer of the group at a time.
A consumer's **lag** is the number of events between its offset and the end of the log, which is the stream's version of a backlog and is computed in the same way.

afterFigure.text: Order is guaranteed only within a partition. Events with the same key, such as one account, go to the same partition and so are read in order, but there is no order between events in different partitions. The number of partitions also caps the parallelism: a group with more consumers than partitions leaves the extra ones idle.

reveal.text: The number of partitions caps the parallelism of a group. A consumer's lag, the events between its offset and the end of its partition, is the stream's version of a backlog.

The charge happened and the record did not, so the second delivery repeats the charge. Writing the id in the same transaction as the effect, or sending an idempotency key to the payment service, makes a repeat harmless.

lessons.orientation: Compute backlog growth and drain time, choose a delivery guarantee, and explain idempotent consumers and streams.
lessons.nextAction: Limit how long a call waits, count how retries multiply load, and see how a circuit breaker stops a failing call.

blocks.text: A queue between two parts of a system lets the producer carry on without waiting for the consumer, and the price is a line of waiting messages whenever the producer sends them faster than the consumer can handle them.
A message that crosses a network can also be lost or delivered twice, so a queue raises a second question, which is what a consumer must be like for a repeated message to do no harm.

intro.promise: By the end you'll compute how a backlog grows and drains, say what the delivery guarantees mean, and explain why an idempotent consumer is the practical answer to repeats.
intro.whyItMatters: A queue is the standard way to let one part of a system fail or fall behind without the rest failing, and the arithmetic says when it stops helping.

recap.keyIdea: A queue absorbs a mismatch of rates only for as long as the spare capacity can clear what it holds, and at-least-once delivery needs an idempotent consumer.

blocks.text: A queue decouples the producer from the consumer, and its backlog changes by the difference of the two rates, so arrivals above capacity grow it without limit and the spare capacity below it sets the drain time. Delivery is at-most-once, which may lose messages, or at-least-once, which may repeat them, and effectively-once processing comes from an idempotent consumer that records each message in the same transaction as its effect. An event stream keeps an ordered, replayable log whose order is guaranteed only within a partition.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson limits how long one service waits for another, and counts how retries multiply load when a dependency is failing.

lessons.title: Timeouts, retries and circuit breakers

reveal.text: The number waiting is the product of the rate and the timeout, here 100 × 30 = 3,000, so shortening the timeout is the direct way to hold fewer.

lead.text: A call to another service can end in three ways: it returns a result, it returns an error, or it returns nothing at all. The third is the awkward one, because silence does not say whether the request was lost on the way, is still being worked on, or was carried out and the reply was lost. The caller cannot wait for ever, since every waiting call holds a thread, a connection and some memory. A **timeout** is a limit on that wait.

Take the service from the question, which makes 100 calls per second to a dependency that has stopped answering. With a timeout of 30 seconds each call waits the full 30, so 100 × 30 = 3,000 calls are in flight at once, and the caller runs out of threads or memory and fails too, though nothing was wrong with it. With a timeout of 1 second only 100 × 1 = 100 are waiting.

afterFigure.text: A timeout also has to fit inside the caller's own deadline. If a user's request must finish within 2 seconds and the call to the dependency is allowed 5, the user has gone long before the call gives up, and any work that finishes late is wasted. Each call in a chain should therefore be given a timeout shorter than the deadline of the call above it.

reveal.text: The user is gone after 2 seconds, but the service keeps a thread and a connection for each attempt, up to 3 × 5 = 15 seconds. Every held call counts, by Little's law, against the threads the service has.

lead.text: Many failures are brief: a lost packet, a server restarting, one slow machine. A **retry**, which repeats the call, turns such a failure into a success. It has two dangers. The first is repeating something that should not be repeated. A call that charged a card may have succeeded before its reply was lost, and a second attempt charges again unless the request carries an idempotency key, as in the previous lesson. The second danger is amplification.

Suppose a request passes through three services in a chain, with A calling B, B calling C and C calling a database, and every caller makes up to 3 attempts. If the database is down, one request to A causes 3 calls to B, each of which causes 3 calls to C, each of which causes 3 calls to the database, so the database receives 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 calls. For k layers with a attempts each, the bottom receives a^k calls, and the dependency that is already struggling gets the most traffic when it can least bear it.

afterFigure.text: The remedies are to retry at only one layer, usually the one nearest the user, to cap retries with a budget, such as a small fraction of the normal traffic, and to stop calling quickly when a dependency is plainly down, which is the job of the circuit breaker described below.

diagram.alt: Four boxes in a chain: service A, service B, service C and a database that always fails, with a bar under each for the calls it receives from one request to A. With one attempt per layer every box receives 1 call. With three attempts per layer the counts are 1, 3, 9 and 27.
diagram.caption: One request to service A while the database is down. Use the buttons to compare one attempt per layer with three.

reveal.text: Each layer repeats the work of the layers below it, so a modest retry count at every layer is a large multiplier at the bottom. The remedy is to retry at one layer only.

lead.text: Retrying at once is poor practice, because a dependency that failed a moment ago has probably not recovered. **Exponential backoff** waits longer after each failure, doubling the wait: 100, 200, 400 and 800 ms before four successive retries, which is 100 + 200 + 400 + 800 = 1,500 ms of waiting in all.

Doubling is not enough when many clients fail together, since they start in step and retry in step, and every retry arrives as a spike. **Jitter** adds a random offset to each wait so that the clients spread out.

afterFigure.text: Backoff with jitter is cheap to add and is the standard way to retry a call that may be failing because the dependency is overloaded.

lead.text: A **circuit breaker** watches the calls to a dependency, and after repeated failures it stops making them. It has three states. While **closed**, calls pass through as normal and failures are counted. After enough failures, for example five in a row, it **opens**, and calls fail at once without being sent, so the failing dependency receives no load and callers do not wait. After a cool-down it becomes **half-open** and lets a single trial request through: if the trial succeeds the breaker closes again, and if it fails the breaker opens for another cool-down.

afterFigure.text: A call that is rejected in a microsecond is much cheaper than one that waits for a timeout, and the dependency is given room to recover.

diagram.alt: A state diagram with three states. Closed moves to open when failures reach the limit. Open moves to half-open after a cool-down. Half-open moves to closed when a trial request succeeds, and back to open when it fails. Each view highlights one state and says what it does with calls.

If it fails, the breaker opens again.</text></svg>

reveal.text: The breaker opens only when the failures in a row reach its limit. After that it rejects calls, and after a cool-down it moves to half-open.

lead.text: Three further tools limit the damage. **Bulkheads** give each dependency its own pool of threads or connections, so that a slow one can exhaust only its own pool and not the whole capacity of the caller. **Load shedding** refuses some requests, usually the least important, when a service is near its limit, so that the rest are served quickly. And **rate limiting** caps how fast a client may call. A common form is the *token bucket*, which holds up to a fixed number of tokens, refills at a steady rate, and takes one token for each request. A bucket of 10 tokens refilling at 5 per second allows 10 requests at once and then 5 per second, which is 10 + 5 × 4 = 30 requests in the first 4 seconds.

afterFigure.text: Each of these is a form of backpressure, the idea from the queue lesson, applied to calls instead of messages.

steps.headline: A makes up to 4 attempts to B, and B makes up to 3 attempts to C. C always fails. How many calls does C receive from one request to A?

workedSteps.text: Every attempt that A makes is a call to B, which is up but fails because C does, so B receives one call per attempt.
Each call that B receives makes up to 3 attempts to C, because C keeps failing.
Multiply the calls to B by the attempts each one makes.
The attempts multiply from layer to layer, and they do not add.

steps.headline: Find the calls that D receives when A, B and C make 3, 2 and 3 attempts, and D always fails.

workedSteps.text: B receives one call for each attempt that A makes, and C then receives 2 attempts for every call B receives.
Each call that C receives makes up to 3 attempts to D.

reveal.text: With a single retrying layer the database receives at most 3 calls for one request instead of 27, and brief failures are still repaired.

lessons.orientation: Set timeouts from Little's law, compute retry amplification and backoff, and read circuit breaker states.
lessons.nextAction: Compute the availability of components in series and in parallel, and see why independent failure domains matter.

blocks.text: Three services in a chain each try a failing call up to three times before giving up, and the database at the end of the chain is down. The first service makes one request, and the database receives 27: three attempts at each of three layers multiply, and a database that is already struggling is handed twenty-seven times the traffic of a single request.

Every call between services can be slow, lost or repeated, and what a caller does about it comes down to a few numbers: how long it waits, how many attempts it makes at each layer and how long it pauses between them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll compute how retries multiply across layers, add up a backoff schedule, and say which state a circuit breaker is in.
intro.whyItMatters: Most large outages grow through calls between services, and these numbers show how a small fault turns into a large one.

recap.keyIdea: A call between services fails safely when it has a short timeout, a retry count that multiplies to a bearable load, backoff with jitter, and a breaker that stops doomed calls.

blocks.text: A timeout limits how long a caller waits, and by Little's law the number of waiting calls is the rate times the timeout. Retries multiply across layers, so three layers of three attempts send 27 calls to the bottom, which is why retries belong at one layer, spaced by exponential backoff with jitter. A circuit breaker moves from closed to open after repeated failures and to half-open after a cool-down to try one request, and bulkheads, load shedding and token buckets limit the damage.

lessons.title: Availability and redundancy

reveal.text: The rule is the share of time that the service may be down, times the length of the period, and the next screen puts the common targets in a table.

lead.text: A service is 99.9% available when it works for 99.9% of the time, which leaves 0.1% for failure. Over 30 days, which is 43,200 minutes, that is 0.001 × 43,200 = 43.2 minutes of downtime. The conversion is the same for any target: the allowed downtime is (1 − availability) × the length of the period.
Targets are often named by their number of nines: 99% is two nines, 99.9% three and 99.99% four, and each added nine multiplies the allowed downtime by one tenth.

afterFigure.text: A target is also a cost, since each extra nine usually needs another layer of redundancy, automation and testing.

diagram.alt: A table of availability targets from 99% to 99.999% and the downtime each allows. Per day: 14.4 minutes, 86.4 seconds, 8.64 seconds and 0.864 seconds. Per 30 days: 7.2 hours, 43.2 minutes, 4.32 minutes and 25.9 seconds. Per year: 3.65 days, 8.76 hours, 52.56 minutes and 5.26 minutes.

reveal.text: The allowance is 0.0005 × 525,600 = 262.8 minutes, about 4.4 hours. The outage of 4.5 hours is 270 minutes, so it is over by 7.2 minutes.

lead.text: Real services are made of parts. When every part must work for the service to work, the parts are in **series**, and their availabilities multiply: three components that are each 99.9% available give 0.999 × 0.999 × 0.999 = 0.997003, or about 99.7%, so a chain is always less available than its weakest link. When the service works if *any* of several replicas works, the replicas are in **parallel**, and the service fails only when all of them fail. If each of two independent replicas is 99% available, each is down 1% of the time, both are down together 0.01 × 0.01 = 0.0001 of the time, and the pair is 1 − 0.0001 = 99.99% available.

afterFigure.text: Series is the reason a long chain of dependencies drains availability, and parallel is the reason replication buys so much: two copies at two nines make four.

diagram.alt: Three arrangements. Three 99.9% components in series give 99.7%. Two independent 99% replicas in parallel give 99.99%. Two replicas that share one 99.9% power supply give about 99.89%, because the supply is in series with the pair.

reveal.text: Each component added in series takes away roughly its own failure rate, so the chain's downtime is close to the sum of the downtimes.
The figure 1 − 0.01 × 0.01 × 0.01 = 0.999999 holds only if the replicas fail independently. Replicas in one rack share its power supply, and that shared part sits in series with them.

lead.text: Replicas fail independently only if there is nothing that can take them down together. A **failure domain** is a set of things that fail as one: a machine, a rack that shares a power feed, a datacentre, a region. Two replicas in the same rack share its power supply, and if that supply is 99.9% available, the replicas cannot do better than that, however many there are. The shared supply sits in series with the pair: the pair on its own is 99.99%, and the whole is 0.9999 × 0.999 = 0.9989, about 99.89%, nowhere near the 99.99% that the pair alone suggests.

afterFigure.text: The remedy is to put replicas in different failure domains, in separate racks, zones or regions, so that the shared component drops out of the series.

reveal.text: The shared supply caps the whole at 99.95% whatever the pair does. Replicas in separate failure domains remove the shared part, so the pair's own 99.99% can show.

lead.text: Availability measures how long a service is down, and two more numbers describe a disaster. The **recovery point objective**, or RPO, is how much data can be lost, measured as time, and the **recovery time objective**, or RTO, is how long the outage may last. Backups every 6 hours mean that a failure just before the next backup loses up to 6 hours of data, so the RPO is 6 hours; a shorter RPO needs more frequent backups or continuous replication. The RTO depends on how fast a restore or failover can be done: restoring a large backup can take hours, and switching to a standby takes minutes.

A standby can be run in two ways. In **active-passive** failover a second copy waits idle and takes over when the first fails, which costs the time to detect the failure and to switch. In **active-active** both copies serve traffic, so there is nothing to switch, but each must be able to carry the whole load alone.

afterFigure.text: A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup, and the RTO is known only by timing one.

steps.headline: Find the availability and 30-day downtime of a 99.99% balancer, two 99% app servers in parallel and a 99.9% database, in series.

workedSteps.text: Combine the two app servers, which are in parallel, first.
Now the three stages are in series, so multiply their availabilities.
Convert to downtime over 30 days, which is 43,200 minutes.
The database is the weakest stage, so it sets most of the downtime.
workedSteps.math: the database alone allows 43.2 of the 52 minutes

steps.headline: Find the availability of a 99.9% web tier, a pair of 99.9% replicas in parallel, and a 99.9% database, all in series.

workedSteps.text: The pair in parallel fails only if both replicas fail.
The web tier, the pair and the database are now three stages in series.

reveal.text: The restore takes 16,000 seconds, about 4.4 hours, so the recovery time objective depends on how fast a restore or failover can be done. A standby takes minutes where a large restore takes hours.

lessons.orientation: Convert availability to downtime, combine components in series and parallel, and relate backups to RPO and RTO.
lessons.nextAction: Choose what to measure, define an SLO, and compute an error budget and its burn rate.

blocks.text: A service that is 99.9% available may be down for 43.2 minutes in 30 days, and one that is 99.99% available for only 4.32, so a single extra digit divides the downtime by ten. Each extra nine also costs more, and a design that cannot say how its components combine cannot say which target it can meet.

The combining is arithmetic: components that all must work multiply their availabilities and so lose ground in a chain, whereas independent replicas fail together only when all of them fail, which is why a second independent copy removes nearly all of the downtime of the first.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn an availability target into downtime, combine components in series and in parallel, and relate a backup schedule to the data that can be lost.
intro.whyItMatters: Availability targets are promises with numbers, and this arithmetic says which promises a design can keep.

recap.keyIdea: Availability is combined by multiplication in series and by multiplying failure probabilities in parallel, and shared failure domains break the independence that parallel relies on.

blocks.text: The allowed downtime is one minus the availability, times the period, so 99.9% allows 43.2 minutes in 30 days and each extra nine divides it by ten. Components in series multiply their availabilities, and independent replicas in parallel multiply their failure probabilities, so two 99% replicas give 99.99% unless they share a failure domain such as one power supply. A backup interval sets the worst-case data loss, the RPO, and recovery is real only when it has been tested.

lessons.title: Observability and SLOs

lead.text: **Logs** record individual events, such as "order 8841 failed: card declined", and are the most detailed and the hardest to search at scale. **Metrics** record numbers over time, such as requests per second or the 99th-percentile latency, and are cheap to store and quick to chart. **Traces** follow a single request across the services it touches and record how long each step took.

Each answers a different question. A metric says *that* the p99 latency has doubled, a trace says *where*, by showing which call in the chain took the time, and a log says *why*, by recording what that call reported.

afterFigure.text: A trace works because each service passes an identifier along with the request, so that the pieces recorded on different machines can be joined into one picture.

reveal.text: Metrics tell you that something is wrong, traces where, and logs why, so the three are used in that order.

lead.text: The SRE book recommends watching four signals for any service that users depend on. **Latency** is how long requests take, reported as percentiles and separately for successes and failures. **Traffic** is how much demand the service receives, such as requests per second. **Errors** are the requests that fail, whether outright or by returning a wrong answer. **Saturation** is how full the service is, the share of its most constrained resource that is in use.

afterFigure.text: Together these say how users are doing, and a figure such as the average processor use does not.

reveal.text: The fleet lesson's utilisation is the same idea: a service that is nearly full is about to slow down.
The allowed failures can be spent, and the next screen names the number and the targets that give rise to it.

lead.text: A signal becomes useful when it has a target. A **service level indicator**, or SLI, is a measurement of one aspect of the service as users see it, such as the fraction of requests that succeed. A **service level objective**, or SLO, is a target for it, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding over 30 days. A service level agreement, or SLA, is a contract with consequences if a target is missed, and it is usually looser than the internal SLO.

The SLO implies a budget. If 99.9% of requests must succeed, 0.1% may fail, and over a window with 10,000,000 requests that is 0.001 × 10,000,000 = 10,000 failed requests. This is the **error budget**, the amount of failure the target allows, and a team may spend it on releases, experiments and outages. A target of 100% would leave a budget of zero, so that no change could ever be made safely, and it could not be met anyway, since the users' own networks fail more often than that.

afterFigure.text: The budget turns an argument about reliability into a number. While there is budget left the team can ship faster, and when it is spent the team slows down and fixes reliability, which gives product and operations a shared rule.

reveal.text: At 99.99% the share that may fail is 0.01%, which is 1,000 of 10,000,000 requests. Each extra nine multiplies the allowed failures by one tenth, and usually needs another layer of redundancy, automation and testing.

lead.text: A budget is spent over time, so the useful question is how fast. The **burn rate** compares the spending so far with spending the budget evenly across the window. With a budget of 10,000 failures over 30 days, the even pace after 3 days is 10,000 × 3 ÷ 30 = 1,000. If 5,000 have failed, the burn rate is 5,000 ÷ 1,000 = 5, five times the even pace, and at that rate the whole budget would be gone after 30 ÷ 5 = 6 days instead of 30.

afterFigure.text: A burn rate of 1 uses exactly the whole budget by the end of the window, a rate below 1 leaves some spare, and a rate above 1 runs out early. Because it is a ratio, the same number means the same urgency for a service with a small budget as for one with a large budget, which is why alerts are written in burn rate and not in raw counts.

reveal.text: An even pace would spend 1/720 of the budget each hour, so 14.4 times that is 2%. Because the burn rate is a ratio, the same number means the same urgency for a small budget as for a large one.

lead.text: Alerting is where telemetry meets people, and more alerts do not mean safer operation: an engineer who is woken by alerts that need no action learns to ignore them. Alert on symptoms that users feel, such as a rising error rate, and not on causes such as a high processor figure, and page a person only when a human must act now. A very high burn rate means the budget will be gone within hours and deserves a page, while a modest one that would exhaust it over weeks can wait for a ticket.
After an incident, a **blameless postmortem** records what happened and what will change, asking what let the failure occur, and not who made it.

steps.headline: An SLO of 99.5% on 4,000,000 requests in 30 days has seen 6,000 failures after 6 days. Find the budget, the burn rate and when the budget runs out.

workedSteps.text: The share that may fail is 0.5%, so the budget is that share of the requests.
The even pace after 6 of the 30 days is the budget times 6 ÷ 30.
The burn rate is the failures so far divided by the even pace.
At this rate the budget lasts the window length divided by the burn rate.

steps.headline: Find the burn rate when 4,000 of a 6,000-failure budget are spent after 10 of 30 days.

workedSteps.text: The even pace after 10 of the 30 days is the budget times 10 ÷ 30.
The burn rate compares the failures so far with that even pace.

reveal.text: A burn rate of 14 would empty a 30-day budget in about two days and users are already being hurt, so it is a page. A modest rate that would exhaust the budget over weeks can wait for a ticket.

lessons.orientation: Choose telemetry and signals, compute an error budget from an SLO, and compute a burn rate.
lessons.nextAction: Carry a whole design from requirements to failure handling, using a number for every choice.

blocks.text: A request that takes 520 ms passes through a gateway and three services, and when it is slow the first question in an incident is which of the four held it up. If every service records when it received the request and when it replied, laying those records side by side on one time axis shows at once that 400 ms went to the payment service, whereas a system that records nothing can only guess.

Knowing where the time went is only half of operating a system. The other half is agreeing in advance how much failure is acceptable, so that a team can tell a bad day from a normal one, and that agreement takes the form of a number: a target for a measurement, and the amount of failure the target allows.

intro.promise: By the end you'll name the telemetry and signals to watch, compute an error budget from an SLO, and compute how fast a budget is being spent.
intro.whyItMatters: An SLO and its burn rate turn an argument about reliability into arithmetic that decides when to ship and when to page.

recap.keyIdea: An SLO turns a signal into a target, its error budget is the failure the target allows, and the burn rate says how fast the budget is being spent.

blocks.text: Logs, metrics and traces say why, that and where something is wrong, and the four golden signals of latency, traffic, errors and saturation say how users are doing. An SLO of 99.9% over 10,000,000 requests gives an error budget of 10,000 failures, and the burn rate compares the failures so far with an even pace, so 5,000 failures after 3 of 30 days is a burn rate of 5 and a budget gone in 6 days. Alerts should follow symptoms and burn rate, and page a person only when one must act.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson uses everything so far to design a URL shortener, with a number behind every component.

lessons.title: Design: a URL shortener

lead.text: The request is the one from the first lesson, a service that shortens links. Its *functional requirements* are two: create a short link for a long URL, and redirect a visitor who opens a short link. Its *quality targets* are that 99% of redirects complete in under 100 ms and that the service is 99.9% available, and it is to be sized for 100 million new URLs a month, with 100 redirects for each URL created, kept for five years.
It also states non-goals: links cannot be edited after they are created, and the only analytics is a count of visits.

Estimation follows the method of the second lesson. A 30-day month has 30 × 86,400 = 2,592,000 seconds, so 100 million new URLs a month is 100,000,000 ÷ 2,592,000 = 38.6 writes per second. The ratio of 100 reads for each write gives 3,858 redirects per second on average, and a peak factor of 3 raises that to about 11,600. A record, which holds a code, a URL and some metadata, takes about 500 bytes, so a month adds 100,000,000 × 500 B = 50 GB and five years hold 60 × 50 GB = 3 TB before any copies.

afterFigure.text: These numbers already rule things out. We assume that a single database node accepts at least hundreds of simple writes per second, so 38.6 writes per second does not call for sharding, and 3 TB fits on a few disks. The reads, at about 11,600 per second at peak, are the load that the design has to take seriously.

steps.headline: Estimate the load and fleet: 100 million new URLs a month, 100 reads per write, peak factor 3, 2,000 redirects per second per server.

workedSteps.text: Turn the monthly writes into a rate by dividing by the seconds in the month.
The ratio of 100 reads to 1 write multiplies the write rate to give the read rate.
Multiply by the peak factor to get the load the fleet must meet.
Plan each server for 70% of the assumed 2,000 per second, divide, and round up.

reveal.text: 10,000,000 ÷ 2,592,000 is about 3.9 writes per second, and 200 reads for each write gives about 770 reads per second. No number here asks for shards or a queue.

lead.text: Each short link needs a code, and the code is the key of the table. Using the 62 characters a to z, A to Z and 0 to 9, a code of length k has 62^k possibilities: 62^6 = 56,800,235,584 and 62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208. Five years of 100 million new URLs a month is 100,000,000 × 12 × 5 = 6,000,000,000 codes. Six characters would hold them, but seven leave 3,521,614,606,208 ÷ 6,000,000,000 ≈ 587 times more room than is needed.

Why room matters depends on how the codes are made. Encoding a counter in base 62 gives each URL the next unused code, so there are no collisions, but the codes can be guessed in sequence and the counter has to be shared by every app server; handing each server a block of 1,000 codes at a time avoids a trip to the counter for each URL. Choosing codes at random hides the order but needs a collision check, and the chance that a random code is already taken equals the share of the space in use: with 7 characters and 6 billion in use it is 0.17%, whereas with 6 characters it would be 10.6%.

afterFigure.text: The length therefore follows from the retention number, as the estimate said.

reveal.text: Six characters would be 10.6% full by the end and seven only 0.17%, about 1 in 587. Both hold the links, so the choice is about how often a new code has to be drawn again.

lead.text: A redirect is a lookup by key, the simplest access pattern, so the store is a table keyed by short code, with no joins or ranges. A request passes through a load balancer to a stateless fleet of 9 app servers, and each looks in a cache first, as in cache-aside. Links rarely change and some are opened far more often than others, so the hit rate is high: at 95%, only 5% of 3,858 reads, about 193 per second, reach the database, and about 579 at peak.
The database is replicated. A leader takes the 38.6 writes per second, followers serve the reads that miss the cache, and they sit in different failure domains.

afterFigure.text: There is no queue and no shard, because no number in the estimate asks for either.

The redirect view highlights the path through the cache to the followers at 193 reads per second. The create view highlights the ID block and the leader at 38.6 writes per second. The cache-down view shows all 3,858 reads per second reaching the store.

reveal.text: At a 95% hit rate, 5% of 3,858 is about 193 reads per second, well inside the 400 the database is sized for. Without the cache it would need to take all 3,858.

lead.text: Failure comes next, one component at a time. If an app server fails, the balancer's health check removes it and the other eight carry on, since 9 were sized with margin. If a follower fails, reads go to the others. If the cache fails, every read becomes a miss, and the database receives 3,858 reads per second instead of 193, twenty times as many, which the replicas must be sized to survive or the app must shed load. If the leader fails, a follower is promoted and writes pause for the time that takes, and the clients retry with backoff and an idempotency key so that a retry does not create two codes.

The 99.9% target allows 43.2 minutes of downtime in 30 days. Counted in requests, it gives an error budget of 0.1% of the 10,000,000,000 redirects a month, which is 10,000,000 failed redirects. The signals to watch are the p99 latency against the 100 ms target, the redirect rate, the error rate, and the cache hit rate and database load as signs of saturation.

reveal.text: The pause touches link creation only, so it is spent against the creation target. The 99.9% target for redirects allows 43.2 minutes of downtime in 30 days, which an outage of the read path would use up.

lead.text: One more choice looks small and is not. The server answers an open link with a redirect, and the status code says what kind. A 301 means *moved permanently*, and browsers may cache it, so a repeat visit from the same browser can go straight to the long URL without asking the service. A 302 means *found*, a temporary redirect that is normally not cached, so every visit reaches the service. If the service wants to count every visit, as its requirements allowed, it must use 302, at the cost of serving that traffic; a 301 saves the traffic and cannot be counted.

afterFigure.text: The choice trades the load that the estimates predicted against a feature. With 302 the 3,858 reads per second include every visit, and with 301 some repeat visits would never arrive and the real rate would be lower than the estimate.

reveal.text: Visit counting and traffic saving pull in opposite directions here, so the requirement decides.

Each number in the chain depends on the one before, so a hundredfold more URLs a month makes a hundredfold more writes, reads and servers, unless the assumptions change. Redoing the estimate from the top is the quickest way to find out which parts of the design still hold.

lessons.orientation: Carry a link shortener from requirements to failure handling, with a number behind each choice.
lessons.nextAction: Compare two ways to build a feed, then review a flawed design for what fails first.

blocks.text: A link shortener that gains a hundred million new links a month is writing 38.6 links per second, and at 100 redirects for every link created it handles 3,858 redirects per second, while five years of records come to 3 TB. Those figures say at once that the writes are small, that the reads are the load to worry about, and that a seven-character code leaves a wide margin, and that is enough to shape most of the design.
What remains is to ask, for each component, which number or requirement calls for it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll carry one design from requirements through estimates, identifiers, storage and caching to failure, and justify each component with a number.
intro.whyItMatters: A design that traces each choice to a number can be defended in review and changed safely when the numbers change.

recap.keyIdea: Every component in a design should trace back to a requirement or an estimate, and the read rate and the retention decide most of it.

blocks.text: The shortener's requirements give 38.6 writes and about 3,900 redirects per second on average, 50 GB a month, and a 62^7 code space of 3.5 trillion for 6 billion links. A cache and a replicated table serve the reads, so that about 193 per second reach the database at a 95% hit rate, and the failure of the cache is the case to plan for, since it multiplies that load by twenty. The redirect status is a choice between traffic and counting visits, and no number justified a queue or a shard.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson compares fan-out on write and on read for a social feed, and ends by reviewing a flawed design for what fails first.

lessons.title: Design: a feed, and a design review

lead.text: A social feed shows each user the recent posts of the accounts they follow. It is read far more often than it is written, since a post is made once and viewed by many, and the design question is where to do the work of assembling a feed: when a post is made, or when a feed is opened. In **fan-out on write**, a new post is copied into the feed of every follower, so a feed is a ready-made list and opening it is a single read. The cost moves to the write: an account with 200 followers that posts 5 times a day causes 200 × 5 = 1,000 feed writes a day.

afterFigure.text: Writes of this kind can be queued and done in the background, since a follower need not see a post in the same second, as in the queue lesson.

diagram.alt: A poster on the left and five boxes standing for many on the right. With fan-out on write, one post from an account with 200 followers becomes 200 feed writes, and from one with 20 million followers 20,000,000 writes. With fan-out on read, one feed view becomes 200 lookups, one for each account followed.

reveal.text: Fan-out on write costs 5 × 200 = 1,000 feed writes plus 10 feed reads, 1,010 in all. Fan-out on read costs 5 post writes plus 10 × 200 = 2,000 lookups, 2,005 in all.

lead.text: The opposite choice is **fan-out on read**. A post is stored once, with its author, and nothing is copied. When a user opens the feed, the service looks up the recent posts of each account that user follows and merges them by time. Writes are now cheap, one per post, but each feed view costs a lookup for every account followed: a user who follows 200 accounts costs 200 lookups for each view, against the single read of fan-out on write.

Put numbers on a platform of 10,000,000 users who each follow 200 accounts, post 5 times a day and open their feed 10 times a day. Fan-out on write makes 10,000,000 × 5 × 200 = 10,000,000,000 feed writes a day, about 115,700 per second, and 100,000,000 feed reads, about 1,160 per second. Fan-out on read makes 50,000,000 post writes, under 600 per second, and 100,000,000 views × 200 = 20,000,000,000 lookups a day, about 231,500 per second.

afterFigure.text: Neither is simply better. Fan-out on write pays when a post is made so that reads are cheap, and suits a platform where feeds are read often. The totals are comparable here, and the difference is in where the work falls and when.

reveal.text: Only the author is sure to notice the gap, since followers do not know the post exists. Merging the author's own recent posts into the feed at read time gives read-your-writes at almost no cost.
That is a little over three minutes, which is tolerable for one post, but a stream of such posts would build a queue that never drains.

lead.text: The averages hide the case that breaks fan-out on write. An account with 20,000,000 followers that posts once causes 20,000,000 feed writes, and at 100,000 writes per second that takes 20,000,000 ÷ 100,000 = 200 seconds, during which the queue of fan-out work grows and ordinary posts wait behind it.

The usual answer is a **hybrid**. Posts from ordinary accounts are fanned out on write, since 200 writes are cheap, and posts from accounts with very large followings are not copied at all: they are fetched at read time and merged into the precomputed feed. A user who follows 300 accounts, 5 of them very large, then costs 1 read for the precomputed feed and 5 lookups for the large accounts, 6 in all, where fan-out on read would cost 300.

afterFigure.text: The threshold for "very large" is a number to be chosen from the estimates, for instance the follower count at which writing a post to every feed costs more than fetching it for the few who open the feed. The hybrid is more code than either strategy alone, and that is the price of having no case that breaks.

reveal.text: The cost of a view is now tied to the number of very large accounts a user follows, which is small.

lead.text: A review asks questions about failure, and three do most of the work. *What is the single point of failure?* Every component that has nothing to take over from it is one. *What is unbounded?* A queue, a timeout, a retry count or a request rate with no limit will in time be exceeded. *What is unmeasured?* A number that nobody has estimated, or a signal that nobody watches, is a place where the design is a guess.

Take a design that looks ordinary: users reach ten web servers, which read and write one database, and sign-up requests call an email provider while the user waits. The figure's second view marks what a review finds. The database has one copy, so it is a **single point of failure**. The email call has no timeout, so a slow provider ties up web-server threads, as in the timeouts lesson. Callers have no limits, and no metric or alert would show any of this happening.

diagram.alt: A design with users, ten web servers, a single database and an email provider that the web servers call while the user waits. A second view marks the flaws: the database has one copy, the email call has no timeout, callers have no limits, and nothing is measured.

reveal.text: The review question is what happens if this component fails, and whether another can take over.

steps.headline: Ten web servers have 50 threads each, and 10% of 200 requests per second call an email provider with no timeout. Find how long the site lasts.

workedSteps.text: Count the threads that are available, which is every server's pool added together.
Each call that hangs holds a thread for ever, so the rate of hanging calls is the rate at which threads are lost.
Divide the threads by the rate at which they are lost.
After 25 seconds there is no thread left for any request, including those that never use email.

steps.headline: Find how long 20 servers of 30 threads last at 500 requests per second, with 10% hanging on an email call.

workedSteps.text: Count the whole pool and the threads lost each second.
The pool is used up at that steady rate.

reveal.text: A timeout of 2 seconds with 20 hanging calls per second holds 20 × 2 = 40 threads by Little's law, instead of all of them. Moving the email onto a queue takes even those off the sign-up path.

lead.text: A design is finished when its trade-offs are stated, and not when it has no faults. For the feed, fan-out on write was accepted for ordinary accounts, at the cost of a short delay before a post reaches every follower. The hybrid was accepted at the cost of a second code path. Eventual consistency of feeds was accepted because a post that arrives a minute late harms nobody.
Every component in the design should be there because a number put it there.

lessons.orientation: Compare feed strategies by their write and read costs, and review a design for what fails first.
lessons.reviewLabel: Design: a feed, and a design review
lessons.nextAction: Run the whole method on a new system: state the requirements, estimate the load, justify each component with a number, and probe it for failure.

blocks.text: An account with 200 followers that posts five times a day causes 1,000 feed writes a day when each post is copied into every follower's feed, which is nothing. An account with 20,000,000 followers causes 20,000,000 writes with a single post, so the same strategy that is trivial for the first account is a storm for the second.
Whether the work of building a feed should be done when a post is made or when a feed is opened turns on how often each happens, and a platform with both kinds of account has to choose with numbers.

intro.promise: By the end you'll compare fan-out on write, fan-out on read and a hybrid with numbers, and review a flawed design by asking what fails first.
intro.whyItMatters: Feeds and reviews are where the earlier lessons meet, since each choice is a trade-off that numbers can settle.

recap.keyIdea: A feed can do its work on write or on read, a hybrid avoids the case that breaks each, and a review asks what fails first.

blocks.text: Fan-out on write copies each post into every follower's feed, so reads are cheap and a post by an account with 20,000,000 followers means 20,000,000 writes, while fan-out on read stores a post once and costs a lookup for every account followed at each view. A hybrid fans out ordinary accounts on write and fetches very large ones on read, so a view costs about 4 reads and lookups instead of 200. A review asks about the single point of failure, what is unbounded and what is unmeasured, and the missing timeout on a synchronous call shows how fast an unbounded call can take a site down.

questions.prompt: A link shortener receives 10 new links per second, and every link that is created is opened about 100 times. Which part of the service carries most of the load?
hints: Compare how many times a link is created with how many times it is opened.
Ask how many times each link is opened for every time it is created.

acceptedIdeas: Opening links, because there are far more opens than creations
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Opening links, because there are far more opens than creations

choices.label: Both about equally, because every link is created once and used afterwards
Creating links, because each one has to be stored safely
Opening links, because there are far more opens than creations

questions.onCorrect: At about 100 opens for each creation, the opens outnumber the creations a hundred to one, so most of the load comes from reading.

misconceptions.feedback: Creating a link is a single write, and only 10 happen each second, whereas each link is opened about 100 times, so about 1,000 opens arrive in the same second.
A link is created once but opened about 100 times, so the opens outnumber the creations a hundred to one and the two sides are far from equal.

questions.prompt: A service has 12 writes per second and 150 reads for each write. What is the read rate, in reads per second?
hints: The ratio gives the reads per write.
Multiply the write rate by the reads per write.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each write brings 150 reads, so the read rate is 12 × 150 = 1,800 per second.

questions.onCorrect: With 1,800 reads against 12 writes, the writes are under 1% of the 1,812 requests per second.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 12 and 150. The rates multiply, because each write brings 150 reads.
That is the write rate, which the question gives. Each write brings 150 reads.
That is the total of reads and writes. The question asks only for the reads.

questions.prompt: A colleague opens a design review by drawing a cache and a message queue in front of the shortener, before anyone has stated a read/write ratio. Which step of the method was skipped?
hints: Ask which step supplies the number that justifies a component.
A cache helps when reads dominate, so something has to be measured first.

acceptedIdeas: Estimating the load, because the load says whether a component is needed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Estimating the load, because the load says whether a component is needed

choices.label: Estimating the load, because the load says whether a component is needed
Probing failures, because every component can fail and should be checked first
Defining the interface, because components need names for their calls
Choosing a database, because storage always comes first in a design

questions.onCorrect: The load estimate is what justifies a component. Without it, the cache and the queue are guesses that may add cost and failure points for nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: Probing comes last, after a sketch exists. The problem here is that the sketch was drawn with nothing to justify it.
The interface does matter, but it does not say whether a cache or a queue is needed. The load does.
No step of the method starts from a technology. Requirements and load choose the technology, not the other way round.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing service sees 3,000 reads per second at a ratio of 150 reads for each write. Its write path, a single database leader, is sized for 25 writes per second. How many writes per second does the service receive?
hints: Here the read rate is known and the write rate is not.
Each write accounts for 150 of the reads.
Divide the read rate by the reads per write.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3,000 ÷ 150 = 20 writes per second, under the 25 that the leader is sized for.

questions.onCorrect: The service receives 20 writes per second, so the leader has 5 per second to spare. Dividing by the ratio recovers the smaller rate, which is the one that decides what the write path must carry.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies, as if the 3,000 were the write rate. The 3,000 is already the reads, so the writes are fewer, not more.
That is the ratio itself. It says how many reads each write brings, not how many writes there are.
That is the read rate, which the question gives.
That is what the write path is sized for. The question asks what actually arrives.

questions.prompt: Each of these services has a stated pattern of reads and writes. Which are read-heavy, and which are write-heavy?
hints: Compare how often each item is read with how often it is written.
Ask whether the work that grows with traffic is looking something up or storing something new.

items.label: A link shortener where each link is opened 100 times for every link created
items.explanation: The same answers are requested again and again, so copies close to the reader pay off.

items.label: A news site where about 2,000 readers open each article the newsroom publishes
items.explanation: One write is followed by thousands of reads.

items.label: A product catalogue that is edited once a week and browsed all day
items.explanation: Changes are rare and lookups are constant.

items.label: A fleet of 50,000 sensors that each upload a reading every second, with an engineer opening a dashboard a few times a day
items.explanation: Nearly every request stores something new, and almost none reads it back.

items.label: A logging service that stores every line from 300 servers and is searched only during incidents
items.explanation: Storing every line safely and in order is the cost that limits it.

items.label: A metrics store that takes a data point from every machine every 10 seconds and is read by a handful of dashboards
items.explanation: Writes arrive continuously and the reads are few.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The link shortener, the news site and the catalogue are read-heavy; the sensor fleet, the logging service and the metrics store are write-heavy.

questions.onCorrect: Where reads dominate, keeping copies of answers close to the reader pays off, and where writes dominate, the cost of storing every item safely is what limits the system.

questions.prompt: A product manager says a new feature will have 4 million daily users who each make 30 requests a day, and asks how many servers to book. You first need the average load. Which is closest to the requests per second?
hints: First find the requests in a whole day, then divide by the seconds over which they arrive.
Check the unit of the total: it is a count per day.

acceptedIdeas: About 1,400 per second, after dividing the daily total by the seconds in a day
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 1,400 per second, after dividing the daily total by the seconds in a day

choices.label: About 33,000 per second, after dividing the daily total by the seconds in an hour
About 46 per second, after dividing the daily total by the seconds in a month
About 1,400 per second, after dividing the daily total by the seconds in a day

questions.onCorrect: The total is 4,000,000 × 30 = 120,000,000 requests a day, and dividing by 86,400 seconds gives about 1,390 per second, which the design then multiplies by a peak factor.

misconceptions.feedback: An hour has 3,600 seconds, but the 120 million requests arrive over a whole day, so dividing by 3,600 overstates the rate 24 times.
A month has about 2.6 million seconds, but the 120 million requests are a day's worth, so dividing by the seconds in a month understates the rate 30 times.

questions.prompt: A team sizes a fleet for the average load of 1,400 requests per second, planning each server at 70% utilisation. Every evening the service slows down and some requests time out, though no server has failed. What is the most likely cause?
hints: The slowdown comes at the same time every day, and no server has failed.
Ask what number the fleet was sized for, and what the busiest hour carries.

acceptedIdeas: Evening traffic is a multiple of the average, so the fleet is overloaded each day
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Evening traffic is a multiple of the average, so the fleet is overloaded each day

choices.label: Evening traffic is a multiple of the average, so the fleet is overloaded each day
The average was worked out wrongly, since averages cannot be used to size a service
Servers slow down in the evening because they have been running all day long
The load balancer cannot spread more than 1,400 requests per second at any time

questions.onCorrect: A peak factor of 2 to 3 would have set the target at 2,800 to 4,200 requests per second, which is the load the servers have to meet.

misconceptions.feedback: The average is the right input for daily totals such as storage and cost. The fleet is sized from the peak, so the average has to be multiplied by a peak factor first.
Nothing in the scenario points at the servers wearing down. A fleet sized for the average slows in the busiest hours with no fault at all.
No balancer limit is mentioned, and a slowdown at the same time every day points at the daily peak, which the fleet was never sized for.

questions.prompt: A service adds 100 million new records a month, and each record takes 500 bytes. Which is closest to the storage it adds each month?
hints: Multiply the number of records by the bytes in each to get a number of bytes, then ask which unit that many bytes fills.
A gigabyte is a billion bytes.

acceptedIdeas: About 50 GB
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 50 GB

choices.label: About 50 GB
About 50 MB
About 5 GB
About 5 TB

questions.onCorrect: 100 million records of 500 bytes come to 50 billion bytes, which is 50 GB.

misconceptions.feedback: A megabyte is a million bytes, so 50 MB would hold only 100,000 records of 500 bytes, a thousandth of the 100 million that arrive.
5 GB would hold 10 million records of 500 bytes, a tenth of the 100 million that arrive each month.
5 TB would hold 10 billion records of 500 bytes, a hundred times the 100 million that arrive each month.

questions.prompt: The estimate says 80 GB are added each month. How many gigabytes does that make over 12 months of retention?
hints: Retention is how long the data is kept.
Twelve months each add the same amount.
Multiply 80 by 12.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 months × 80 GB per month = 960 GB.

questions.onCorrect: Retention multiplies the monthly figure, so keeping a year of data needs twelve times the monthly storage.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 12 to 80. Each month adds its own 80 GB, so the total is the monthly amount times 12.
That is a single month. A year of retention holds twelve of them.

questions.prompt: How many terabytes does the service hold in all? Use 1 TB = 1,000,000,000,000 bytes.
hints: Find the bytes added in one day.
A day adds 2,000,000,000 bytes, which is 2 GB, and the retention is 365 × 5 days.
Multiply the daily bytes by the number of days, then divide by 10^12.
questions.onCorrect: A daily 2 GB over 1,825 days is 3,650 GB, so a few terabytes, which fits on one large disk.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the figure in gigabytes. The question asks for terabytes, so divide by 1,000.
That uses one year of retention. The service keeps its records for five.
That is the daily amount in gigabytes. The retention of 1,825 days has not been applied.

questions.prompt: A vendor lists a network link as 10 Gbit/s. A teammate plans on it carrying 10 GB of responses every second. Which statement is right?
hints: The rating counts bits, and the plan counts bytes.
Divide the bits per second by the 8 bits in a byte.

acceptedIdeas: The link carries at most about 1.25 GB per second, as each byte is 8 bits
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The link carries at most about 1.25 GB per second, as each byte is 8 bits

choices.label: The plan holds, because 10 Gbit/s is just another way of writing 10 GB/s
The link carries at most about 1.25 GB per second, as each byte is 8 bits
The link carries about 80 GB per second, because each byte is 8 bits long
The link carries about 125 MB per second, which is its real top speed

questions.onCorrect: 10,000,000,000 bits ÷ 8 is 1,250,000,000 bytes per second, and a real link carries somewhat less once protocol overhead is counted.

misconceptions.feedback: A gigabit is an eighth of a gigabyte. Network speeds count bits and file sizes count bytes, so the two numbers differ by a factor of 8.
Converting bits to bytes divides by 8 and does not multiply. Multiplying overstates the capacity 64 times.
125 MB per second is the capacity of a 1 Gbit/s link, and this link is ten times faster.

questions.prompt: One machine has a 1 Gbit/s link, which is 125 MB/s, and can process 5,000 requests per second. A service must send 3,000 responses per second of 60,000 bytes each. Which resource runs out first?
hints: Work out the bytes per second that the responses need, then compare with 125 MB/s.
Compare the request rate with the 5,000 per second that the machine can process.

acceptedIdeas: The network, because the responses need more than the link can carry
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The network, because the responses need more than the link can carry

choices.label: Neither, because the machine can process more than 3,000 requests per second
Processing, because 3,000 requests per second is a high rate
The network, because the responses need more than the link can carry

questions.onCorrect: Processing has headroom, at 3,000 of 5,000 requests per second, whereas the link cannot carry what the responses need.

misconceptions.feedback: 3,000 requests per second is below the 5,000 that the machine can process, so processing still has headroom.
Processing is within its limit, but the responses add up to 3,000 × 60,000 bytes, or 180 MB per second, which is more than the 125 MB per second that the link carries.

questions.prompt: A team estimates storage for 30 million new records a month at 2,000 bytes each, kept for 3 years, with three copies of everything for durability. Use 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes. Which estimate should they book disks for?
hints: A month adds 30,000,000 × 2,000 bytes. Convert that to gigabytes before multiplying by the months.
Retention is 36 months, and each record is stored three times.

acceptedIdeas: About 6.5 TB, from three years of records at 2.2 TB, tripled for the copies
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 6.5 TB, from three years of records at 2.2 TB, tripled for the copies

choices.label: About 2.2 TB, from three years of records, because the copies are the database's concern
About 6.5 TB, from three years of records at 2.2 TB, tripled for the copies
About 2.2 TB, from one year of records held in three copies

questions.onCorrect: A month adds 60 GB, 36 months add 2,160 GB, and three copies make 6.48 TB, so the disks are booked for about 6.5 TB and not for the 2.2 TB of records alone.

misconceptions.feedback: The copies occupy disk too. An estimate shows what has to be bought, which is three times the 2.16 TB of records.
Three years is 36 months, not 12. A year of records in three copies comes to 2.16 TB, the same figure by coincidence, and the retention is the longer one.

questions.prompt: A service sends 600 responses per second of 150,000 bytes each over one 1 Gbit/s link, which carries 125 MB per second. A teammate says the link is fine because the traffic is 90 MB per second. What have they left out?
hints: The 90 MB per second is the average, and the link has to carry the busiest moment.
Apply a peak factor of 2 and compare with 125 MB per second.

acceptedIdeas: The peak: a peak factor of 2 takes 90 MB per second to 180, over the link's 125
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The peak: a peak factor of 2 takes 90 MB per second to 180, over the link's 125

choices.label: Nothing, because 90 MB per second is below 125, so the link is fine at every load
The factor of 8, because 90 MB per second is really 720 Gbit/s and cannot fit
The peak: a peak factor of 2 takes 90 MB per second to 180, over the link's 125

questions.onCorrect: At the average the link has 35 MB per second to spare, but at twice that it is 55 MB per second short, so the network runs out before anything else does.

misconceptions.feedback: That compares the average with the link's limit. The link has to carry the peak, and a peak factor of 2 would take the traffic to 180 MB per second.
The conversion gives 720 Mbit/s, which is 0.72 Gbit/s, so the average does fit. The unit slip is the other way: the missing step is the peak.

questions.prompt: In 100 requests, 98 took 10 ms and 2 took 1,000 ms. Which is closest to the mean latency?
hints: Add up the time taken by all 100 requests, then divide by 100.
Ask how far two very slow requests can pull an average over 100 requests.

acceptedIdeas: About 30 ms, above a typical request but far below the slow ones
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 30 ms, above a typical request but far below the slow ones

choices.label: About 500 ms, halfway between the two groups of requests
About 30 ms, above a typical request but far below the slow ones
About 10 ms, since 98 of the 100 requests took that long to finish
About 1,000 ms, since the slow requests dominate the whole sample

questions.onCorrect: The two slow requests add about 20 ms to the average of the fast ones, which gives 29.8 ms, a figure that matches no request in the sample.

misconceptions.feedback: The two slow requests add 2 × 990 = 1,980 ms beyond the 10 ms of the others, and spread over 100 requests that raises the mean by about 20 ms.
A mean of 500 ms would need about half of the requests to be slow, and only 2 in 100 are.
A mean near 1,000 ms would need almost every request to be slow, and 98 of the 100 took 10 ms.

questions.prompt: A checkout service has a target of p99 under 200 ms. In the last hour 98% of requests took 20 ms and 2% took 900 ms, which makes the mean about 38 ms. The dashboard shows only the mean, and the team says the target is met. Is it?
hints: Sort the requests and find which group holds the 99th position out of 100.
A mean is pulled toward the slow group, but it equals no request.

acceptedIdeas: No, because the slowest 2% take 900 ms and the p99 falls among them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because the slowest 2% take 900 ms and the p99 falls among them

choices.label: Yes, because the mean of 38 ms is far below the 200 ms target for p99
No, because the slowest 2% take 900 ms and the p99 falls among them
Yes, because 98% of requests were fast and only a few were slow
No, because the mean has to equal the p99 for a target to be met

questions.onCorrect: The p99 here is 900 ms, four and a half times the target, while the mean looks healthy at 38 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: The two slow requests in every hundred lift the mean by only about 18 ms, and it matches no request that a user saw. A target stated as p99 has to be checked against the p99.
Two in every hundred are slow, and the p99 is the value that 99% of requests beat. Positions 99 and 100 in the sorted list are both slow, so the p99 is 900 ms.
A mean and a p99 describe different things and are rarely equal, and nothing requires them to match. The target concerns the p99 alone.

questions.prompt: A service receives 400 requests per second, and each normally takes 50 ms. Its dependency slows down, and each request now stays 250 ms. The service has a pool of 80 worker threads, and every request holds one thread. How many requests are in the service on average once the slowdown has settled?
hints: Little's law says that the average number in the system is the arrival rate times the time each request stays.
Keep the units consistent: 250 ms is 0.25 seconds.
Multiply 400 by 0.25.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 400 × 0.25 = 100 requests in the service, more than the 80 threads.

questions.onCorrect: At 100 requests in flight against 80 threads the pool is used up, so requests queue and the slowdown spreads. Before it the figure was 400 × 0.05 = 20, a quarter of the pool.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number in flight before the slowdown, 400 × 0.05. The question asks for the number after each request has slowed to 250 ms.
That is the size of the pool, not the demand on it. The demand is the arrival rate times the time spent.
That multiplies by 250 and leaves the time in milliseconds. A rate per second needs a time in seconds.

questions.prompt: A request must wait for 100 backends, called in parallel. Each backend is slow 1% of the time, independently of the others. Roughly how often is the whole request slow?
hints: The request is fast only if every one of the 100 backends is fast.
Chances that must all hold multiply, and they do not add.

acceptedIdeas: Well over half of the requests
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Well over half of the requests

choices.label: About 10%, one request in ten
About 1%, the same as for a single backend
Nearly every request, because 100 chances of 1% add up to 100%
Well over half of the requests

questions.onCorrect: The request is fast only when all 100 backends are, which happens about 37% of the time, so it is slow about 63% of the time.

misconceptions.feedback: A single backend is slow 1% of the time, but this request has 100 chances to meet a slow one, and any one of them makes the whole request slow.
That is close to the answer for 10 backends. With 100 backends the chance of meeting at least one slow call is far higher.
The 100 chances overlap, because one request can meet several slow backends at once, and the overlap is counted only once, so the total stays below 100%.

questions.prompt: A request waits for 20 backends, each slow 1% of the time, independently. To the nearest percent, how often is the whole request slow?
hints: Work out the chance that all 20 are fast first.
Raise 0.99 to the power 20, which is 0.99 multiplied by itself 20 times.
Subtract that from 1 and write it as a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0.99^20 ≈ 0.818 is the chance that all are fast, so the request is slow 1 − 0.818 = 0.182, about 18%.

questions.onCorrect: Twenty backends make slow requests 18 times as common as a single backend does.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share of requests in which all 20 backends are fast. The question asks for the share that are slow.
That adds 1% twenty times. Chances do not add, because one request can have several slow calls.
That is the chance for a single backend.

questions.prompt: A service takes 30 ms per request and has 20 worker threads. Arrivals rise from 250 to 500 requests per second, and the time per request does not change. What happens?
hints: Little's law: the number in flight is the arrival rate times the time each request stays.
Work out the count at 250 per second and at 500 per second, with the time in seconds.

acceptedIdeas: The number in flight doubles from 7.5 to 15, which leaves the pool three quarters full
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The number in flight doubles from 7.5 to 15, which leaves the pool three quarters full

choices.label: Nothing changes, because each request still takes 30 ms and the pool is large enough
Latency doubles to 60 ms, because twice as many requests arrive each second at the service
The number in flight stays near 8, because the threads cap the throughput of the service
The number in flight doubles from 7.5 to 15, which leaves the pool three quarters full

questions.onCorrect: The count follows the arrival rate as well as the time, so doubling the arrivals doubles it even when each request is as fast as before.

misconceptions.feedback: The time per request is unchanged, but the number inside the service is the arrival rate times that time, so it doubles.
The question says the time per request is unchanged. Little's law ties the count to the rate and the time, and it does not slow each request.
Twenty threads could hold up to 20 requests, so a cap matters only above that. The count follows the arrival rate, and it is 15 here.

questions.prompt: A search page waits for 30 backends in parallel, and each backend is slow 1% of the time, independently of the others, so about 26% of pages are slow. The team can either cut the page down to 10 backends, or make each backend slow only 0.1% of the time. Which lowers the share of slow pages more?
hints: Use 1 − (1 − p)^n for each plan, with p as the chance that one backend is slow.
Compare the two results, not the changes made.

acceptedIdeas: Making each backend slow only 0.1% of the time, which brings slow pages to about 3%
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Making each backend slow only 0.1% of the time, which brings slow pages to about 3%

choices.label: Cutting to 10 backends, which brings slow pages down to about 10% of all pages
Both lower it by the same amount, because each removes a share of the risk
Making each backend slow only 0.1% of the time, which brings slow pages to about 3%
Neither helps, because a page is only as fast as its slowest backend, whatever is done

questions.onCorrect: Both numbers in 1 − (1 − p)^n can be reduced. Here a tenfold rarer slow call gives about 3%, against about 10% for a third of the backends.

misconceptions.feedback: Ten backends at 1% give 1 − 0.99^10, about 9.6%. That helps, and the tenfold rarer slow call gives a smaller share still.
The two are not equal: 1 − 0.99^10 is about 9.6%, and 1 − 0.999^30 is about 3.0%.
The formula 1 − (1 − p)^n shows two numbers that can be reduced, and each one lowers the result.

questions.prompt: A service's latency has stayed flat at 40 ms, yet the number of requests inside it at any moment has doubled since yesterday. What is the most likely explanation?
hints: Little's law: the count in the system is the arrival rate times the time each request spends there.
One of the two factors is unchanged, so the other one explains the change.

acceptedIdeas: Traffic has about doubled, since the count is the arrival rate times the time spent
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Traffic has about doubled, since the count is the arrival rate times the time spent

choices.label: Each request now takes twice as long, which is how the count in the system doubles again
Throughput has fallen, so requests are now waiting in a queue inside the service for longer
The p99 has doubled, and that raises the count of requests
Traffic has about doubled, since the count is the arrival rate times the time spent

questions.onCorrect: With the time per request unchanged, only a higher arrival rate can double the count, and that is a traffic change worth checking before touching the service.

misconceptions.feedback: That would double the count, but the latency has stayed at 40 ms. The other factor in Little's law must have changed.
Waiting in a queue would show up as longer latency, and the latency is flat.
A p99 describes the slow tail; the count is the arrival rate times the average time, and the average has not moved.

questions.prompt: The chance that all 5 backends are fast is about 0.951. As a decimal, what is the chance that at least one of them is slow?
hints: Either every backend is fast or at least one is slow, and nothing else.
The two chances add up to 1.
Subtract 0.951 from 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two events cover every case between them, so the chances sum to 1, and the answer is 1 − 0.951 = 0.049.

questions.onCorrect: The two events leave no other case, so subtracting from 1 turns the chance that all are fast into the chance that the request is slow.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance that all 5 are fast. The question asks for the opposite event.
That is the chance for one backend. The request has five chances to meet a slow one.

questions.prompt: A balancer spreads a peak of 2,400 requests per second over 6 servers that each saturate at 500 requests per second. One server fails its health check and is removed. At what percentage utilisation does each remaining server run?
hints: The load is shared by the servers that are left.
Five servers remain.
Divide 2,400 by 5, then divide by 500.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2,400 ÷ 5 = 480 requests per second each, and 480 ÷ 500 = 96%.

questions.onCorrect: Each survivor carries 480 of its 500 requests per second, which is 96%, and the mean time in the system is then 1 ÷ (500 − 480) = 50 ms, against 10 ms at the 80% the fleet ran at before.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the utilisation before the failure, 2,400 ÷ 6 ÷ 500. The question asks for the survivors.
That is the load on each survivor in requests per second. The question asks for the percentage of its capacity.
That is the load on each server before the failure, in requests per second.

questions.prompt: A server that handles 100 requests per second has a mean time in the system of 20 ms when 50 requests arrive each second. When 90 requests arrive each second, what is the mean time likely to be?
hints: Think about what happens to a request that arrives while the server is still busy with the ones before it.
Use 1 ÷ (service rate − arrival rate) at both loads and compare.

acceptedIdeas: Several times longer, 80 ms or more
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Several times longer, 80 ms or more

choices.label: A little longer, under 40 ms, in proportion to the load
Several times longer, 80 ms or more
About the same, near 20 ms

questions.onCorrect: With little room left at 90 requests per second, requests queue behind one another, and the delay grows much faster than the load.

misconceptions.feedback: The server is no slower, but at 90 arrivals per second a request often finds others already being served and must wait for them, so the delay cannot stay at 20 ms.
In proportion to the load, 90 arrivals instead of 50 would give about 36 ms. The delay grows faster than the load, because less room is left for bursts, and it reaches 100 ms.

questions.prompt: A server handles 100 requests per second, and 90 arrive each second, which gives a mean time in the system of 100 ms. To save money a team moves the service onto fewer servers so that 95 arrive each second, 'only 5% more load'. Using 1 ÷ (service rate − arrival rate), what happens to the mean time in the system?
hints: Work out 1 ÷ (100 − 90) and 1 ÷ (100 − 95), in seconds.
Compare the two denominators.

acceptedIdeas: It doubles, from 100 ms to 200 ms
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It doubles, from 100 ms to 200 ms

choices.label: It rises by about 5%, in line with the extra load
