It doubles, from 100 ms to 200 ms
It rises by about 50%, to 150 ms
It stays the same, because the server is still below 100 requests per second

questions.onCorrect: A server at 95% utilisation has twice the delay of one at 90%, which is why a small rise in load near the limit costs so much.

misconceptions.feedback: Delay does not rise in proportion to load. The denominator falls from 10 to 5, so the delay doubles.
At 95 per second the denominator is 100 − 95 = 5, and 1 ÷ 5 is 200 ms, not 150 ms.
Being below the limit does not hold the delay constant. It grows without bound as the arrivals approach the service rate.

questions.prompt: Why is the fleet size of 17.14 servers rounded up to 18 and not down to 17?
hints: Share the 6,000 requests per second over 17 servers and compare with the planned 350.
Ask which limit is crossed: the capacity of 500, or the plan.

acceptedIdeas: With 17 servers each would run at about 70.6%, above the 70% planned
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With 17 servers each would run at about 70.6%, above the 70% planned

choices.label: With 17 servers each one would pass the 500 requests per second it can handle
With 17 servers each would run at about 70.6%, above the 70% planned
The extra server is the spare that covers the failure of one server

questions.onCorrect: Servers come whole, and rounding down would run each above the plan, which on the steep part of the delay curve is not free.

misconceptions.feedback: Seventeen servers would carry about 353 requests per second each, well under the 500 they can handle. What they would pass is the 70% in the plan.
The extra server comes from rounding. Spare capacity for a failure is a separate decision, with its own calculation.

questions.prompt: How many servers do you need, rounded up to a whole number?
hints: First find what each server should carry at the target.
Each should carry 600 × 0.6 requests per second.
Divide 8,000 by that and round up.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each should carry 600 × 0.6 = 360, and 8,000 ÷ 360 ≈ 22.2, which rounds up to 23.

questions.onCorrect: With 23 servers each runs at about 58% at peak, a little under the 60% target.

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds 22.2 down, which runs each server above the 60% target. Servers are rounded up.
That divides by the full 600 and ignores the target utilisation.
That is 8,000 ÷ 600 rounded down. The target utilisation has not been applied.

questions.prompt: A fleet of 18 servers handles a peak of 6,000 requests per second. Each server saturates at 500 and is planned at 70%, which is 350. The team plans to update by taking 3 servers out at once at peak. A colleague says it is safe because 15 servers can handle 7,500 requests per second in all. What is wrong with the plan?
hints: Share 6,000 requests per second over the servers that stay.
Compare each server's load with the 350 it was planned for, not with the 500 it can handle.

acceptedIdeas: The 15 servers would run at 80%, above the planned 70%, and one more failure would take them to 86%
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 15 servers would run at 80%, above the planned 70%, and one more failure would take them to 86%

choices.label: Nothing, because the total capacity of 7,500 exceeds the 6,000 that arrive, so every server is safe
The 15 servers would run at 80%, above the planned 70%, and one more failure would take them to 86%
The balancer cannot remove three servers at once without dropping the connections they hold

questions.onCorrect: A smaller batch, or an update outside the peak, keeps the servers near their planned 70% and leaves room for a failure during the update.

misconceptions.feedback: That compares the load with total capacity. The plan is for 70% on each server, and at 80% the margin that the plan kept is already used.
A balancer stops sending new requests to servers that are drained or fail their health checks, and removing servers is routine. The risk lies in the load the others must carry.

questions.prompt: A web shop is being moved behind a load balancer so that it can scale out. Which of these parts hold state that has to survive between requests, and which can be copied freely?
hints: Ask what would be lost if that part were replaced by a fresh copy.
State that every server can reach has moved to a store, and the store itself is now the part that holds state.

items.label: An app server that keeps each customer's cart in its own memory
items.explanation: The cart lives in one server, so a request that reaches another server cannot see it.

items.label: The orders database
items.explanation: Orders have to survive restarts and be visible to every server.

items.label: The shared session store that every app server reads
items.explanation: The state has moved here from the servers, so this store is now the part that must be fast, large and safe.

items.label: An app server that reads the cart from the shared store on every request
items.explanation: It keeps nothing between requests, so any server can answer any request.

items.label: A service that turns an uploaded photo into a thumbnail and returns it
items.explanation: Its output depends only on the request, so a failed copy loses nothing.

items.label: A fleet where a signed cookie carries the user's id, so any server can verify it
items.explanation: The client holds the state and sends it back with each request.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The cart-in-memory server, the orders database and the shared session store hold state; the server that reads the shared store, the thumbnail service and the cookie-checking fleet can be copied freely.

questions.onCorrect: Servers can be copied once the state they depend on sits in a shared store, and the store is then the part that has to be fast, large and safe.

questions.prompt: A service runs on one machine that reaches 85% processor use at peak, and traffic is expected to double within six months. The team also cannot accept an outage when that machine fails. Which change deals with both problems?
hints: The change has to add capacity and leave something running when one machine fails.
Ask what each option does when the one machine breaks.

acceptedIdeas: Add two more identical servers behind a load balancer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Add two more identical servers behind a load balancer

choices.label: Replace it with a machine twice the size, which doubles the capacity
Put a second load balancer in front of the one machine
Add health checks to the machine so that failures are noticed sooner
Add two more identical servers behind a load balancer

questions.onCorrect: Horizontal scaling adds capacity by about the capacity of each server and lets the others carry on when one breaks.

misconceptions.feedback: A bigger machine fixes capacity for a while, but it leaves one machine to fail, and vertical scaling has a ceiling.
A balancer in front of one machine adds no capacity and no second machine to take over.
Health checks detect a failure, but with a single machine there is nothing to send the traffic to.

questions.prompt: An autoscaler adds servers when utilisation passes 90%, and a new server takes four minutes to start and warm up. During a sudden surge users see slow responses long before the new servers arrive. Which change helps most?
hints: A new server needs time before it can help, so the existing servers carry the surge first.
Ask what keeps the delay low while the new servers start.

acceptedIdeas: Plan for a lower utilisation, so the servers that exist can carry the surge
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Plan for a lower utilisation, so the servers that exist can carry the surge

choices.label: Raise the trigger to 95%, so that servers are added only when they are needed
Plan for a lower utilisation, so the servers that exist can carry the surge
Check utilisation every second, so that new servers appear at once

questions.onCorrect: The margin of a target utilisation below 100% is what carries the service across the gap, because autoscaling always lags behind the load.

misconceptions.feedback: At 90% a server's delay is already ten times its service time, and at 95% it is twenty times, so waiting longer makes the surge worse.
Faster checks start the four minutes earlier, but they do not remove the time a server needs to start and warm up.

questions.prompt: A cache lookup takes 1 ms and a database read takes 20 ms, and every request does the lookup. The hit rate is 90%. Which is closest to the average latency?
hints: Every request pays for the lookup, and only the requests that miss pay for the database as well.
Every request pays for the lookup, and only the misses pay for the database as well.

acceptedIdeas: A few milliseconds, much nearer a hit than a database read
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A few milliseconds, much nearer a hit than a database read

choices.label: A few milliseconds, much nearer a hit than a database read
About 10 ms, halfway between the time of a hit and of a database read
About 1 ms, as fast as a hit
About 19 ms, almost as slow as the database alone

questions.onCorrect: One request in ten misses and adds a 20 ms database read, which adds 2 ms to the average and makes it 3 ms.

misconceptions.feedback: An average of 10 ms would need about half of the requests to miss. Only one in ten does, so only a tenth of the requests pay for the database.
An average near 19 ms would need almost every request to go to the database. Here only one in ten does.
Every hit costs 1 ms, but the one request in ten that misses also pays 20 ms for the database, and that adds about 2 ms to the average.

questions.prompt: A customer opens a product page whose entry is not in the cache. The service has a load balancer, an app server, a cache and a database, and uses cache-aside. In what order does the request travel?
hints: The cache is asked before the database.
A miss has to be known before the database is read, and the copy can only be stored after it has been read.

items: The load balancer sends the request to an app server
The app server looks the product up in the cache
The lookup misses, because the cache has no entry
The app server reads the product from the database
The app server stores the product in the cache
The app server returns the page to the customer

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The balancer chooses a server first. The app server tries the cache, sees a miss, reads the database, stores the copy for the next reader and only then answers.

questions.onCorrect: The copy goes into the cache before the page is returned, so the next request for the same product finds it there, while the database stays the source of truth.

questions.prompt: A product database is sized for the 500 requests per second that reach it when the cache hits 95% of 10,000 requests per second. The cache cluster is restarted during the busiest hour. What happens next?
hints: Ask what the hit rate is for a cache that has just restarted.
The load on the database follows the miss rate, not the hit rate.

acceptedIdeas: The empty cache hits nothing, so the database takes all 10,000 requests, 20 times its load
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The empty cache hits nothing, so the database takes all 10,000 requests, 20 times its load

choices.label: Nothing visible, because the database is replicated and the replicas share all the extra load
The database sees a few per cent more requests for a short time while the cache warms
The empty cache hits nothing, so the database takes all 10,000 requests, 20 times its load
The cache refills at once from the database, so the hit rate recovers within a second

questions.onCorrect: Warming the cache before it takes traffic, or shedding load while it fills, keeps the database from facing 20 times the load it was sized for.

misconceptions.feedback: Replicas serve the misses they receive, and the whole group is sized for about 500 requests per second. Twenty times that load overwhelms it whichever replica answers.
The hit rate falls to zero, not to a slightly lower figure, so the miss rate goes from 5% to 100%.
An entry enters the cache only when a request misses and reads the database, so refilling takes a miss for every key that is needed, and the database serves each of them.

questions.prompt: A shop caches each product page for 300 seconds. A price changes at second 120 after the page was cached, and customers keep seeing the old price for 180 seconds. The shop wants the new price to show at once, without sending many more requests to the database. Which change does that?
hints: The old price shows from the change until the entry expires.
Look for a change that removes the entry when the data changes, and not one that only shortens the wait.

acceptedIdeas: Delete the cached page in the same code that changes the price
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Delete the cached page in the same code that changes the price

choices.label: Delete the cached page in the same code that changes the price
Cut the TTL to 1 second for every product
Raise the TTL to one hour, so the page rarely expires
Remove the cache, since stale prices cannot be avoided with one

questions.onCorrect: Explicit invalidation gives the freshest answers, at the price that every code path that changes the price must remember to remove the entry.

misconceptions.feedback: A 1-second TTL keeps prices fresh, but nearly every request would miss, so the database takes almost the full load again.
A longer TTL keeps each copy for longer, so customers would see an old price for up to an hour.
A cache can be kept fresh. Explicit invalidation removes the entry when the data changes, and removing the cache gives up the load it saves.

questions.prompt: A popular product key expires at noon. For the 200 ms that one database read takes, every request for it misses and reads the same row, about 200 reads in all. What is this called?
hints: The burst arrives because no request can see that a refresh is already under way.
The word describes a crowd rushing at the same place.

acceptedIdeas: stampede
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: stampede

questions.onCorrect: Coalescing, serving stale and jittered expiry all aim to make the database see one read for a hot key instead of hundreds.

misconceptions.feedback: A hit is a request the cache answers. This burst is made of misses.
A cold cache is one that has just started and holds nothing. Here one hot key expired while the rest of the cache was fine.

questions.prompt: A cache lookup takes 1 ms and a database read takes 20 ms, and the hit rate is 99%. What is the average latency in milliseconds?
hints: The miss rate is 1 minus the hit rate.
The miss rate is 0.01.
Add 1 ms to the miss rate times 20 ms.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The miss rate is 1%, so the average is 1 + 0.01 × 20 = 1.2 ms.

questions.onCorrect: At a 99% hit rate the database adds only 0.2 ms to the average, so almost all of the latency is the lookup.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the share contributed by misses. Every request also pays the 1 ms lookup.
That weights the database time by the hit rate, 0.99 × 20 + 1. The misses are the ones that read the database.
That adds both times for every request. Only the misses go on to the database.

questions.prompt: A cache lookup takes 4 ms and a database read takes 40 ms. A team puts this cache in front of a report query that is almost never repeated, and measures a hit rate of 8%. What should they do?
hints: Every request does the lookup, whether it hits or misses.
The break-even hit rate is the lookup time divided by the database time.

acceptedIdeas: Rework or remove the cache, as the average is now 40.8 ms, slower than the database alone
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Rework or remove the cache, as the average is now 40.8 ms, slower than the database alone

choices.label: Rework or remove the cache, as the average is now 40.8 ms, slower than the database alone
Keep it, because every hit saves 36 ms of database time and so the cache can only ever help
Keep it, because the hit rate will rise as traffic grows and more keys are repeated

questions.onCorrect: The break-even is 4 ÷ 40 = 10%, and a cache that hits less often than that makes the average request slower than having no cache.

misconceptions.feedback: Every request pays the 4 ms lookup, and the 92% that miss pay for the database as well, so below a 10% hit rate the lookups cost more than the hits save.
A hit rate depends on how often the same key repeats and not on volume, so queries that are almost never repeated stay near zero however much traffic arrives.

questions.prompt: A team caches user profiles and removes a profile's entry whenever the profile service updates it. A new import job writes to the profiles table directly, and afterwards users still see their old details until the TTL runs out. What is the cause?
hints: Ask which code removes a cache entry, and which code changes the data.
A cache entry is a copy, so it stays as it was until something removes it or it expires.

acceptedIdeas: The import never removes the cached entries, because only the profile service does
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The import never removes the cached entries, because only the profile service does

choices.label: The TTL is too long, and shortening it would fix the cause of the stale details
The cache evicted entries too early and refilled them from an out-of-date database
Replication lag on the database, which delays the new details reaching the replica read
The import never removes the cached entries, because only the profile service does

questions.onCorrect: With explicit invalidation every code path that changes the data has to remove the entry, and a new writer that skips it leaves the cache stale until the TTL runs out.

misconceptions.feedback: A shorter TTL would shorten the window and leave the cause in place. The entries go stale because the import never removes them.
Early eviction would send users to the database, which already holds the new details. Stale details mean the old entries stayed.
Replication lag is a gap between copies of the database. Here the cache holds the old values, whichever replica is read.

questions.prompt: Which measure reduces a stampede when a popular key expires?
hints: A stampede is many requests doing the same refresh at once.
Look for the measure that makes one request do the work.

acceptedIdeas: Letting one request refresh the key while the others wait
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Letting one request refresh the key while the others wait

choices.label: Shortening every TTL so that keys are refreshed sooner
Adding more databases so the duplicate reads are spread out
Letting one request refresh the key while the others wait
Clearing the whole cache whenever a popular key expires

questions.onCorrect: One refresh is enough for every waiting request, so the database sees a single read for the key.

misconceptions.feedback: A shorter TTL makes keys expire more often, which gives the burst more chances to happen.
Clearing the cache makes every key miss at once, which is a larger stampede.
More databases raise the capacity but leave the duplicate reads in place, and the cost grows with the burst.

questions.prompt: Why is the database load found by multiplying the request rate by the miss rate, 20,000 × 0.1, and not by the hit rate?
hints: Ask which requests actually reach the database.
The hit rate counts requests the cache answers on its own.

acceptedIdeas: Only the requests that miss go on to read the database, and the miss rate is 1 − hit rate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the requests that miss go on to read the database, and the miss rate is 1 − hit rate

choices.label: Requests that hit the cache are the ones that cost the database the most to serve, since they arrive in the largest numbers
Only the requests that miss go on to read the database, and the miss rate is 1 − hit rate
The database must also store every request that hits the cache, as a record of use

questions.onCorrect: The load on the database follows the miss rate, which is why a small fall in the hit rate can multiply it.

misconceptions.feedback: A hit is answered by the cache and never reaches the database, so the load follows the misses.
A hit is served from the copy. Only a miss reads the database, and it then stores the result in the cache.

questions.prompt: A table has 1,000,000 rows and 100 rows fit on a page. A query with no index must read every page. About how many pages does it read?
hints: A page holds 100 rows, so one page read covers 100 rows of the table.
Divide the number of rows by the rows that fit on a page.

acceptedIdeas: About 10,000 pages
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 10,000 pages

choices.label: About 100 pages
About 10,000 pages
About 1,000,000 pages, one for each row

questions.onCorrect: A page holds 100 rows, so 1,000,000 rows fill 10,000 pages, and a scan reads each of them.

misconceptions.feedback: 100 is the number of rows on one page. The table has 1,000,000 rows, so it fills 10,000 such pages.
A page holds 100 rows, so a scan reads each page once and not once for each row, which makes 100 times fewer reads than rows.

questions.prompt: A table with 1,000,000 rows has a B-tree index with a fan-out of 100, so a lookup reads 3 pages of the index and 1 for the row. The table grows a hundredfold, to 100,000,000 rows. How many pages does a lookup read now?
hints: The depth is the smallest number of levels whose reach covers the keys.

acceptedIdeas: 5 pages, one more level of the index
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 5 pages, one more level of the index

choices.label: 400 pages, a hundred times as many as before
5 pages, one more level of the index
4 pages, no different from before
30 pages, ten times as many

questions.onCorrect: Depth grows very slowly, so a lookup through an index costs a handful of page reads however large the table becomes.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the lookup like a scan, which grows with the table. The depth of the index grows with the logarithm of the rows.
The depth is the smallest L with 100^L at least the number of keys, and 100^3 = 1,000,000 no longer covers 100,000,000, so one more level is needed.
The depth grows by one level for each hundredfold increase in rows, not by a multiple of the page count.

questions.prompt:
A page that lists 80 orders takes 3 seconds to load. The query log for one page view begins like this.

`SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 12 LIMIT 80`
`SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = 301`
`SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = 417`
`SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = 301`
`... 77 more queries on customers`

Which change helps most?
hints: Count the queries in one page view, and ask which part of the time they spend.
Each query pays a round trip to the database, however fast it is.

acceptedIdeas: Fetch the customers for all 80 orders in one query, by id or with a join
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fetch the customers for all 80 orders in one query, by id or with a join

choices.label: Add an index on `customers.id`, so that each of the lookups is faster than now
Move the customers table to a larger server with more memory and faster disks
Fetch the customers for all 80 orders in one query, by id or with a join
Add a follower database, so that the 81 queries are spread out across two machines

questions.onCorrect: The pattern is N+1, 1 + 80 = 81 queries, and asking for the related rows together takes the page down to two queries, or to one with a join.

misconceptions.feedback: Each query is already a lookup by key, so it is fast. The cost is the 80 round trips, and an index does not remove them.
A larger server speeds each query a little and leaves the 80 round trips in place.
A follower spreads the same 81 queries across machines, and the page still waits for each one.

questions.prompt: With a fan-out of 100, how many levels does a B-tree need to index 100,000,000 keys?
hints: Each level multiplies the reach by 100.
Find the smallest L with 100^L at least equal to the number of keys.
100^3 is 1,000,000, which falls short.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100^3 = 1,000,000 is too small and 100^4 = 100,000,000 is enough, so 4 levels.

questions.onCorrect: Four levels reach exactly 100,000,000 keys, so the lookup reads 4 pages and one more for the row.

misconceptions.feedback: Three levels reach only 1,000,000 keys.
Five levels reach 10,000,000,000 keys, which is more than needed.

questions.prompt: An audit table takes 20,000 inserts per second and is searched by hand about once a week. A teammate proposes an index on every column, so that any search is fast. What is the cost?
hints: An insert has to leave every index in sorted order.
Compare how often the table is written with how often it is searched.

acceptedIdeas: Every insert must also update every index, which multiplies the write work
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every insert must also update every index, which multiplies the write work

choices.label: None, because an index only helps the queries and never slows anything else down
Every insert must also update every index, which multiplies the write work
Only disk space, because the indexes are brought up to date in the background

questions.onCorrect: An index speeds up the reads it serves and costs work on every write, so it belongs where the reads are frequent enough to earn it.

misconceptions.feedback: An insert changes the table and every index, so a table with five indexes turns one insert into six writes.
Index updates are part of each insert. The cost is paid in write time as well as in disk.

questions.prompt: A social app needs the friends of a user's friends. What is this access pattern called?
hints: The query follows links from one record to the next.
A graph store is built for this pattern.

acceptedIdeas: traversal
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: traversal

questions.onCorrect: A traversal follows links, and a graph store is built for it, whereas a relational database does joins and a key-value store does lookups by key.

misconceptions.feedback: A join combines rows from tables by a shared value. This query follows links from one record to the next, and then again, which is a different pattern.
A range reads the records between two keys. Friends of friends is found by following links from record to record.

questions.prompt: A write reaches the leader at 0 ms and a follower applies it at 80 ms. What does a read from that follower at 50 ms return?
hints: Compare the time of the read with the time at which the follower applies the write.
Ask what the follower holds at 50 ms, given when it applies the write.

acceptedIdeas: The old value, because the follower has not applied the write yet
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The old value, because the follower has not applied the write yet

choices.label: An error, because the leader and the follower disagree about the value
The new value, because the leader already has it
The old value, because the follower has not applied the write yet

questions.onCorrect: The follower holds the old value until 80 ms, so a read before then returns it.

misconceptions.feedback: The leader has the new value, but a read sent to the follower returns what the follower holds, and it does not apply the change until 80 ms.
A follower does not know that it is behind, so it answers with the value it holds. The read succeeds and returns the old value.

questions.prompt: A leader can accept at most 1,000 writes per second. Four followers are added to the cluster. What is the most that the cluster can now accept?
hints: Ask which machine accepts each write, and what the followers do with it.
Ask which machine has to make every write.

acceptedIdeas: 1,000 writes per second, because the leader still has to make every write
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 1,000 writes per second, because the leader still has to make every write

choices.label: 2,000 writes per second, because the followers share the work of accepting writes
5,000 writes per second, because each of the five machines can accept 1,000
1,000 writes per second, because the leader still has to make every write

questions.onCorrect: Every write is made by the leader and then repeated on each follower, so followers add read capacity and leave the write limit at 1,000.

misconceptions.feedback: Followers do not accept writes. They only apply the changes that the leader sends them, so they cannot share the work of accepting.
Only the leader accepts writes, and each follower repeats every change instead of adding capacity for new ones.

questions.prompt: Keys 0 to 19 are placed on 4 shards with k mod 4. The cluster grows to 5 shards and the keys are placed with k mod 5. Roughly how many of the 20 keys stay on the same shard number?
hints: Work out the shard of keys 4, 5 and 6 under both rules and see whether they agree.
List the keys from 0 to 19 whose remainder is the same under both rules.

acceptedIdeas: Only a few of them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only a few of them

choices.label: About three quarters of them
Nearly all of them, since only one shard was added
About half of them
Only a few of them

questions.onCorrect: Only keys 0 to 3 stay, because their remainders agree under both rules, so 16 of the 20 keys have to move.

misconceptions.feedback: Adding a shard changes the modulus for every key, and a key stays only if its two remainders agree. Key 4, for instance, is on shard 0 under mod 4 and on shard 4 under mod 5.
Three quarters would be 15 keys. Keys 4 to 19 all have different remainders under the two rules, so only keys 0 to 3 stay.
Half would be 10 keys. Only keys 0 to 3 have the same remainder under both rules.

questions.prompt: A cache cluster of 8 nodes places keys with hash modulo the number of nodes. A ninth node is added. How do hash-mod and consistent hashing compare for this change?
hints: Under hash-mod, count the keys among 0 to 71 for which k mod 8 equals k mod 9.
On a ring, a node that joins takes over only the arc between itself and its predecessor.

acceptedIdeas: Hash-mod moves nearly nine keys in ten, and consistent hashing about one in nine
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Hash-mod moves nearly nine keys in ten, and consistent hashing about one in nine

choices.label: Both move about one key in nine, because one node in nine is new
Hash-mod moves about one key in nine, and consistent hashing moves nearly all of them
Hash-mod moves nearly nine keys in ten, and consistent hashing about one in nine
Both move nearly all of the keys, because every key is rehashed

questions.onCorrect: A growing cluster that uses hash-mod copies almost all of its data, and one that uses consistent hashing copies about its share of the new node.

misconceptions.feedback: That holds for consistent hashing only. With hash-mod the divisor changes for every key, and a key stays only when k mod 8 equals k mod 9, which is one key in nine.
The two are the wrong way round. Consistent hashing moves only the arc taken by the new node.
Consistent hashing leaves each key on its old node except those on the arc the ninth node takes, about 1/9 of them.

questions.prompt: Keys 0 to 23 are placed with k mod 4. The cluster grows to 6 shards and the keys are placed with k mod 6. How many of the 24 keys stay on the same shard number?
hints: Compare the two rules for k = 0 to 3.
The two rules realign every 12 keys, since 12 is the smallest number that both 4 and 6 divide.
Count the agreeing keys in 0 to 11 and in 12 to 23.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: k mod 4 and k mod 6 agree for k = 0 to 3, then again for k = 12 to 15, and for k = 24 onward, so within 0 to 23 the keys 0 to 3 and 12 to 15 stay, which is 8.

questions.onCorrect: Four keys in each block of 12 stay, so one third of the keys keep their shard and two thirds move.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the first block of 12 keys. The two rules realign after 12, so keys 12 to 15 also agree.
That is the number of keys that move. The question asks for the number that stay.
That treats every key where the rules agree on its remainder as one of six. Compare the rules key by key.

questions.prompt: A team shards its orders table across ten shards by order date, so that daily reports read one shard. After launch, one shard sits at 95% processor use while the other nine are idle. What is the cause?
hints: Ask which shard receives a new order, and what the shard key of that order is.
Think about where all of one day's writes go.

acceptedIdeas: All of today's orders are written to the shard that holds today's date
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: All of today's orders are written to the shard that holds today's date

choices.label: Hash-mod spreads keys unevenly, so the fix is to change the modulus used
All of today's orders are written to the shard that holds today's date
Replication lag on that shard is making followers repeat writes
Ten shards are too few, and adding more would spread today's writes

questions.onCorrect: A shard key that follows time sends all the new writes to one shard, whereas a key such as the customer id spreads them.

misconceptions.feedback: The table is sharded by date and not by hash-mod, and date ranges send every current write to one place.
Lag affects what followers show. It does not change how many writes a shard takes.
Today's writes all share one key range, so extra shards would sit idle and today's shard would stay as busy.

questions.prompt: A user saves a new profile photo in a service with one leader and two followers. In what order do these things happen?
hints: Every write is made by the leader before the followers see it.
A follower can return the new value only after it has applied the change.

items: The client sends the write to the leader
The leader applies the write
The leader sends the change to its followers
Each follower applies the change, in the same order as the leader
A read from a follower returns the new photo

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every write goes to the leader first. The leader applies it and passes the change on, the followers apply it in the leader's order, and only after that does a follower return the new photo.

questions.onCorrect: Between the third and the last step a follower still returns the old photo, and that gap is the replication lag.

questions.prompt: Under the rule k mod 3, which shard holds key 11?
hints: The shard is the remainder after dividing the key by 3.
3 × 3 = 9, which is below 11 by a small amount.
Subtract 9 from 11.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 11 = 3 × 3 + 2, so the remainder when 11 is divided by 3 is 2, and key 11 lives on shard 2.

questions.onCorrect: Under k mod 4 the same key goes to shard 3, so key 11 moves when the cluster grows from 3 shards to 4.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the quotient, the number of times 3 goes into 11. The shard is the remainder.
That is the key itself. The shard is its remainder after division by 3.

questions.prompt: A like counter shows 1,204 on one phone and 1,210 on another, and an hour later both phones show 1,213. What kind of consistency does the counter give? Answer with two words.
hints: The copies disagreed for a while and then agreed once writes stopped.
The promise is weaker than a single copy, and cheaper to keep.

acceptedIdeas: eventual consistency
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: eventual consistency

questions.onCorrect: A like count a few seconds behind harms no one, and the weaker the promise, the cheaper it is to keep.

misconceptions.feedback: A strongly consistent system would behave as if there were a single copy, so the two phones could never disagree. These did, for a while.
Read-your-writes promises only that a user sees their own writes at once. Here two readers disagreed, and the copies agreed later.

questions.prompt: A store keeps N = 3 replicas, and a write is acknowledged once W = 2 of them have it. What is the smallest number of replicas that a read must ask to be sure of seeing the latest acknowledged write?
hints: Ask how many replicas can lack the write, and how large a read must be to avoid choosing only those.
Ask how many replicas can have missed a write that reached 2 of the 3.

acceptedIdeas: Two replicas, since only one replica can have missed the write
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two replicas, since only one replica can have missed the write

choices.label: Two replicas, since only one replica can have missed the write
All three replicas, since any smaller set might miss it entirely
One replica, since the write reached most of them

questions.onCorrect: Only one replica can lack the write, so any two replicas include at least one that has it.

misconceptions.feedback: The one replica asked might be the one that missed the write, and then the read returns the old value. Most replicas having the write does not make any single one of them reliable.
Asking all three would work but is more than needed. Only one replica can lack the write, so two replicas cannot both be without it.

questions.prompt: A store like Dynamo keeps 3 replicas of each item. Its common setting acknowledges a write after 2 replicas have it and asks 2 on a read. To make both faster, a teammate sets both numbers to 1. What is the risk?
hints: A read and a write share a replica only when R + W is more than N.
Check 1 + 1 against 3.

acceptedIdeas: A read can reach a replica that missed the latest write and return a stale value
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A read can reach a replica that missed the latest write and return a stale value

choices.label: Reads become slower, because one replica must now answer every request on its own
Nothing changes, because three replicas still hold every write
A read can reach a replica that missed the latest write and return a stale value

questions.onCorrect: Dynamo's common setting of (N, R, W) = (3, 2, 2) makes every read set share a replica with the latest write set, and (3, 1, 1) gives that up for speed.

misconceptions.feedback: Asking fewer replicas makes reads faster and not slower.
Holding a copy is not the same as being asked. With R = 1 and W = 1 the two sets need not overlap, because 1 + 1 is not more than 3.

questions.prompt: A team runs a consensus group of 4 nodes and says it can survive 2 failures. Is that right?
hints: A majority of n nodes is more than half of them.
Count how many nodes can be down while a majority is still up.

acceptedIdeas: No, a majority of 4 is 3, so it survives 1 failure, and 2 needs 5 nodes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, a majority of 4 is 3, so it survives 1 failure, and 2 needs 5 nodes

choices.label: Yes, because 2 nodes remain and that is half of the group, enough to go on
No, a majority of 4 is 3, so it survives 1 failure, and 2 needs 5 nodes
Yes, because every even-sized group tolerates half its nodes failing

questions.onCorrect: Five nodes need 3 and tolerate 2 failures, while four nodes also need 3 and tolerate only 1, so the fourth node adds cost and no resilience.

misconceptions.feedback: Half is not a majority. With 2 of 4 nodes up, no group of 3 can be formed, so the group stops accepting changes.
A majority is more than half, so a group of 4 needs 3, the same as a group of 3, which is why consensus groups usually have an odd size.

questions.prompt: With N = 5 replicas and W = 3, why is R = 2 not enough for every read to see the latest write?
hints: Count how many replicas can have missed a write that reached 3.
A read must ask more replicas than that to be sure of reaching one that has it.

acceptedIdeas: A write reached 3 replicas and 2 did not, and a read of 2 might ask those 2
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A write reached 3 replicas and 2 did not, and a read of 2 might ask those 2

choices.label: A write reached 3 replicas and 2 did not, and a read of 2 might ask those 2
Two replicas can never agree, so a read of 2 always fails
R must equal W, so that reads and writes use the same number of replicas each time

questions.onCorrect: Five replicas minus the 3 that have the write leaves 2 that may not, so a read must ask 3 to be sure of overlapping.

misconceptions.feedback: A read of 2 does not fail. The trouble is that it might ask only replicas that missed the latest write.
R and W need not be equal. They need R + W to be more than N, which here means R + 3 > 5.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest R that guarantees a read overlaps the latest write?
hints: The condition is R + W > N.
R + 4 must exceed 7.
R must be larger than 7 minus 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: R + 4 must be more than 7, so R must be more than 3, and the smallest whole number is 4.

questions.onCorrect: With W = 4 and R = 4 the sum is 8, and either side can lose three replicas.

misconceptions.feedback: With R = 3 the sum is 7, which is not more than 7.
R = 5 also works, but a smaller R already satisfies the condition.
That adds N and W. The condition compares R + W with N.

questions.prompt: A store keeps N = 3 replicas, acknowledges a write only when all W = 3 have it, and reads from R = 1. A rack failure takes one replica down. What happens?
hints: Writes tolerate N − W unavailable replicas, and reads tolerate N − R.
Work out N − W and N − R.

acceptedIdeas: Every write fails until the replica returns, while reads from the other two work
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every write fails until the replica returns, while reads from the other two work

choices.label: Writes keep working on the two replicas that remain, and reads are unaffected
Reads fail too, because a read needs the same replicas as a write
Reads can return stale values, because the replica that is down missed the writes
Every write fails until the replica returns, while reads from the other two work

questions.onCorrect: W = 3 makes reads fast and always current, and the price is that no replica may be down for a write to succeed.

misconceptions.feedback: W = 3 means all three replicas must acknowledge, so two are not enough.
R = 1 needs only one replica, so reads continue.
Every acknowledged write reached all three replicas, so the replicas that are up hold all of them.

questions.prompt: During a network partition, a system keeps answering reads and writes on both sides. Which property did it give up?
hints: Both sides are answering, so the copies can diverge.
One property is kept by answering, and the other is the one that is lost.

acceptedIdeas: Consistency
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Consistency

choices.label: Partition tolerance
Availability
Consistency
Durability

questions.onCorrect: Answering on both sides keeps the system available, and the copies may then disagree, so consistency is what is lost.

misconceptions.feedback: Answering every request means that availability is kept.
The partition has happened regardless of what the system chooses, so tolerating it is not what is traded.
Durability concerns data surviving. Answering on both sides does not delete accepted data.

questions.prompt: Messages arrive at 150 per second and the consumers process 100 per second, starting from an empty queue. How does the number of waiting messages change over the next two minutes?
hints: Count how many more messages arrive in one second than the consumers handle, and ask whether that number changes as the queue grows.
Compare the arrival rate with the consumers' rate, second by second.

acceptedIdeas: It grows by the same number of messages every second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It grows by the same number of messages every second

choices.label: It stays short, because the consumers are busy the whole time
It grows slowly at first and faster as the queue gets longer
It grows for a while and then levels off
It grows by the same number of messages every second

questions.onCorrect: The queue gains the same 50 messages every second, because the gap between the two rates does not depend on how long the queue is.

misconceptions.feedback: Consumers that are busy all the time still handle only 100 messages a second, so the 50 extra messages that arrive each second wait in the queue.
Each second adds the same 50 extra messages whatever the length of the queue, so the growth is steady and does not speed up.
The queue levels off only if the consumers speed up or the arrivals slow down. At these fixed rates the gap of 50 messages per second never closes.

questions.prompt: A queue's broker holds at most 90,000 messages and then starts refusing new ones. Messages arrive at 130 per second and the consumers process 100 per second, starting from an empty queue. After how many minutes does the broker start refusing messages?
hints: The backlog grows by the difference between the two rates.
That difference is 30 messages per second, and the broker is full at 90,000.
90,000 ÷ 30 is a number of seconds, so convert it to minutes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: (130 − 100) = 30 per second; 90,000 ÷ 30 = 3,000 seconds = 50 minutes.

questions.onCorrect: At 30 messages per second the queue fills in 3,000 seconds, which is 50 minutes, so an alert on the backlog well before then leaves time to add consumers or to shed load.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time in seconds. The question asks for minutes.
That divides the limit by the arrival rate alone. The backlog grows by the difference between arrivals and processing.
That divides 90,000 by 120 messages per second. The growth is the difference of the rates, 30 per second.

questions.prompt: Consumers process 100 messages per second and arrivals have fallen to 60 per second. By how many messages per second does the backlog shrink?
hints: The backlog shrinks by what leaves minus what arrives.
Messages leave at 100 per second.
Subtract the arrival rate from the processing rate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The consumers remove 100 per second and 60 per second arrive, so the backlog shrinks by 100 − 60 = 40 per second.

questions.onCorrect: The net drain rate is the spare capacity, and the drain time is the backlog divided by it.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two rates. The backlog shrinks by their difference.
That is the arrival rate. The backlog shrinks by the processing rate minus the arrival rate.

questions.prompt: How many seconds until the queue is empty?
hints: Find the rate at which the backlog shrinks.
The backlog shrinks by 40 messages per second.
Divide the backlog by that rate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The backlog shrinks by 100 − 60 = 40 per second, so it empties in 9,000 ÷ 40 = 225 seconds.

questions.onCorrect: The drain time is the backlog divided by the spare capacity, so doubling the spare capacity halves it.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the backlog by the processing rate of 100. The backlog shrinks by the spare capacity, not the whole rate.
That divides the backlog by the arrival rate. The backlog shrinks by the difference between the rates.
That is the backlog itself. Divide it by the rate at which it shrinks.

questions.prompt: A metrics agent sends each reading once and does not resend it. If the network drops a reading it is lost, but no reading is ever counted twice. Which delivery guarantee is that?
hints: The agent never resends, so a drop is final.
Ask which of the failures, loss or repetition, the agent allows.

acceptedIdeas: at-most-once
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: at-most-once

questions.onCorrect: At-most-once suits readings where a gap matters less than a repeat, and at-least-once with an idempotent consumer suits work that must not be lost.

misconceptions.feedback: At-least-once delivery resends until the message is acknowledged, so nothing is lost but a message can arrive twice. This agent never resends.
Exactly once would neither lose nor repeat a message, and a sender cannot tell a lost message from a lost acknowledgement. This agent loses readings.

questions.prompt: A topic has 4 partitions, and a consumer group of 6 consumers reads it. What happens to the work?
hints: A partition is read by one consumer of the group at a time.
Compare the number of consumers with the number of partitions.

acceptedIdeas: Four consumers each read one partition, and two sit idle
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Four consumers each read one partition, and two sit idle

choices.label: Four consumers each read one partition, and two sit idle
All six consumers read in parallel, because more consumers always mean more throughput
Two partitions are read twice, so that every consumer has something to do

questions.onCorrect: A group can use at most as many consumers as the topic has partitions, and more partitions raise that cap.

misconceptions.feedback: Each partition is read by one consumer of the group at a time, so the number of partitions caps the parallelism.
Reading a partition twice within a group would process its events twice. The group gives each partition to one consumer.

questions.prompt: A consumer reads a payment message, charges the card, and then writes the message id to its 'processed' table. The queue delivers at least once. The consumer crashes after charging the card and before writing the id. What happens when the message is delivered again, and what prevents it?
hints: Ask what the queue does with a message that was never acknowledged.
The effect and the record that it happened have to succeed or fail together.

acceptedIdeas: The card is charged again, which recording the id in the same transaction would prevent
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The card is charged again, which recording the id in the same transaction would prevent

choices.label: Nothing happens, because the queue delivers each message only once
The card is charged again, which recording the id in the same transaction would prevent
The payment is lost, because the crash cancelled the message
The card is charged again, which switching the queue to at-most-once delivery would prevent

questions.onCorrect: A consumer becomes idempotent by recording the message id in the same transaction as the effect, so a repeat finds the record and does nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: At-least-once delivery means a message can arrive twice, because a crash before the acknowledgement makes the queue send it again.
The message is delivered again after a crash, because it was never acknowledged.
At-most-once avoids repeats by accepting loss, so a payment could be dropped instead of repeated. An idempotent consumer avoids both.

questions.prompt: A queue delivers each message at least once, so some messages arrive twice. What must the consumer be for a repeat to do no harm?
hints: A repeat must have the same effect as the first delivery.
Look for the property that makes a second processing harmless.

acceptedIdeas: Idempotent
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Idempotent

choices.label: Single-threaded
Stateless only
Faster
Idempotent

questions.onCorrect: An idempotent consumer treats a repeated message as already done, so at-least-once delivery produces an effect only once.

misconceptions.feedback: Speed does not change what a repeat does. The second delivery would still have an effect.
A single thread can still process the same message twice, one after the other.
Statelessness does not stop a repeat having an effect, and the consumer needs a record of what it has handled.

questions.prompt: A service makes 100 calls per second to a dependency that has stopped answering, and each call waits for its timeout of 30 seconds before failing. Once the service has settled, about how many calls are waiting at any moment?
hints: Picture the calls that arrived in the last 30 seconds and have not yet timed out.
Little's law: arrivals per second times the seconds each call stays.

acceptedIdeas: A few thousand, because calls keep arriving during the 30 seconds each one waits
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A few thousand, because calls keep arriving during the 30 seconds each one waits

choices.label: About 100, the calls that arrive in one second
A few thousand, because calls keep arriving during the 30 seconds each one waits
The number grows without limit, because none of the calls ever finishes or gives up
About 30, one for each second of the timeout

questions.onCorrect: Each call waits 30 seconds while 100 more arrive every second, so about 100 × 30 = 3,000 are waiting at any moment.

misconceptions.feedback: 100 is the number of calls that arrive in a single second, but each call stays for 30 seconds, so the calls of 30 different seconds are waiting together.
30 is the length of the timeout in seconds. Calls arrive 100 times a second, so far more than 30 are waiting.
Each call ends when its timeout runs out, so calls leave as well as arrive, and the number waiting settles at a fixed value.

questions.prompt: A user's request must finish within 2 seconds. The service calls a dependency with a timeout of 5 seconds and retries it twice, which makes three attempts. The dependency stops answering. What happens?
hints: Add up the time that three attempts of 5 seconds can take.
Compare that total with the 2 seconds the user will wait.

acceptedIdeas: The user leaves at 2 seconds, and the service holds threads for up to 15 seconds
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The user leaves at 2 seconds, and the service holds threads for up to 15 seconds

choices.label: The user waits 5 seconds and then gets an error
The call fails at 2 seconds, because the user's deadline cancels it automatically
The user leaves at 2 seconds, and the service holds threads for up to 15 seconds
The retries succeed, because the dependency was only briefly unavailable

questions.onCorrect: A timeout has to fit inside the caller's deadline, and so does the whole retry schedule. Here 15 seconds of work is allowed for a request worth 2.

misconceptions.feedback: Three attempts of 5 seconds each can take up to 15 seconds, so the service waits far past 5.
A timeout fires only when it is set. A deadline does not cancel a call that has its own, longer timeout.
The dependency has stopped answering, so each retry waits for its full timeout and fails.

questions.prompt: A calls B, B calls C and C calls a database, and each of A, B and C makes up to 3 attempts at the next service. The database is failing, and when healthy it can take 300 calls per second. 20 requests per second reach A. If the database fails every call, how many calls per second does it receive?
hints: Each attempt at one layer is a call to the next layer.
Three layers with 3 attempts each give 3 × 3 × 3 calls for one request.
Multiply that by the 20 requests per second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 calls per request, and 27 × 20 = 540 calls per second.

questions.onCorrect: 540 calls per second is almost double the 300 the database can take, so retries turn a failing database into an overloaded one. The Amazon Builders' Library describes five layers of three tries, where the database sees 243 times its load.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 20 × 3, which counts the attempts at one layer only. The attempts at B and C multiply on top of it.
That is 20 × 9, which stops after two layers.
That is the number of calls for one request. The question asks for the rate with 20 requests per second.

questions.prompt: One thousand clients lose their connection to a service at the same moment. Each retries after 100 ms, then after 200 ms, then after 400 ms, with no randomness. What does the service see?
hints: Every client uses the same schedule and started at the same moment.
Ask what separates one client's retry from another's.

acceptedIdeas: Waves of about a thousand retries at the same moments, which jitter would spread
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Waves of about a thousand retries at the same moments, which jitter would spread

choices.label: Retries spread over time, since exponential backoff alone prevents any overload
Waves of about a thousand retries at the same moments, which jitter would spread
A steady trickle of retries, because each client's waits differ from the others

questions.onCorrect: Jitter adds a random offset to each wait so that the clients spread out, and backoff with jitter is the standard way to retry a call that may be failing because the dependency is overloaded.

misconceptions.feedback: Backoff spaces out one client's attempts. Clients that started together stay in step, so each retry arrives as a spike.
The waits are the same for every client, so nothing separates them.

questions.prompt: A chain A, B, C and a database has three layers. The team wants retries, since many failures are brief, but is worried about the load on the database. Which policy keeps both?
hints: Work out how many calls the database receives if every layer retries three times.
Then work it out if only one layer retries.

acceptedIdeas: Retry at one layer only, so one request causes at most 3 database calls
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Retry at one layer only, so one request causes at most 3 database calls

choices.label: Retry at one layer only, so one request causes at most 3 database calls
Retry at every layer, so that each service can recover by itself
Never retry, because any retry risks overloading the database
Retry at every layer with a short timeout, so that the waits limit the extra calls

questions.onCorrect: Retrying at a single point keeps the benefit for brief failures and removes the multiplication.

misconceptions.feedback: Three layers with 3 attempts each send up to 27 calls to the database for one request, because the attempts multiply.
Many failures are brief and a retry turns them into successes. The answer is to limit where the retries happen.
A short timeout does not change the multiplication, and each layer still repeats everything below it.

questions.prompt: A circuit breaker has stopped calling a failing service and is now letting a single trial request through. Which state is it in?
hints: One state passes every call and one rejects every call.
The trial request is how the breaker checks for recovery.

acceptedIdeas: Half-open
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Half-open

choices.label: Half-open
Closed, with all calls passing
Open, rejecting all calls
Tripped, waiting out a cool-down

questions.onCorrect: The half-open state sends one trial request, and its result decides whether the breaker closes or opens again.

misconceptions.feedback: A closed breaker passes every call through. This one is limiting calls to a single trial.
An open breaker rejects every call. This one lets one through.
Tripped is a common name for the open state in ordinary speech, but it is not one of the three states, and this one is sending a trial.

questions.prompt: A service must be 99.5% available over 30 days, which is 43,200 minutes. Which is closest to the downtime that allows?
hints: Find the share of time the service may be down, then take that share of 43,200 minutes.
The allowed downtime is (1 − availability) × 43,200 minutes.

acceptedIdeas: About 3½ hours
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 3½ hours

choices.label: About 20 minutes
About 15 hours
About 3 days
About 3½ hours

questions.onCorrect: The service may be down for 0.5% of the period, and 0.5% of 43,200 minutes is 216 minutes, or about three and a half hours.

misconceptions.feedback: About 20 minutes is 0.05% of the period. A target of 99.5% leaves 0.5% for downtime, which is ten times as much.
About 15 hours is 900 minutes, or about 2% of the period. A target of 99.5% leaves only 0.5% for downtime.
About 3 days is a tenth of the period. A target of 99.5% leaves 0.5% for downtime, which is far less.

questions.prompt: A contract promises 99.95% availability over a 365-day year, which is 525,600 minutes. The service had one outage of 4.5 hours and nothing else all year. Did it meet the promise?
hints: The allowed downtime is (1 − availability) × the length of the period.
Convert 4.5 hours to minutes and compare.

acceptedIdeas: No, because 99.95% allows 262.8 minutes of downtime and 4.5 hours is 270
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because 99.95% allows 262.8 minutes of downtime and 4.5 hours is 270

choices.label: Yes, because 4.5 hours is a tiny part of the year and the service ran well otherwise
No, because 99.95% allows 262.8 minutes of downtime and 4.5 hours is 270
Yes, because 99.95% allows about 44 hours of downtime in a year

questions.onCorrect: The outage used 270 of the 262.8 minutes allowed, so the promise was missed by just over seven minutes.

misconceptions.feedback: A small fraction can still exceed a tight target. 99.95% leaves only 0.05%, which is 262.8 minutes.
That reads 99.95% as 0.5% downtime. The allowance is 0.05%, which is 262.8 minutes, about 4.4 hours.

questions.prompt: A request passes through a CDN, a load balancer, an application tier and a database in turn, and each is 99.9% available. The product team wants to promise 99.95%. What availability does the chain give, in percent, to one decimal place?
hints: Every component must work for the request to succeed.
Multiply the four availabilities.
0.999 to the power of 4 is about 0.996.
questions.onCorrect: The chain gives 99.6%, below the 99.95% wanted and below every single component, because in series the availabilities multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the availability of one component. A chain of four is lower than any of its parts.
That is the figure the product team wants. The four components together give less.

questions.prompt: A team runs three replicas that are each 99% available and says the service is 99.9999% available, since all three would have to fail together. What does that figure assume?
hints: The product 0.01 × 0.01 × 0.01 treats the three failures as separate events.
Ask what could take down several replicas at once.

acceptedIdeas: That the replicas fail independently, which a shared rack or power feed would break
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That the replicas fail independently, which a shared rack or power feed would break

choices.label: That the replicas fail independently, which a shared rack or power feed would break
That each replica is at least 99.99% available, so that the arithmetic comes out right
That the replicas are in series, so that all of them must work together

questions.onCorrect: Replicas fail independently only if nothing can take them down together, which is why they are placed in different failure domains.

misconceptions.feedback: The figure uses 1% for each replica, as stated: the calculation is 1 − 0.01 × 0.01 × 0.01.
In series the availability would fall, to about 97%. The service works if any one replica works, which is parallel.

questions.prompt: Two replicas make a pair that is 99.99% available, but both sit behind one power supply that is 99.95% available, which puts the whole at about 99.94%. Which change raises the availability most?
hints: The shared supply is in series with the pair.
Look for the change that removes the supply from the series.

acceptedIdeas: Move the replicas to racks with separate power supplies
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Move the replicas to racks with separate power supplies

choices.label: Add a third replica in the same rack
Buy faster servers for the pair
Raise the pair from 99.99% to 99.999% with better software
Move the replicas to racks with separate power supplies

questions.onCorrect: Putting replicas in separate racks, zones or regions drops the shared component out of the series.

misconceptions.feedback: A third replica behind the same supply still depends on it, so the supply caps the whole at 99.95%.
Speed does not change availability, and the shared supply is the limit.
The pair is already far more available than the supply, so raising it changes the whole by almost nothing: the supply sits in series with it.

questions.prompt: Two independent replicas are each 90% available, and the service works if either does. Why is the combined availability found from 1 − 0.1 × 0.1 and not from 0.9 × 0.9?
hints: Ask when the service as a whole is down.
Work with the chance of failure, not of working.

acceptedIdeas: The service is down only if both replicas are down, and 0.1 × 0.1 is the chance of that
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The service is down only if both replicas are down, and 0.1 × 0.1 is the chance of that

choices.label: The service is down only if both replicas are down, and 0.1 × 0.1 is the chance of that
Parallel components add their availabilities, so 0.9 + 0.9 is used and then capped
0.9 × 0.9 is used for parallel components, and 1 − 0.1 × 0.1 for series ones

questions.onCorrect: Parallel replicas fail the service only together, so the failure chances multiply and the availability is what remains.

misconceptions.feedback: Availabilities are not added, and a sum of 1.8 could not be a probability.
It is the other way round. Series components multiply their availabilities, and parallel ones multiply their failure chances.

questions.prompt: What is the availability of the whole, in percent, to one decimal place?
hints: Combine the pair in parallel first.
The pair is about 0.999999.
Multiply 0.999 by the pair and by 0.999.
questions.onCorrect: The pair adds almost nothing to the downtime, and the two single stages account for nearly all of it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one stage. The two single stages in series already take it below that.
That multiplies three stages of 99.9% as though the pair were a single one. The pair is much better than one replica.
That is about the availability of the pair alone, or of two of the stages in parallel. The three stages are in series.

questions.prompt: Checkout is slow for some users. For one slow request you need to see which of the six services in the chain took the time. Which kind of telemetry shows that? Answer with one word.
hints: You are following a single request across several services.
Each service passes an identifier along with the request.

acceptedIdeas: trace
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: trace

questions.onCorrect: A metric says that latency has doubled, a trace says where, and a log says why.

misconceptions.feedback: A log records an individual event and says why a call failed. It does not join the steps of one request across six services.
A metric says that the p99 latency has doubled. It does not show which call in the chain took the time.

questions.prompt: A service's processor sits at 95% and requests are queueing, though errors are zero and latency is still fine. Which of the four golden signals does this show? Answer with one word.
hints: The question describes how full a resource is.
Latency and errors are normal, so they are not the signal.

acceptedIdeas: saturation
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: saturation

questions.onCorrect: Saturation is the share of the most constrained resource in use, and it often rises before latency or errors do.

misconceptions.feedback: Traffic is how much demand the service receives. Nothing here says the demand changed.
Latency is how long requests take, and it is still fine. The signal that is moving is how full the service is.
Errors are requests that fail, and there are none.

questions.prompt: An SLO says that 99.9% of requests must succeed. In a window with 5,000,000 requests, about how many may fail?
hints: Find the share of requests that may fail, then take that share of 5,000,000.
The share that may fail is 1 minus the target.

acceptedIdeas: About 5,000
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 5,000

choices.label: About 500
None, because a promise of 99.9% means that no request may fail
About 50,000
About 5,000

questions.onCorrect: A target of 99.9% lets 0.1% of requests fail, and 0.1% of 5,000,000 is 5,000.

misconceptions.feedback: A target of 99.9% is below 100%, so it allows a small share of failures. Only a target of 100% would allow none.
500 is 0.01% of 5,000,000. A target of 99.9% leaves 0.1% for failures, which is ten times as much.
50,000 is 1% of 5,000,000, which a target of 99% would allow. A target of 99.9% leaves only 0.1%.

questions.prompt: A service has an SLO of 99.9% over a window of 10,000,000 requests, which gives an error budget of 10,000 failures. The product owner asks for 99.99% to impress customers. What does that change?
hints: The share that may fail is 1 minus the target.
Multiply that share by the 10,000,000 requests.

acceptedIdeas: The budget falls to 1,000 failures, a tenth of the room for releases and incidents
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The budget falls to 1,000 failures, a tenth of the room for releases and incidents

choices.label: The budget falls by a tenth, to 9,000 failures, so a little less room for releases remains
The budget falls to 1,000 failures, a tenth of the room for releases and incidents
The budget stays at 10,000, and only the alerts become stricter

questions.onCorrect: The budget turns the argument about reliability into a number: a tenth of it means a tenth of the room for releases, experiments and outages.

misconceptions.feedback: Each added nine multiplies the allowed failures by one tenth. It does not remove a tenth of them.
The budget is worked out from the target, so a stricter target gives a smaller budget.

questions.prompt: The Site Reliability Workbook suggests paging when a service burns its 30-day error budget at 14.4 times the even pace for one hour. What percentage of the whole 30-day budget is spent in that hour?
hints: An even pace spends the whole budget over the 720 hours of 30 days.
At 14.4 times that pace, one hour spends 14.4 hours' worth.
Divide 14.4 by 720 and write it as a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 14.4 ÷ 720 = 0.02, which is 2% of the budget in one hour.

questions.onCorrect: Two percent in one hour would empty the budget in about 50 hours, 720 ÷ 14.4, which is why this rate deserves a page and not a ticket.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the burn rate itself. The question asks what share of the whole budget one hour at that rate spends.
That divides by 100 where the 720 hours of the window are needed.
That is the number of hours the budget lasts at this rate, not the share spent in one hour.

questions.prompt: A 30-day budget is 20,000 failures. How many failures would an even pace have spent after 6 days?
hints: The even pace spends the budget in proportion to the time.
Six days is a fraction of 30 days.
Multiply the budget by 6 and divide by 30.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Six of the 30 days is a fifth of the window, and a fifth of 20,000 is 4,000.

questions.onCorrect: The even pace is the yardstick against which the failures so far are compared.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole budget. After 6 days an even pace has used only part of it.
That multiplies 6 days by 100 for no reason. The even pace is the budget times 6 over 30.

questions.prompt: How many times faster than an even pace is the budget being spent?
hints: Find the even pace for day 10 first.
Ten of the 30 days is a third of the window.
Divide the failures so far by that even pace.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The even pace after 10 days is 6,000 × 10 ÷ 30 = 2,000, and 4,000 ÷ 2,000 = 2.

questions.onCorrect: At a burn rate of 2 the budget runs out at day 15, halfway through the window.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the even pace by the failures. The burn rate is failures over the even pace.
That compares the failures with 1,000. The even pace after 10 days is larger than that.
That compares the failures with the whole budget.

questions.prompt: It is 3 am. Which of these should wake the on-call engineer?
hints: Page a person only when a human must act now.
Alert on symptoms that users feel and not on causes.

acceptedIdeas: The error budget is burning at 14 times the even pace and checkouts are failing
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The error budget is burning at 14 times the even pace and checkouts are failing

choices.label: The error budget is burning at 14 times the even pace and checkouts are failing
One server's processor use has passed 80%, though latency and errors are still normal
A deployment has finished successfully
The disk on a log server is 70% full and will fill in two weeks

questions.onCorrect: A very high burn rate means the budget will be gone within hours and deserves a page, while a slow one can wait for a ticket.

misconceptions.feedback: A cause that users do not feel can wait. Page on symptoms, such as a rising error rate.
A finished deployment needs no action from a person.
A problem that is two weeks from mattering is a ticket for the morning, not a page.

questions.prompt: A marketing email doubles the number of checkout requests that arrive each second. Which of the four golden signals has moved? Answer with one word.
hints: The change is in how much work arrives.
One of the four signals counts the requests the service receives each second.

acceptedIdeas: traffic
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: traffic

questions.onCorrect: Traffic is the demand on the service, and a rise in it can push saturation and then latency up.

misconceptions.feedback: Saturation is how full the service is. It may rise as a result, but the signal that moved first is the demand itself.
Latency is how long requests take, and it may or may not change. What changed is the number arriving.

questions.prompt: A variant of the shortener receives 10 million new URLs a month, with 200 reads for each write. A colleague wants a sharded database and a queue 'because 10 million a month is a lot'. Use 2,592,000 seconds in a month. What do the rates say?
hints: Divide the monthly total by the seconds in the month, then apply the ratio.
Compare the rates with what one database node can take.

acceptedIdeas: About 4 writes and 770 reads per second, which one replicated database and a cache can serve
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 4 writes and 770 reads per second, which one replicated database and a cache can serve

choices.label: About 4 writes and 770 reads per second, which one replicated database and a cache can serve
About 4 writes and 770 reads per second, which is high enough to need sharding and a queue
About 23,000 reads per second, from reading the 10 million as a daily figure

questions.onCorrect: A count that sounds large is judged by the rate it makes, and about 4 writes per second is far below what one node accepts.

misconceptions.feedback: A single database node accepts at least hundreds of simple writes per second, so 4 per second needs no shards. A number calls for a component only when it is large against what one component can do.
The 10 million is a monthly figure. A day has 86,400 seconds and a month has 2,592,000, and the month is what the question gives.

questions.prompt: The shortener expects 6,000,000,000 links over five years and chooses each code at random from 62 symbols, checking for a collision before it saves. One designer proposes 6 characters, which give 62^6 = 56,800,235,584 codes, and another proposes 7, which give 62^7 = 3,521,614,606,208. What is the difference in practice?
hints: The chance that a random code is already taken equals the share of the space in use.
Divide 6,000,000,000 by each of the two sizes.

acceptedIdeas: With 6 characters about 1 new code in 10 collides by the end, and 7 cut that to under 1 in 500
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With 6 characters about 1 new code in 10 collides by the end, and 7 cut that to under 1 in 500

choices.label: None, because 6 characters hold all 6 billion codes with plenty of room to spare, so collisions are rare
With 6 characters about 1 new code in 10 collides by the end, and 7 cut that to under 1 in 500
7 characters are needed, because 6 cannot hold 6 billion codes

questions.onCorrect: Room matters because random codes collide in proportion to how full the space is: about 10.6% at 6 characters and 0.17% at 7.

misconceptions.feedback: Six characters do hold them, but a random code collides with a chance equal to the share of the space already used, which reaches 10.6% by the end.
62^6 is almost ten times 6 billion, so six characters can hold every link.

questions.prompt: The shortener receives 3,858 redirects per second on average, and its database is sized for 400 reads per second. A reviewer asks whether the cache is justified. Which answer is right?
hints: Compare the redirect rate with what the database is sized for.
A cache at a 95% hit rate lets only the misses through.

acceptedIdeas: Yes, because without it the database would face ten times the 400 reads per second it is sized for
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Yes, because without it the database would face ten times the 400 reads per second it is sized for

choices.label: No, because 3,858 reads per second is small enough for any modern database to serve easily without a cache
Yes, because without it the database would face ten times the 400 reads per second it is sized for
No, because most of the traffic is writes

questions.onCorrect: A 95% hit rate lets 5% through, about 193 reads per second, which is within 400, so the number justifies the cache.

misconceptions.feedback: Whether a number is small depends on what the component can take, and this database is sized for 400. 3,858 is almost ten times that.
The estimate has 100 reads for each write, so reads are almost all of the load.

questions.prompt: In the shortener, a failover to a new database leader pauses link creation for 90 seconds. Redirects keep being served from the cache and the followers. Does the pause count against the 99.9% target for redirects?
hints: Ask which requests the pause affects, and which it does not.
A target is stated for one behaviour, as measured from the user's side.

acceptedIdeas: Little, because redirects are still served and link creation needs its own target
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Little, because redirects are still served and link creation needs its own target

choices.label: Yes in full, because any pause in link creation means the whole service is down
Little, because redirects are still served and link creation needs its own target
No, because a failover is a normal event and never counts against a target

questions.onCorrect: Redirects and link creation are different behaviours, so each gets its own target, and a pause in one does not spend the budget of the other.

misconceptions.feedback: Reads go to the cache and the followers, which stay up. Counting the pause against redirects would hide where the failures are.
A target counts what users experience, whatever the cause. Link creations that fail during the pause count against the target for creation.

questions.prompt: A team prints short links on posters, wants as few repeat visits as possible to reach its servers, and has no need to count them. Which redirect status should the service send?
hints: The team wants browsers to remember the redirect.
Only the permanent redirect may be cached by browsers.

acceptedIdeas: 301, moved permanently, which browsers may cache
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 301, moved permanently, which browsers may cache

questions.onCorrect: A service that must count every visit makes the opposite choice and sends 302.

misconceptions.feedback: A 302 is a temporary redirect that browsers normally do not cache, so every repeat visit would reach the servers, which is the load this team wants to avoid.

choices.label: 302, found, a temporary redirect that is not normally cached
301, moved permanently, which browsers may cache

questions.prompt: The shortener is asked to handle a hundred times more traffic, and you redo the estimate from the start. In what order do you work out these numbers, each from the one before?
hints: Each number is computed from the one before it.
The fleet size comes last, because it needs the peak load.

items: New URLs per month
Writes per second, from the monthly total
Average redirects per second, from the read/write ratio
