Peak redirects per second, from the peak factor
Servers needed, from what one server carries at the target utilisation

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The monthly total gives the write rate, the ratio turns that into the average read rate, the peak factor raises it to the load that must be met, and the fleet size follows from what each server can carry.

questions.onCorrect: Every number is built from the one before it, so a change at the start of the chain, such as a hundredfold more URLs, flows through to the number of servers.

questions.prompt: In a social feed, a typical user follows 200 accounts, has about 200 followers, posts 5 times a day and opens the feed 10 times a day. Compare the two designs for the work such a user causes in a day. Which statement is right?
hints: For fan-out on write, count the feed writes caused by the user's posts and the reads of the feed.
For fan-out on read, count the post writes and one lookup per followed account on each view.

acceptedIdeas: Fan-out on write does about 1,010 operations and fan-out on read about 2,005
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fan-out on write does about 1,010 operations and fan-out on read about 2,005

choices.label: Fan-out on read is cheaper, because a post is stored once
Both do the same work, because every follower still sees every post of the account
Fan-out on write does about 1,010 operations and fan-out on read about 2,005

questions.onCorrect: Here the feed is opened often enough that writing ahead is cheaper, though neither design is simply better.

misconceptions.feedback: Storing a post once does make writes cheap, but each feed view then costs a lookup for each of the 200 accounts followed, 2,000 a day.
Both deliver the same posts, but the work differs: it happens at write time in one design and at read time in the other.

questions.prompt: A feed fans posts out through a background queue. A user publishes a post, opens their own feed straight away, and the post is missing for a few seconds. Which fix costs least?
hints: Ask who is sure to notice the gap.
Look for a fix that works for the author without changing what followers see.

acceptedIdeas: Merge the user's own recent posts into their feed when it is read
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Merge the user's own recent posts into their feed when it is read

choices.label: Merge the user's own recent posts into their feed when it is read
Make the fan-out finish for every follower before replying to the author
Switch to fan-out on read for everyone, which removes the delay

questions.onCorrect: Read-your-writes promises only that users see their own writes at once, and it is cheaper than making every copy current.

misconceptions.feedback: Waiting for every follower's copy would make posting as slow as the largest fan-out, and it would fail whenever a feed store is down.
That removes the delay but gives up the cheap reads that made fan-out on write worth choosing, to close a gap that only the author notices.

questions.prompt: An account with 20,000,000 followers posts once, and feed writes are done at 100,000 per second. About how long does it take to fan out the post?
hints: Divide the number of feed writes by the number of writes done in one second.
Divide the number of followers by the rate of feed writes.

acceptedIdeas: A few minutes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A few minutes

choices.label: Well under a second
A few minutes
A few seconds
Several hours

questions.onCorrect: The post needs 20,000,000 writes, which at 100,000 per second takes 200 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: 100,000 writes per second is fast, but this post needs 20,000,000 writes, which is 200 times as many as one second's worth.
A few seconds would complete only a few hundred thousand writes, and this post needs 20,000,000.
At 100,000 writes per second an hour of work completes 360,000,000 writes, so 20,000,000 take a small fraction of an hour.

questions.prompt: A user follows 200 accounts, of which 3 are very large and are fetched at read time. The other accounts are fanned out on write into one precomputed feed. What work does one feed view cause?
hints: Ask which posts are already in the precomputed feed and which still have to be fetched when the feed is opened.
Count the precomputed feed as one read, then add the accounts fetched at read time.

acceptedIdeas: One read of the precomputed feed and 3 lookups for the large accounts
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One read of the precomputed feed and 3 lookups for the large accounts

choices.label: One read of the precomputed feed and 3 lookups for the large accounts
3 lookups, one for each large account
One read of the precomputed feed, since the feed holds everything the user needs
200 lookups, one for each account the user follows

questions.onCorrect: The view reads the precomputed feed once and looks up the 3 large accounts, which is 4 operations where fan-out on read would need 200.

misconceptions.feedback: Looking up every followed account is fan-out on read. Here the posts of the other 197 accounts are already in the precomputed feed.
The precomputed feed still has to be read, since it holds the posts of the other 197 accounts.
The very large accounts are not copied into feeds, so their posts have to be fetched at read time.

questions.prompt: A design has one database with no replica, so that if the database fails the whole service stops. What is such a component called?
hints: The component has nothing to take over from it.
The review asks what happens if this component fails.

acceptedIdeas: Single point of failure
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Single point of failure

questions.onCorrect: The remedy is a second copy in another failure domain, with a way to promote it, which the availability lesson priced in nines.

misconceptions.feedback: A bottleneck limits throughput. The component described is one whose failure stops the whole service.
A failure domain is a set of things that fail together, such as a rack. It is not the name for a component with nothing to take over from it.
A hot key is one key that receives far more requests than the others. It says nothing about what happens when a component fails.

choices.label: Bottleneck, the part that limits throughput
Single point of failure
Failure domain, the set of things that fail together
Hot key, a key that gets most of the load

questions.prompt: A site handles 200 requests per second, and 10% of them call an email provider that has stopped answering, with no timeout. How many calls per second hang?
hints: Only the requests that call the provider are affected.
That is 10% of the 200 requests.
Multiply 200 by 0.1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 10% of 200 is 0.1 × 200 = 20 calls per second.

questions.onCorrect: Each hanging call holds a thread, so this rate is the rate at which threads are used up.

misconceptions.feedback: That is all the requests. Only 10% call the provider.
That takes 1% of the requests. The share is 10%.

questions.prompt: In the review, sign-up requests call an email provider with no timeout, and the web threads run out when the provider stops answering. Which change closes the hole best?
hints: Ask what holds the threads, and for how long.
Look for a change that limits the wait and takes the call off the sign-up path.

acceptedIdeas: A short timeout, and the email sent through a queue so sign-up does not wait
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A short timeout, and the email sent through a queue so sign-up does not wait

choices.label: Add more web servers, so that there are more threads to lose when the provider hangs
A short timeout, and the email sent through a queue so sign-up does not wait
Retry the email call until it succeeds, so that no email is lost

questions.onCorrect: A timeout bounds how long a thread is held and a queue takes the email out of the sign-up path, so a slow provider no longer takes the site down.

misconceptions.feedback: More servers only delay the point where the threads are used up, because each hanging call still holds a thread for ever.
Retrying a call that hangs holds more threads for longer and multiplies the load on a provider that is already failing.

questions.prompt: A design review of a video upload service lists findings. Which of the three review questions does each finding answer: what is the single point of failure, what is unbounded, or what is unmeasured?
hints: Ask whether the finding is about a part with no backup, a quantity with no limit, or a number nobody has.
A queue or a retry count with no cap is unbounded, not a single point of failure.

items.label: Every upload is written to one storage server that has no replica
items.explanation: If that server fails, nothing takes over from it.

items.label: One load balancer receives every request and has no standby
items.explanation: Every request passes through it, and nothing can take its place.

items.label: A failed transcoding job is retried until it succeeds, with no maximum
items.explanation: A retry count with no limit will in time be exceeded.

items.label: The queue of videos waiting for transcoding has no size limit
items.explanation: A queue with no limit grows until something else fails.

items.label: Nobody has estimated how many uploads arrive at the evening peak
items.explanation: A number nobody has estimated is a place where the design is a guess.

items.label: No metric shows how long a video waits before it is transcoded
items.explanation: A signal nobody watches cannot show a problem as it grows.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The single storage server and the lone balancer are single points of failure; the unlimited retries and the unlimited queue are unbounded; the unestimated peak and the missing waiting-time metric are unmeasured.

questions.onCorrect: Three questions do most of the work in a review: what has nothing to take over from it, what has no limit, and what nobody has measured.

questions.prompt: Which kind of requirement is the statement "Link owners can see how many times each short link was opened"?
hints: Ask whether the statement says what the service does or how well it does it.
Ask whether the statement could be checked by trying it once.

acceptedIdeas: A functional requirement, because it names something the service does
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A functional requirement, because it names something the service does

questions.onCorrect: A functional requirement can be tested once, and any numbers belong to separate quality targets for the same behaviour.

choices.label: A quality target, because it involves counting something in the service
A functional requirement, because it names something the service does
Neither kind, because it carries no number or threshold

misconceptions.feedback: Counting is not what makes something a quality target. A quality target says how well something must be delivered, with a threshold, and this statement gives none.
A requirement does not need a number to be a requirement. Only a quality target does, while a functional requirement is checked by trying the behaviour once.

questions.prompt: Which property does this statement describe: "after a user changes their display name, the next profile page that anyone opens shows the new name"?
hints: Ask what the statement says about the version a reader sees.
Match the statement to one of the four properties the lesson named.

acceptedIdeas: Consistency
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Consistency

questions.onCorrect: Consistency concerns whether a reader sees the most recent write, which is what the statement asks for.

choices.label: Availability
Durability
Latency
Consistency

misconceptions.feedback: Availability is the fraction of requests that succeed. Here the request succeeds either way; the statement is about which version of the name the reader is shown.
Durability is whether accepted data can still be read later. The statement is about which version of the name is shown, not about whether it survives a failure.
Latency is how long a request takes. The statement puts no limit on time, only on which version of the name is shown.

questions.prompt: Why is the read rate found by multiplying the 5 writes per second by 200?
hints: Ask what the ratio of 200 to 1 says about one write.
Think about what happens to the read rate when the write rate doubles.

acceptedIdeas: Each of the 5 writes brings its own 200 reads, so the 200 is counted 5 times.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each of the 5 writes brings its own 200 reads, so the 200 is counted 5 times.

questions.onCorrect: Each write brings its own 200 reads, so 5 writes bring 5 groups of 200, which is repeated addition and therefore multiplication.

choices.label: The 200 reads are shared among the 5 writes, so each write receives only a part of them.
The 200 is a number of reads that arrive every second, and it is added to the 5 writes.
Each of the 5 writes brings its own 200 reads, so the 200 is counted 5 times.

misconceptions.feedback: Sharing would put fewer than 200 reads against each write, but the ratio of 200 reads to 1 write says that reads are the larger number.
The 200 is a ratio, the reads for each write. It is not a separate rate of reads arriving every second on top of the writes.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a measurable quality target?
hints: A measurable target names a quantity, a threshold and a share of requests.
Look for the line you could test by counting requests in the logs.

acceptedIdeas: 99.9% of link creations succeed in each month
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 99.9% of link creations succeed in each month

questions.onCorrect: The statement fixes a share of requests that must succeed over a period, so counting the logs is enough to check it.

choices.label: The service should be highly available at all times
99.9% of link creations succeed in each month
Link creation should feel instant
Users can delete their own links

misconceptions.feedback: Highly available has no figure, so no measurement could show whether it had been met.
Instant has no threshold and no share of requests, so no measurement could show whether it had been met.
That is a behaviour, a functional requirement, and it is met by trying it once.

questions.prompt: A team starts the design of a photo-sharing service and follows the method of this lesson. In what order do they take these steps?
hints: Each step needs a result from an earlier one.
A sketch has to exist before it can be probed for failures.

items: Clarify the scope: behaviours, quality targets and non-goals
Estimate the load in requests per second, storage and bandwidth
Define the interface that clients call
Define the data and how it is found
Sketch the components
Probe the sketch for its bottleneck and for what happens when a part fails

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The scope comes first because the load cannot be estimated until it says what counts as a request. The interface and the data follow the estimate, the components come only then, and the probe is last because it needs a sketch to test.

questions.onCorrect: Each step needs a result from the one before: a component is chosen from the load, and the load is estimated from the scope.

questions.prompt: A news app expects 5 million daily users who each make 40 requests a day. Plan for a peak factor of 3, and for servers that handle 2,000 requests per second each and are planned at 70% utilisation at peak. Use 86,400 seconds in a day. How many servers do you book?
hints: Turn the daily total into a rate first, then apply the peak factor.
Each server should carry 70% of 2,000 requests per second at peak.
Divide the peak load by what one server should carry, and round up to a whole server.
questions.onCorrect: The peak is about 6,900 requests per second and each server should carry 1,400, so 4.96 servers rounds up to 5. That leaves almost no spare capacity, and if one server fails the other four would run at about 87%.

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds 4.96 down. Four servers would each carry 1,736 requests per second, 87% of their capacity against the 70% planned.
That is the peak load in requests per second. The question asks for the number of servers that carry it.
That is the average load. The fleet has to be sized for the peak, and then divided by what one server carries.

questions.prompt: A service runs in two regions. A dashboard shows each region's p99 latency, 200 ms and 800 ms, and a report gives the service's p99 as their average, 500 ms. Why can that figure not be trusted?
hints: A percentile is a position in a sorted list of requests.
Two regions with different amounts of traffic would give a different combined list.

acceptedIdeas: Percentiles cannot be averaged, because the combined p99 depends on the traffic mix
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Percentiles cannot be averaged, because the combined p99 depends on the traffic mix

choices.label: Percentiles cannot be averaged, because the combined p99 depends on the traffic mix
Averaging is fine, but the report should have averaged the two means instead of the p99s
The service's p99 must equal the larger of the two, so it is exactly 800 ms
A p99 can only be measured within one region, so no figure for the service exists

questions.onCorrect: The combined p99 lies somewhere between 200 and 800 ms depending on the traffic mix, so the 500 ms in the report is a guess. Merge the requests, or their histograms, and read the p99 from the result.

misconceptions.feedback: The mean hides the slow requests, which is the reason latency is stated as a percentile. A mean of means has the same flaw.
The combined p99 lies between 200 and 800 ms, and where it falls depends on how much traffic each region carries.
A service-wide percentile can be read from the combined requests or from merged histograms. It cannot be got by averaging the regional figures.

questions.prompt: A search page waits for 40 shards in parallel. Each shard answers within the target 98% of the time, independently of the others. To the nearest percent, how often does the page miss the target?
hints: Each shard is fast with probability 0.98, and the page is fast only if all 40 are.
Multiply: 0.98 to the power of 40 is about 0.446.
The page misses the target whenever at least one shard does, which is the opposite event.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 0.98^40 ≈ 0.446, so the page is slow 1 − 0.446 ≈ 0.554, which is 55%.

questions.onCorrect: The page misses the target 55% of the time, so if it is meant to meet it at least 80% of the time, each shard would have to be fast about 99.4% of the time and not 98%.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance for a single shard. The page waits for 40 of them, so the chances compound.
That adds the 2% forty times. Probabilities of independent events do not add like this; the page is fast only if all 40 shards are fast, and those chances multiply.
That is the share of pages that are fast, 0.446. The question asks how often the page misses the target.

questions.prompt: A service stores each user's login session in the memory of the server that created it, and its servers sit behind a load balancer. Which change would let the service be scaled out by adding servers?
hints: Think about what happens when the balancer picks a different server for the next request.
The cart example failed because the second server lacked something.

acceptedIdeas: Keep the sessions in a shared cache that every server reads
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Keep the sessions in a shared cache that every server reads

questions.onCorrect: Once no session lives in a single server's memory, the balancer can send any request anywhere, and a new server is useful at once.

choices.label: Keep the sessions in a shared cache that every server reads
Replace each server with a machine that has more memory
Send each user's requests to a different server every time they arrive
Add a second load balancer in front of the servers

misconceptions.feedback: A bigger machine is vertical scaling. It leaves each session in one server's memory, so the other servers still cannot answer for that user.
Round robin spreads the requests, but a server that did not create a session has no record of it, so spreading harder makes the missing sessions more frequent.
A second balancer removes a single point of failure at the front, but each session still sits in the memory of one server.

questions.prompt: The database behind a shop can serve 1,500 requests per second. At peak 10,000 requests per second arrive, and the team puts a cache in front of the database. What is the lowest hit rate, in percent, that keeps the database within its limit?
hints: The database should receive no more than 1,500 of the 10,000 requests.
That share is the miss rate.
The hit rate is 1 minus the miss rate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 1,500 ÷ 10,000 = 15% may miss, so the hit rate has to be at least 85%.

questions.onCorrect: At 85% the 1,500 requests that miss are exactly what the database can take, with no margin, so a real design would aim higher and would also plan for the cold cache after a restart, when the hit rate is zero.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the miss rate, the share allowed through to the database. The question asks for the hit rate.
That is the database's limit in requests per second. The question asks for a percentage of the requests.
That is the hit rate of the earlier example. Here the limit of 1,500 sets the figure.

questions.prompt: A new feature stores a login session for each user, found by a token on every request, about 50,000 times per second. Sessions are never joined to anything and expire after 30 minutes. Which store fits the access pattern?
hints: Write down how the data is read: by key, by range, by join or by following links.
Ask which of those the feature does on every request.

acceptedIdeas: A key-value store, because every request is a lookup by key
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A key-value store, because every request is a lookup by key

choices.label: A key-value store, because every request is a lookup by key
A relational database, because sessions belong to users and will need joins
A graph store, because a session links a user to a device

questions.onCorrect: A lookup by key with no joins or ranges is the simplest access pattern, and a key-value store is built for it.

misconceptions.feedback: The sessions are never joined to anything. A join is a reason to choose a relational database, and this feature has no use for one.
A graph store suits traversal, such as the friends of friends of a user. No request here follows links from one record to the next.

questions.prompt: A table has an index on `(store_id, sold_at)`. Which query can use the index efficiently?
hints: The index is sorted first by store, then by date within each store.
A query has to give the first column to use the sorted order.

acceptedIdeas: Sales at store 12 on 3 March
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sales at store 12 on 3 March

questions.onCorrect: The query names the first column and then the second, so the database can jump to store 12 and read the entries for 3 March in sequence.

choices.label: All sales on 3 March, at every store
Sales whose amount is above 100
Sales at store 12 on 3 March
Stores whose name starts with A

misconceptions.feedback: The dates are sorted only within each store, so the sales for one date are scattered through the index.
The amount is not in the index at all, so the database would have to read the rows.
The store name is not in the index, and the table it belongs to may be a different one.

questions.prompt: A table has 30,000,000 rows, and 100 rows fit on a page. How many pages does a full scan read?
hints: A scan reads every page.
Divide the rows by the rows per page.
30,000,000 ÷ 100 removes two zeros.
questions.onCorrect: The scan reads 300,000 pages, and an index would need only 4 levels for the same table.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of rows. A page holds 100 of them.
That divides by 10. Each page holds 100 rows.
That is the number of index levels, not the pages of a scan.

questions.prompt: A bank needs to list a customer's transactions for a month, join them to merchant details, and move money between two accounts so that either both changes happen or neither does. Which store fits?
hints: Write down the access patterns the bank needs.
Ask which store gives a transaction across two accounts as standard.

acceptedIdeas: A relational database, since it gives joins, ranges and transactions
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A relational database, since it gives joins, ranges and transactions

choices.label: A key-value store, because each transaction can be fetched by its id
A graph store, because accounts are linked to each other
A relational database, since it gives joins, ranges and transactions

questions.onCorrect: Joins, ranges and transactions are what a relational database provides as standard, and they decide the choice here.

misconceptions.feedback: A key-value store fetches one record by key. A month of transactions is a range, the merchant details need a join, and an atomic transfer needs a transaction.
A graph store follows links from one record to the next. The queries here are a range, a join and a transaction, which a relational database provides as standard.

questions.prompt:
A query for one customer's orders is slow on a table of 5,000,000 rows. The database reports this plan.

`Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..95310.00 rows=48 width=24)`
`  Filter: (customer_id = 7)`

What should you do?
hints: The plan names the way the table is read.
Look at which column the filter uses.

acceptedIdeas: Create an index on `customer_id`, so the filter no longer scans the table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Create an index on `customer_id`, so the filter no longer scans the table

choices.label: Create an index on `customer_id`, so the filter no longer scans the table
Add more memory to the server, since a scan is only a memory problem for the server
Create an index on `id`, which is the primary key

questions.onCorrect: A sequential scan reads every page, whereas an index on the filtered column lets the database walk a few pages to the 48 matching rows.

misconceptions.feedback: More memory may speed up the scan a little, but it still reads every page of the table. An index avoids the scan.
The filter is on `customer_id`. An index on another column cannot serve a filter on this one.

questions.prompt: A table holds 6 TB and takes 24,000 writes per second at peak. One shard can hold at most 500 GB and take at most 2,500 writes per second. What is the smallest number of shards that satisfies both limits?
hints: Each limit gives its own minimum number of shards, so work them out separately.
6 TB is 6,000 GB, and 24,000 writes per second need shards that each take 2,500.
Take the larger of the two minimums.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 6,000 ÷ 500 = 12 shards for storage and 24,000 ÷ 2,500 = 9.6, so 10, for writes. The larger is 12.

questions.onCorrect: Storage needs 12 shards and writes need only 10, so storage sets the count. With 12 shards each takes 2,000 writes per second, 80% of its limit.

misconceptions.feedback: That meets the write limit alone. At 10 shards each would hold 600 GB, over the 500 GB limit.
That is the unrounded figure for writes only. Shards come whole, and storage needs more of them.
That divides 6 TB by 250 GB or adds the two counts. The limits are separate, and the larger of the two applies.

questions.prompt: A user posts a comment, and the page that loads straight afterwards does not show it. Ten seconds later a reload shows it. Which cause is most likely?
hints: The comment appeared later, so it was stored. Ask which machine answered the first read.
Think about replication lag.

acceptedIdeas: A follower that had not yet applied the write answered the read
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A follower that had not yet applied the write answered the read

questions.onCorrect: The leader had the comment, but the follower that answered had not applied it yet, so the data was late and not lost.

choices.label: The write failed, so the comment was never stored
The disk was full, so the comment could not be saved
The cache was cold, so the first read took longer than usual for that user
A follower that had not yet applied the write answered the read

misconceptions.feedback: A comment that was never stored would stay missing however long you waited, and this one appeared.
A write that could not be saved would not appear later, and this comment did.
A cold cache makes a read slow. It does not return a version from before the write.

questions.prompt: A bank's cash machines decline every withdrawal while they cannot reach the other replicas of an account balance, because a stale balance could let money be withdrawn twice. What does the bank give up while that lasts?
hints: Ask what a customer at a cash machine experiences when the withdrawal is declined.
Ask who gets no answer while the machines refuse.

acceptedIdeas: Availability, because some customers get no answer
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Availability, because some customers get no answer

questions.onCorrect: Declining keeps the balances from drifting apart, and the price is that some customers get no answer.

choices.label: Consistency, because the replicas may disagree about the balance
Durability, because balances that were already stored are lost
Availability, because some customers get no answer

misconceptions.feedback: Declining withdrawals keeps the replicas from holding different balances, which preserves consistency.
Nothing that was stored has been lost. Durability concerns data that was accepted, and no balance has been deleted.

questions.prompt: A product team lists features of an online shop. Which need strong consistency, and which can use eventual consistency?
hints: Ask what goes wrong if a reader sees an out-of-date value.
A number that can be a few seconds behind without harm is a candidate for eventual consistency.

items.label: Checking an account balance before approving a withdrawal
items.explanation: A stale balance could let a withdrawal go through twice.

items.label: Reserving the last seat on a flight
items.explanation: Two buyers must not both be told that the seat is theirs.

items.label: Claiming a username that has to be unique
items.explanation: Two accounts with the same name would break the rule the feature exists for.

items.label: The like count under a post
items.explanation: A number a few seconds behind harms no one.

items.label: The number of times a video has been watched
items.explanation: A count that catches up later is as useful as an exact one.

items.label: The list of suggested people to follow
items.explanation: A suggestion that is a minute old is as good as a fresh one.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The balance check, the seat reservation and the unique username need strong consistency; the like count, the watch count and the suggestions can be eventually consistent.

questions.onCorrect: The right guarantee depends on the data: where a stale read causes harm the system pays for strong consistency, and where it does not the weaker, cheaper promise is enough.

questions.prompt: A consensus group of 3 nodes is split by a network partition, with 2 nodes on one side and 1 on the other. What happens?
hints: A group makes progress while a majority of its nodes can talk to each other.
Count the nodes on each side against the majority of 3.

acceptedIdeas: The side with two nodes keeps working, and the lone node stops taking changes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The side with two nodes keeps working, and the lone node stops taking changes

choices.label: Both sides keep accepting changes, so that the service stays available to users
Neither side can accept changes, because every node must agree
The side with two nodes keeps working, and the lone node stops taking changes
The side that held the leader keeps working, wherever the majority is

questions.onCorrect: This is CAP's choice made visible: the group keeps one history by refusing to make progress on the side that has no majority.

misconceptions.feedback: Two sides accepting changes would produce two histories. Consensus keeps one by refusing to make progress without a majority.
A majority is enough, and 2 of 3 is a majority.
The leader alone does not decide. It needs a majority to commit a change, and a lone node cannot form one.

questions.prompt: Each of these describes what a queue and its consumer do when a message goes missing or arrives twice. Which delivery guarantee is each?
hints: Ask whether the system may lose a message, repeat one, or neither in effect.
Effectively-once needs a repeated message to do no harm.

items.label: The producer sends each message once and does not resend it if no acknowledgement comes
items.explanation: Nothing is repeated, so a dropped message is gone.

items.label: A log shipper loses a line when the network drops it, and never sends a line twice
items.explanation: Loss is allowed and repetition is not.

items.label: The broker resends a message until the consumer acknowledges it, so a lost acknowledgement produces a duplicate
items.explanation: Nothing is lost, and a repeat is possible.

items.label: A job runner reruns a task whose completion was never confirmed
items.explanation: It prefers a repeat to a missing task.

items.label: The broker resends until acknowledged, and the consumer records each message id with its effect in one transaction
items.explanation: A repeat finds the record and does nothing, so the effect happens once.

items.label: A payment service stores the idempotency key of each request, so a repeated request charges once
items.explanation: Delivery may repeat while the effect happens once.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The producer that never resends and the log shipper are at-most-once; the resending broker and the job runner are at-least-once; the transactional consumer and the idempotency key give effectively-once.

questions.onCorrect: Effectively-once is what systems achieve in practice: at-least-once delivery together with a consumer that is idempotent.

questions.prompt: A queue receives 150 messages per second and its consumers process 100 per second, so its backlog grows every minute. The team raises the queue's size limit tenfold. Does that fix the problem?
hints: Work out how fast the backlog grows and what a larger limit changes.
Ask what happens once the larger queue is full.

acceptedIdeas: No, because the backlog still grows by 50 per second and only fills ten times later
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because the backlog still grows by 50 per second and only fills ten times later

choices.label: No, because the backlog still grows by 50 per second and only fills ten times later
Yes, because a larger queue can absorb the extra messages indefinitely without trouble
Yes, because messages in a longer queue are processed faster
No, because the size limit never affects how many messages are accepted in total

questions.onCorrect: Only more consumer capacity, fewer arrivals or backpressure on the producers remove the shortfall, and a bigger queue postpones the point at which it fills.

misconceptions.feedback: A queue absorbs bursts, but it is safe only while arrivals stay below the capacity of the consumers on average. Here the shortfall is permanent.
A longer queue means a longer wait for each message and not faster processing.
The limit decides when the broker starts refusing messages, so it does matter for that. It does not remove the shortfall.

questions.prompt: A circuit breaker opens after 5 failures in a row. So far it has seen 3 failures in a row. Which state is it in?
hints: Ask whether the failures have reached the limit.
One state passes calls, one rejects them, and one lets a single trial through.

acceptedIdeas: Closed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Closed

questions.onCorrect: Until the failures reach the limit the breaker stays closed, passes every call through and keeps counting.

choices.label: Closed
Open
Half-open

misconceptions.feedback: A breaker opens only when the failures reach its limit, and 3 is short of 5.
Half-open is the state a breaker enters after a cool-down, when it has been open. This one has not opened.

questions.prompt: Why does C receive 4 × 3 calls and not 4 + 3?
hints: Follow one call from A to B and ask how many attempts it causes at C.
Then ask what happens to the next call from A.

acceptedIdeas: Each call that B receives makes its own 3 attempts to C.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each call that B receives makes its own 3 attempts to C.

questions.onCorrect: Each of the 4 calls to B makes 3 attempts to C, so the attempts multiply: 4 groups of 3.

choices.label: Each call that B receives makes its own 3 attempts to C.
B makes its 3 attempts only after A has finished its 4 attempts.
Multiplying always gives the safer figure for a count.

misconceptions.feedback: Nothing makes B wait for A to finish. B acts on each call as it arrives.
A count is multiplied or added according to how the attempts are related, not because one gives a bigger number.

questions.prompt: How many calls does D receive from one request to A?
hints: Count the calls that each layer receives, starting from A.
B receives 3 calls and C receives 6.
Each call to C makes 3 attempts to D.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: B receives 3 calls, C receives 3 × 2 = 6, and D receives 6 × 3 = 18.

questions.onCorrect: The attempts multiply down the chain, and the last layer, the one that is failing, receives the largest count.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 3, 2 and 3. The attempts multiply from layer to layer.
That is the number of calls C receives. Each of those makes 3 attempts to D.
That gives C only 2 attempts to D. C makes 3.

questions.prompt: A dependency fails and later recovers while a circuit breaker watches the calls to it. In what order do these things happen?
hints: The breaker opens only after the failures have been counted.
It becomes half-open after a cool-down, and closes only when the trial succeeds.

items: Calls pass through and five failures in a row are counted
The breaker opens, and calls fail at once without being sent
After the cool-down the breaker becomes half-open and lets one trial request through
The trial request succeeds
The breaker closes, and calls pass through again

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The failures are counted while the breaker is closed, and the fifth opens it. After the cool-down one trial request goes through, and when it succeeds the breaker closes.

questions.onCorrect: While the breaker is open the failing dependency receives no load, and the single trial request is how it finds out that the dependency has recovered.

questions.prompt: A client sends a request to charge a card, and the call times out with no reply. It sends the same request again, and the request carries no idempotency key. What can go wrong?
hints: A timeout means no reply arrived, which is not the same as the request not running.
Ask what the server could use to recognise the second request as a repeat.

acceptedIdeas: The first attempt may have worked before its reply was lost, so the card is charged twice
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first attempt may have worked before its reply was lost, so the card is charged twice

choices.label: Nothing, because a timeout shows that the first request never ran at all
The server rejects the second request automatically as a duplicate of the first one
The first attempt may have worked before its reply was lost, so the card is charged twice

questions.onCorrect: A request with side effects is safe to retry only when it carries an idempotency key, which guarantees that the side effects happen once however often it is retried.

misconceptions.feedback: Silence does not say whether the request was lost on the way, is still being worked on, or was carried out and the reply was lost.
A server can recognise a repeat only if the request carries a key to match it against.

questions.prompt: Your database is 2 TB and would be restored from a backup over a 1 Gbit/s link, which carries 125 MB per second. The business needs the service back within 1 hour of a total loss. Use 1 TB = 1,000,000 MB. How many hours does the restore alone take, to one decimal place?
hints: Convert the size to megabytes, and use the 125 MB per second that the link carries.
2,000,000 MB at 125 MB per second is a number of seconds.
Divide by 3,600 to turn seconds into hours.
questions.onCorrect: A 4.4-hour restore misses a recovery time objective of 1 hour by a wide margin, so the RTO needs a standby that takes over, or replication, rather than a restore from backup.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the link as 1 GB per second. A 1 Gbit/s link carries 125 MB per second, one eighth of that.
That is the time in seconds. The question asks for hours.
That divides by 125 gigabits where megabytes are meant, or multiplies by 8 in the wrong place; the link carries 125 MB per second.

questions.prompt: A checkout service needs five other services, each 99.95% available, and every one of them must answer for a checkout to succeed. The product owner wants to promise customers 99.95%. Why can the service not keep that promise?
hints: If every service must work, the services are in series.
Multiply 0.9995 by itself five times.

acceptedIdeas: Five required services in series give about 99.75%, lower than any one of them
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Five required services in series give about 99.75%, lower than any one of them

choices.label: It can, because the weakest dependency is 99.95%
It can, because the availabilities of services add up when the services are combined
Five required services in series give about 99.75%, lower than any one of them

questions.onCorrect: A long chain of dependencies drains availability, which is why each hard dependency has to be justified or given a fallback.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the figure for one dependency. A chain is always less available than its weakest link.
Series availabilities multiply and do not add, and the product is lower than each factor.

questions.prompt: A request meets these arrangements of components. In which does every component have to work (series), and in which does any one working keep the service up (parallel)?
hints: Ask whether one failure stops the request or another component can take over.
Components that all have to answer are in series.

items.label: A request passes a balancer, an application server and a database in turn
items.explanation: The request needs every one of them, so their availabilities multiply.

items.label: Checkout calls the payment provider and the inventory service, and needs both
items.explanation: If either is down the checkout fails.

items.label: Login needs the identity service and the session store
items.explanation: Both must answer for a login to succeed.

items.label: Any of three replicas can answer a read
items.explanation: The read fails only if all three are down.

items.label: Clients are given two regions and use whichever responds
items.explanation: One region is enough to keep the service up.

items.label: Either of two application servers behind a balancer can handle a request
items.explanation: The request fails only if both servers are down.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The balancer chain, the checkout needing two services and the login needing two services are series; the three replicas, the two regions and the two application servers are parallel.

questions.onCorrect: A chain is always less available than its weakest link, and replicas in parallel fail the service only when all of them fail.

questions.prompt: Backups run every 4 hours. Which statement about the recovery point objective is correct?
hints: The worst case is a failure just before the next backup.
The data since the last backup is what is lost.

acceptedIdeas: The RPO is 4 hours, because a failure just before a backup loses a full interval
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The RPO is 4 hours, because a failure just before a backup loses a full interval

questions.onCorrect: The RPO is therefore at best 4 hours, and a smaller RPO needs more frequent backups or continuous replication.

choices.label: The RPO is 2 hours, because failures are spread evenly across the backup interval
The RPO is 4 hours, because a failure just before a backup loses a full interval
The RPO is 8 hours, because a failed backup would add a second whole interval

misconceptions.feedback: The RPO is the most data that can be lost, so it is set by the worst case and not by the average.
The loss cannot exceed the time since the last backup, which is at most one interval.

questions.prompt: Users report failing checkouts. Average processor use across the fleet is 40%. What do you check next?
hints: Think of the four golden signals.
Choose the measurement that users would notice.

acceptedIdeas: Checkout's error rate and p99 latency, which show what users feel
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Checkout's error rate and p99 latency, which show what users feel

choices.label: Nothing is wrong, because average processor use is low
Restart the servers until processor use rises
Add servers, because failures mean that the fleet is too small for the load
Checkout's error rate and p99 latency, which show what users feel

questions.onCorrect: Latency, traffic, errors and saturation say how users are doing, and a figure such as the average processor use does not.

misconceptions.feedback: Average processor use says little about how users are doing. Errors and latency can be bad while it is low.
Restarting changes the processor figure and says nothing about what users see, and it can drop requests.
More servers help if saturation is the cause, but nothing in the figures says so. Check the signals first.

questions.prompt: Halfway through a 30-day window, a service has spent 90% of its error budget. What should the team do?
hints: Ask how fast the budget is being spent compared with an even pace.
The budget exists to decide how much risk the team can take.

acceptedIdeas: Slow down risky releases and spend effort on reliability until the budget recovers
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Slow down risky releases and spend effort on reliability until the budget recovers

choices.label: Carry on releasing as before, since the SLO is only a goal and not a hard limit on anything
Lower the target to 99%, so that the budget is bigger
Slow down risky releases and spend effort on reliability until the budget recovers

questions.onCorrect: At 90% spent by the halfway point the burn rate is 1.8, nearly twice the even pace, so risk has to come down until the budget recovers.

misconceptions.feedback: The budget is the failure the target allows. At 90% spent, the next incident or release could break the objective.
Changing the target to cover a miss makes the number meaningless. The budget is a decision made in advance.

questions.prompt: Why is the monthly total divided by the seconds in the month rather than by the days?
hints: Think about the unit in which a server's capacity is given.
The result is later compared with the 2,000 redirects per second that one server handles.

acceptedIdeas: Server capacity is quoted per second, so the load has to be a rate per second too.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Server capacity is quoted per second, so the load has to be a rate per second too.

questions.onCorrect: A load in writes per second can be compared directly with what one server handles each second.

choices.label: Months differ in length, and a count of seconds is exact where a count of days is not.
Dividing by the larger number gives a lower load, and a lower load is the safer estimate.
Server capacity is quoted per second, so the load has to be a rate per second too.

misconceptions.feedback: The estimate already treats every month as 30 days, so it is not exact either way. Exactness is not what the division is for.
A lower load is not a safer one: an estimate that is too low leaves the fleet too small.

questions.prompt: A shortener receives 60 million new URLs a month, with 150 reads for each write. Use a 30-day month of 2,592,000 seconds and a peak factor of 3. Servers handle 2,000 redirects per second each and are planned at 70% utilisation at peak. How many servers do you need?
hints: Turn the monthly writes into a rate, then use the ratio and the peak factor.
Each server should carry 70% of 2,000 redirects per second.
Divide the peak load by what one server should carry, and round up.
questions.onCorrect: Eight servers carry the peak of about 10,400 redirects per second at 65% each, whereas seven would run at 74%, above the 70% plan.

misconceptions.feedback: That rounds 7.4 down. Seven servers would each run at about 74%, over the 70% plan.
That is the peak load in redirects per second. The question asks for the number of servers.
That is the average read rate. The fleet has to be sized for the peak.

questions.prompt: A customer finds that by changing the last character of her short link she can open other people's links. Which code scheme allows that, and what does fixing it cost?
hints: Changing the last character reaches a neighbour, which means the codes run in sequence.
Ask what a scheme that hides the order has to check.

acceptedIdeas: A base-62 counter, whose codes run in order; random codes hide it but need a collision check
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A base-62 counter, whose codes run in order; random codes hide it but need a collision check

choices.label: A base-62 counter, whose codes run in order; random codes hide it but need a collision check
Random codes, which can be guessed in order, whereas a counter would need no collision check at all
Any scheme, since a short code can always be guessed

questions.onCorrect: A counter gives each URL the next unused code with no collisions and a guessable order, and random codes trade that for a collision check.

misconceptions.feedback: It is the other way round. Random codes hide the order, and the counter's codes follow one another.
Random codes give no order to follow, so a guess lands on a used code only as often as the share of the space in use.

questions.prompt: A service sometimes changes the long URL that a short link points to, and wants every browser to ask it again on each visit. Which redirect status should it send?
hints: One redirect code may be cached by browsers and one is normally not cached.
A browser that remembers the redirect never asks the service again.
questions.onCorrect: A 302 is not normally cached, so every visit reaches the service and sees the current destination.

misconceptions.feedback: A 200 returns a page and does not redirect the visitor to the long URL.
A 301 may be cached by browsers, so a browser could keep sending visitors to the old URL without asking the service.
A 404 reports that the link does not exist.

questions.prompt: The email provider has stopped answering, and calls have no timeout. After how many seconds are all threads in use?
hints: Count the threads, then the rate at which they are lost.
There are 600 threads, and 50 are lost each second.
Divide the threads by the rate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are 20 × 30 = 600 threads, and 500 × 0.1 = 50 are lost each second, so they are gone after 600 ÷ 50 = 12 seconds.

questions.onCorrect: A bigger pool buys only seconds, because the loss continues at the same rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the number of threads. Divide it by the rate at which they are lost.
That divides the threads by 500, the whole request rate. Only 10% of requests hang.
That is the number of threads per server. The whole pool is 600 threads.

questions.prompt: A feed uses fan-out on write for every account. An account with 5,000,000 followers posts once, and the fan-out runs at 50,000 writes per second, which takes 100 seconds. What happens to the posts of ordinary accounts in the meantime?
hints: The fan-out work goes through one queue.
Ask what is ahead of an ordinary post in that queue.

acceptedIdeas: They wait behind the celebrity's fan-out work in the same queue
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They wait behind the celebrity's fan-out work in the same queue

choices.label: They are unaffected, because each post is fanned out on its own
They wait behind the celebrity's fan-out work in the same queue
They are lost, because the queue drops work it cannot finish

questions.onCorrect: The usual answer is a hybrid: ordinary accounts fan out on write, and very large accounts are fetched at read time.

misconceptions.feedback: The fan-out work shares one queue, so ordinary posts wait behind the 5,000,000 writes ahead of them.
Nothing in the design drops work. The posts wait, and a hybrid keeps them from waiting by not fanning out the very large accounts at all.

questions.prompt: A search service sends each query to 20 shards and waits for every answer, with no timeout. One shard becomes very slow. What is the main risk?
hints: Think about what a waiting call holds.
Each call that waits keeps a thread busy.

acceptedIdeas: Waiting queries hold threads until none are left for new queries
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Waiting queries hold threads until none are left for new queries

questions.onCorrect: Without a timeout, calls to a stalled shard hold threads until none remain for any query.

choices.label: Waiting queries hold threads until none are left for new queries
The other 19 shards slow down until they match the slow one shard
The data held by the slow shard is lost from the index
Queries return at once with that shard's results missing

misconceptions.feedback: The healthy shards still answer at their normal speed. It is the callers waiting on the slow shard that suffer.
A slow shard still holds its data. Slowness is not loss, and the risk here is the wait.
Without a timeout, nothing makes a query give up early, so it keeps waiting for the slow shard.

flashcards.front: What do you call the number of reads that arrive for every write?
flashcards.back: It is the read/write ratio, and it fixes one rate from the other.

acceptedIdeas: read/write ratio
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: read/write ratio

flashcards.front: A link shortener is opened about 100 times for every link created. Which way does its load lean?
flashcards.back: It is read-heavy, so keeping copies of answers close to the reader pays off.

acceptedIdeas: read-heavy
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: read-heavy

flashcards.front: In a sentence, why do you ask for the read/write ratio before choosing components?
flashcards.back: It shows whether the design should favour fast reads, with copies of answers, or fast writes.

flashcards.front: How many seconds are in a day?
flashcards.back: 24 × 60 × 60 = 86,400, close enough to 100,000 for an estimate.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 24 × 60 × 60 = 86,400, close enough to 100,000 for an estimate.

flashcards.front: What do you call the multiplier applied to the average load to find the load the design must meet?
flashcards.back: It is the peak factor, commonly assumed to be two to three.

acceptedIdeas: peak factor
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: peak factor

flashcards.front: In a sentence, why must you multiply bytes per second by 8 before comparing with a network link?
flashcards.back: Links are rated in bits per second, and each byte is 8 bits.

flashcards.front: In the nearest-rank method, which sorted position gives the p99 of 100 requests?
flashcards.back: The position is 0.99 × 100 = 99, so it is the 99th value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The position is 0.99 × 100 = 99, so it is the 99th value.

flashcards.front: Which law says that the average number in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time spent there?
flashcards.back: Little's law, L = λW.

acceptedIdeas: Little's law
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Little's law

flashcards.front: In a sentence, why can a request be slow far more often than each of the backends it waits for?
flashcards.back: It is slow if any one backend is slow, so the small chances of 100 backends combine into a large one.

flashcards.front: A fleet sizes out at 17.14 servers. Which direction do you round the count?
flashcards.back: You round up, because servers come whole and rounding down would run each above the planned utilisation.

acceptedIdeas: round up
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: round up

flashcards.front: What do you call the small requests a load balancer sends to each server to decide whether to keep sending it traffic?
flashcards.back: Each one is a health check, and a server that fails them is taken out of rotation.

acceptedIdeas: health check
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: health check

flashcards.front: In a sentence, why is a server at 90% utilisation fragile and not efficient?
flashcards.back: Its delay is already ten times the time to serve one request, and a small rise in load makes the delay climb steeply.

flashcards.front: What do you call the fraction of lookups that a cache answers?
flashcards.back: It is the hit rate, and the load on the backend follows its complement, the miss rate.

acceptedIdeas: hit rate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: hit rate

flashcards.front: What is the hit rate of a cache that has just restarted?
flashcards.back: It is zero, so the database must serve every request until the cache fills.

acceptedIdeas: zero
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: zero

flashcards.front: In a sentence, why must the database stay the source of truth when a cache sits beside it?
flashcards.back: Cache entries are copies that can expire, be evicted or be lost on restart, so the database is the only place guaranteed to hold the latest value.

flashcards.front: What do you call a sorted structure such as a B-tree that finds rows without scanning the table?
flashcards.back: It is an index, and it costs extra space and extra work on every write.

acceptedIdeas: index
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: index

flashcards.front: Roughly how many extra levels does a hundredfold increase in rows add to a B-tree with a fan-out of 100?
flashcards.back: One level, because a hundred times as many keys needs one more factor of 100.

acceptedIdeas: one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: one

flashcards.front: In a sentence, why can a query that is fast on 1,000 rows be slow on 100 million?
flashcards.back: Without an index it reads every page, and that work grows in step with the table.

flashcards.front: What is the term for the gap between a write on the leader and its application on a follower?
flashcards.back: It is replication lag, and a read from a follower within that gap can return older data.

acceptedIdeas: replication lag
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: replication lag

flashcards.front: About what percentage of keys move when a fourth node joins a three-node ring?
flashcards.back: The new node takes about 1/4 of the keys, which is 25%.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The new node takes about 1/4 of the keys, which is 25%.

flashcards.front: In a sentence, why does adding followers not make writes faster?
flashcards.back: Every write still goes through the single leader and is then repeated on each follower.

flashcards.front: What name is given to the agreement of nodes on a value despite failures?
flashcards.back: It is consensus, and it needs a majority of the nodes to proceed.

acceptedIdeas: consensus
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: consensus

flashcards.front: N = 3, W = 2. What is the smallest R that guarantees a read sees the latest write?
In a sentence, what does CAP say a system must choose between during a partition?
flashcards.back: It must either answer every request, with possibly stale data, or refuse some requests to stay consistent.

flashcards.front: What is the name for a queue where messages that repeatedly fail are set aside for inspection?
flashcards.back: It is a dead-letter queue, and it stops one poison message from blocking the rest.

acceptedIdeas: dead-letter queue
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: dead-letter queue

flashcards.front: By what quantity does a queue's backlog change each second?
flashcards.back: The backlog changes by the arrival rate minus processing rate: when arrivals exceed what the consumers process, it grows.

acceptedIdeas: arrival rate minus processing rate
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: arrival rate minus processing rate
acceptedAlternatives: the difference between the arrival rate and the processing rate

flashcards.front: In a sentence, why does an unbounded queue only postpone failure?
flashcards.back: If arrivals stay above capacity the backlog and the wait grow without limit, so the queue only delays the moment the slowness shows.

flashcards.front: What name is given to waiting longer after each failure, for example 100, 200, 400 ms?
flashcards.back: It is exponential backoff, and jitter adds a random offset so clients do not retry in step.

acceptedIdeas: exponential backoff
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: exponential backoff

flashcards.front: Three layers each make up to 3 attempts, and the bottom service always fails. How do the attempts combine across the layers on the way down?
flashcards.back: They multiply, so the bottom service receives 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 calls for one request.

acceptedIdeas: multiply
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: multiply

flashcards.front: In a sentence, why is a timeout of 30 seconds not a safe default?
flashcards.back: At a high request rate, calls that wait 30 seconds pile up in the thousands and exhaust the caller's threads or memory.

flashcards.front: What is the term for the set of things that fail together, such as a rack that shares a power feed?
flashcards.back: It is a failure domain, and replicas in the same one are not independent.

acceptedIdeas: failure domain
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: failure domain

flashcards.front: Components that must all work are in series. How does the chain's availability compare with that of its weakest component?
flashcards.back: It is less available, because the availabilities multiply and each factor is below 1.

acceptedIdeas: less
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: less

flashcards.front: In a sentence, why is a backup that has never been restored not a backup?
flashcards.back: Without a restore drill nobody knows that the files are usable or how long recovery takes.

flashcards.front: What is the amount of failure that an SLO allows over its window called?
flashcards.back: It is the error budget, for example 10,000 failed requests for 99.9% of 10,000,000.

acceptedIdeas: error budget
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: error budget

flashcards.front: What do you divide the failures so far by to get the burn rate?
flashcards.back: The failures so far are divided by the even pace, the failures an even pace would have spent by now.

acceptedIdeas: the even pace
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: the even pace
acceptedAlternatives: the failures at an even pace
the budget spent at an even pace

flashcards.front: In a sentence, why should an SLO not be 100%?
flashcards.back: It would leave no error budget, so no change could be made safely, and no real service can meet it.

flashcards.front: When codes are chosen at random, what does the chance of a collision equal?
flashcards.back: The chance that a random code is already taken equals the share of the space in use.

acceptedIdeas: the share of the space in use
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: the share of the space in use
acceptedAlternatives: share of the space already used
the fraction of the code space in use
share of the code space in use

flashcards.front: Which redirect status code is temporary and normally not cached, so that every visit reaches the service?
flashcards.back: It is 302, which lets the service count visits.

flashcards.front: In a sentence, why does the design have no queue and no shards?
flashcards.back: Neither is justified by a number: 38.6 writes per second is small, and the reads are served by a cache and replicas.

flashcards.front: What do you call a component with nothing to take over when it fails?
flashcards.back: It is a single point of failure, and the fix is a second copy in another failure domain.

acceptedIdeas: single point of failure
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: single point of failure

flashcards.front: Fan-out on write copies each post into every follower's feed. Which accounts make that too slow?
flashcards.back: An account with millions of followers breaks it, because one post causes millions of feed writes.

acceptedIdeas: millions
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: millions

flashcards.front: Recall one question that finds single points of failure when reviewing a design.
flashcards.back: What happens if this component fails, and is there another that can take over?
